item.title: Gary Anderson's verdict on McLaren's 2027-leaning upgrade
item.author: Gary Anderson
item.content:encoded: No team wants to show its dirty washing in public, so McLaren calling its new front wing effectively a 2027 concept seems strange.In that position, assuming the numbers on track and the simulation tools show it has potential, I’d be using it now and considering it very much a 2026 part. With (perhaps) four races remaining and roughly five months before the start of next season, I’d be learning as much as possible from it and would hopefully make a step or two as a result of it before next season kicks off.The intersection between the mainplane and the lower foot of the endplate, highlighted with the red ellipse, is what caught my eye. Red Bull started the season with this concept, and Mercedes and others have followed. Making it more of a single lower surface reduces the sensitivity of the endplate footplate to the track, so in high-speed corners the front of the car should produce more consistent downforce. Basically, it should feel less snatchy, making the rear of the car more stable.The slot gap profile between the forward and central elements, highlighted with the green arrow, has also been altered. This is in line with the profile change highlighted with the light blue arrow and the positioning of the longest chord section of the third element. With that section slightly more inboard, this will alter where the mass flow reaches the leading edge of the floor.What confuses me a little is the change from reducing the angle of the second and third elements in straight mode to reducing only the angle of the third when straight mode is activated. It means that the front wing is less powerful in corner mode, but that comes at the expense of overall downforce.When the wing is in cornering mode (max downforce), the low pressure on the lower surface will pull more of its airflow through the slot gap between the first and second elements. To compensate for this, McLaren has reduced the chord length of the mainplane, highlighted with the green arrow, and increased the chord length of the second element, highlighted with the light blue arrow.Mounting the wing on the second element, as highlighted with the red ellipse is sensible with this concept as it’s the best stiffness-to-weight compromise, but only if you don’t use the mid-flap as part of the straight-line mode wing angle reduction. So perhaps that, together with the fact that the car seems to be struggling with the balance between low- to medium-speed corners and high-speed corners, has led McLaren to this concept.There are also small additions to the rear wing trailing edge, highlighted with the green arrows. I can’t really see enough to tell if it’s a completely new package, but I’ve highlighted the small additions. These will improve the airflow on the wing’s underside, which is affected by the twin mounting pillars. A small airflow separation problem behind those mountings can very easily spread across a much wider section of the wing’s underside.McLaren has also declared a new diffuser and a re-profiled rear beam wing. This year the beam wing has a much shorter chord than in previous seasons, but it’s still very powerful when it comes to improving the performance of the diffuser. I don’t have the visual information to go into much detail on the diffuser. It’s basically the component that has a major influence on the overall performance of the car, so teams tend to keep these components well hidden."The upgrades, even though I had half and then half, and we’re going to put everything together for tomorrow, the upgrades seem to have given what we hoped for, I would say," was Lando Norris's early verdict on Friday."Ultimately, the upgrades are there to bring laptime and bring performance. They’re not set out just to improve handling. A perfect upgrade is one that brings laptime and at the same time brings a handling upgrade, especially with how tricky the car’s been. "I would say maybe there’s a small change in the right direction; it seems just a little bit more straightforward to drive. "But I don’t think we can ever judge things over just one track. But so far, for today, things have seemed a little bit more straightforward, which is a good thing." Let’s see how it all performs when it matters on Saturday and Sunday and if McLaren keeps all these components on the car as the weekend progresses.

Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and approval decisions on 117 more in September 2026, amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient details for regulation and monitoring. It is not alone in reconsidering datacentre projects. item.title: The PM’s small measures aim to help the public take back control – and we know how powerful that can be | Gaby Hinsliff
item.author: Gaby Hinsliff
item.content:encoded: E-bikes, noisy headphones, flytipping: Burnham is weighing in on areas that make a difference to how people feel about lifeImagine waking up one morning to find a humiliating video of you, filmed without your knowledge or control, plastered all over social media. Maybe you were sweating at the gym; or maybe at work, in a bar, or walking down the street, where you never realised the stranger hassling you for your number was covertly filming for his social media channel dedicated to shaming women who won’t date him.This week ministers hinted at a potential crackdown on so-called pervert glasses, wifi-enabled spectacles that let the wearer capture video of people around them, after multiple reports of men using them to harass women. (Though a small flashing light on the frame is meant to warn that the user is filming, it’s easily missed and worryingly easily disabled.) If so, it would be a small win, admittedly, in the context of what feels like an endless losing battle against big tech. But it would give young women back some small sense of control in life, and that matters perhaps more than we think.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistContinue reading...

item.title: Freezer meltdowns and airline hoaxes are a taste of things to come. Hoping for the best is no longer an option | Elisabeth Braw
item.author: Elisabeth Braw
item.content:encoded: Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilientIt was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up, many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarterand more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable.Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. When Transport for London suffered a devastating hack two years ago, the culprits turned out to be two British teenagers. Governments regularly warn retailers and other companies about cyber-attacks and even provide cyber-defence training to businesses. The lessons of costly ransomware and cyber-attacks also mean many big organisations and retailers have become much better at keeping their payments and logistics systems safe.Continue reading...

item.title: What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?
item.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya, Turkey
item.content:encoded: Its key temperature goal has been missed but experts say the agreement is still proving a vital moral compass for progressIt was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.”Continue reading...

item.title: Yankees news: Cody Bellinger wins Platinum Glove honors
item.author: Kento Mizuno
item.content:encoded: SABR: The Yankees’ Cody Bellinger was already awarded his second career Gold Glove for his excellent work in left field in 2026, but now he’s taken home an even higher honor. Since 2011, Rawlings has also given out one Platinum Glove per league each year to honor the best of the best. Until last night, 2022 catcher Jose Trevino was the only Yankees player to take home the award. Now, they have two, as Bellinger was named the AL’s best defender, joining the truly outstanding Pete Crow-Armstrong, the NL winner and likely MVP. Congrats to Cody!MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: Elite pitching, lackluster bats; such was the story of the 2026 Yankees. If the 2027 squad is to progress further into the postseason, offensive upgrades are a must. Here, Hoch examines a number of positions where the Bombers should seek more thump. To my eyes, the position that is most in need is also the spot with the most intriguing option – third base, where Ryan McMahon stunk it up this past year, and where NPB slugger Teruaki Sato is seeking to make a splash in free agency. It’s been a hot minute since the Yankees acquired NPB talent, so I’m not sure how seriously the Yankees will participate in the Sato sweepstakes (especially if they’re unsure about his glovework at the hot corner), but a blogger can hope.FanGraphs | Eric Longenhagen: If you want more info on Teruaki Sato, Eric Longenhagen has you covered. The FanGraphs lead prospect analyst covered Sato as part of his overview on notable players from the NPB and KBO, had this to say about the 2026 Central League Triple Crown winner – “Though Sato isn’t a five-tool superstar – he’s going to strike out a lot and play below-average defense – he should hit for enough power to be a productive, heart-of-the-order power hitter with 25-30 home runs.”Another potential upgrade for the Yankees, albeit at second base, is Shugo Maki of the Yokohama BayStars, who expressed his desire to play stateside last offseason, though he hasn’t been officially posted yet. Says Longenhagen: “Maki projects as an everyday second baseman in the Brandon Lowe mold, and you could make a pretty good argument that his hit-tool stability (Maki has a single-digit miss rate against fastballs compared to Sato’s whopping 32 percent) makes him a superior “prospect” when compared to Sato.”NJ.com | Bob Klapisch: With yet another postseason run cut short, Yankees fans are understandably frustrated with Brian Cashman. However, former Athletics GM Billy Beane of “Moneyball” fame considers Cashman to be “one of the best that’s ever done this job. Period.” While your mileage may vary on Cashman’s maneuvering in recent years, one must acknowledge that his overall body of work remains very impressive. If you’re up in arms about Hal Steinbrenner handing Cashman another extension, maybe Beane’s words can offer you some reassurance. Or not. Lastly, in case you missed Madison’s column, the Yankees are down a key member of the 2026 coaching staff. Tanner Swanson has gained a reputation since being hired away from the Twins in 2020 as one of the best catching instructors in baseball. As noted above Trevino became a Platinum Glove winner under his watch, and most impressively, he’s helped transform Austin Wells from a guy who might not stick behind the plate into a legitimately great defensive catcher who was a Gold Glove finalist himself in 2026. But his contract was up, and he’ll be heading to the Pacific Northwest because new Mariners skipper Jason Kanzler offered the Seattle native a job as his bench coach. Best of luck to him — and to the Yankees on finding his replacement.

item.title: Herta finally clears his last F1 superlicence hurdle
item.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
item.content:encoded: Colton Herta has cleared the final hurdles to qualifying for a Formula 1 superlicence with his penalty-free and productive Friday practice outing for Cadillac at the Brazilian Grand Prix.Herta replaced Sergio Perez in FP1 at Interlagos, where he and Cadillac were seeking to seal the final point needed for Herta to be eligible for a superlicence.He is a contender to race for the team next season but even if 2027 comes too soon getting a superlicence now would also make it much easier for Herta to remain an option in the years that follow, too.A driver needs to accrue 40 superlicence points when applying for the first time. Cadillac thought this had already been achieved after his Mexico FP1 appearance a week ago, but Herta was still one short after a mix-up over a previous IndyCar result.He was immediately back in the car for Brazil to seal the deal, though, so long as he completed 100km and did not get any penalty points on his licence in the session.Herta could have been tripped up on either count. The red flag that emerged early in FP1 could have shortened running significantly enough that he did not do enough laps for it to count – and it also caused a brief scare when Herta went past the pit entry after the session had been red-flagged.No action was taken as it was clear the red light panels came on too late for him to react and get into the pitlane.Cadillac’s Marc Hynes said on Friday evening that the team wanted to be absolutely clear whether the 100km limit comes from total mileage or only mileage from timed laps, but either way Herta would be safe.The Race understands the FIA is satisfied with what he did in FP1 so the superlicence point will be earned and his eligibility will be confirmed in due course.Herta ran a full programme in FP1 with early laps on hard tyres hampered by some lock-ups before a switch to softs, which yielded a best lap 0.904s slower than Valtteri Bottas over one lap and 0.275s slower than the target Cadillac set him.Herta was due to speak to media at the end of the day but withdrew from those activities as Cadillac said he was feeling unwell.When Hynes spoke, though, he said Herta was making good progress with his F1 work dovetailed alongside a disappointing Formula 2 campaign in which he is only 19th in the standings."It was a huge step to come to Europe chasing the F1 dream, and I hugely admire that," Hynes said."F2 is difficult. You’ve got the guys that have come through in the same peer set from karting, they know all the tracks – you get very little mileage in F2 practice, they know the tyre very well, and the driving style is baked in. So to come into that is tough."FP1 is a good opportunity to get some mileage, and he’s got better every time. The nerves aren’t there that you have for the first one, and he’s really looking assured out there now."

item.title: The Guardian view on the AI backlash: American voters want a say in their future | Editorial
item.author: Editorial
item.content:encoded: Tech stocks have lost trillions while voters have rejected the industry’s political champions. The billionaire-led boom is facing a democratic reckoningThis week’s midterms showed that the political bill for the AI boom is falling due. The Democratic sweep intensified fears over runaway spending, mounting debt and resistance to datacentres, sending tech shares tumbling. On Thursday Wall Street suffered its worst day since the pandemic as $3.2tn was wiped from markets. Anthropic, developer of the Claude chatbot, is hoping to float within the next fortnight for $1.5tn (£1.1tn), but it may not now get even a trillion dollars. The dominant AI chipmaker Nvidia saw its value crash by more than $400bn. The world’s richest man, Elon Musk, lost $113bn in two days.While a few very rich people may be a little less wealthy, the sell-off may not be a bad thing. It brings a needed dose of reality to an industry whose spending plans and valuations depend on heroic expectations of future profits. That is a view held by many influential figures – from Goldman Sachs’ research boss to Nobel laureate Daron Acemoğlu. AI may transform the economy. That does not guarantee investors will earn back the sums being poured into it.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? item.title: Winners & losers from F1 2026 Brazilian GP Friday practice
item.author: Ben Anderson
item.content:encoded: A familiar name at the top of the timesheet, but not your run of the mill F1 Friday at the Brazilian Grand Prix, as one struggling frontrunner got back in the groove again while the usual kings of Friday practice produced their worst result of the season.Here are our winners and losers from the first day of F1 track action at Interlagos.Loser: Ferrari (6th & 7th)Charles Leclerc and Ferrari had been fastest in Friday practice at three of the past four races, going back to October’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and a 6-7 FP2 result in Brazil (with Leclerc behind Lewis Hamilton) was the first time all season Ferrari has finished Friday outside the top five on the timesheet.Leclerc called it a “very, very difficult Friday” and described the feeling inside the car as “strange” and “very poor”.“We were losing in the straights, but I think the car in the corners just felt probably one of the worst Friday feelings of the season," he added.“So I think there's a lot to be found in corners, more than in the straights, where we know we have a deficit. Normally we are very fast in corners and today was not the case.”Team boss Fred Vasseur joked this was a Friday when Ferrari “have 200 kilos” of fuel inside the cars in order to flip the script, such is their usually prodigious form in free practice, but in a serious moment then admitted Ferrari has “a lot of work to do on the balance”.“The drivers, they were not happy,” he confirmed, while also saying he was “not less optimistic than last week” when Leclerc topped Friday in Mexico.“We had a couple of times a deployment issue in the lap,” Vasseur added. “We have to fine-tune everything.“On his fastest lap, he [Leclerc] lost a couple of tenths in a straight line. I would say that it’s not a drama. It’s more for you [the media] to be focused on page one [of the timing screen], but we are not.“We know that we have a lot to do on the balance. The balance was not good. The tarmac is the opposite of one week ago. It’s creating a lot of work to do and a difference compared to last week.” - Winner: McLaren (2nd & 5th)Fastest in FP1 and looking competitive on longer runs - McLaren's upgrade package for Brazil appears to be working well, with the usual caveat that Fridays don't always offer perfect insight into the order.Senior racing director Randy Singh said it's "very likely" the upgrades - led by a new front wing - will stay on the car, and Friday went "really well" for the team, while Lando Norris cautioned that the team still looks two-tenths off Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes but "pretty good" compared to the other teams.Norris also felt gently encouraged that McLaren's new 2027-ethos front wing had begun to address the long-standing edginess of the car's balance."I would say maybe there’s a small change in the right direction, that it seems just a little bit more straightforward to drive," he said."I don’t think we can ever judge things over just one track. But so far, for today, things have seemed a little bit more straightforward."After missing FP1, Singh says Oscar Piastri was also "immediately on the pace" - something which hasn't always happened this year - but the usual rule from recent races applies: the team needs to optimise qualifying, where its knife-edge car has let its long-run pace down all too often. - Winner: Gabriele Mini (7th in FP1)Every now and then, a lesser-known Friday driver pops up high on the timesheets in an FP1 outing, which is exactly what Gabriele Mini did on his second appearance for Alpine by setting the seventh-fastest time to head the midfield pack. "Gabby did a very good job to be a little bit quicker than his team-mate," said Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen. "[It's the] second weekend in a row for him and he looks like a seasoned campaigner already. He literally didn't put a foot wrong, which is really good."The 21-year-old Italian, when he wasn't reading from the standard FP1 driver script about focusing on doing a good job for the team, showed that he wasn't keen to rest on his laurels after making a positive impression and admitted to areas where he knew his lap, quick as it was, could have been better. "There were a few things that, let’s say, didn’t allow me to make the best lap," said Mini when asked by The Race to break down his lap. "The lap of your life, it’s really hard to get in an FP1, but where I had some margin was in corners like Turn 1, because there was never a clear run before the actual push, so I never really had an idea, so I took a bit of margin there, which I know I have. "And then some other corners, a bit in the braking points, some slides that I got that could have been better. It’s hard to really say how much time. I don’t [say] one second, but for sure a few tenths are easy. "Something that we could have done better with the switches as well, so not only my side. But that’s something that, as I said, you get in FP1 to then improve in FP2, both driver- and engineer-wise. So it’s normal to have those kinds of things, I’d say."Mini, who was a star name in his karting career and has since won the 2020 Italian F4 title and races at every level up to and including F2, has shown that not only is he quick but also determined to improve. And those are two key prerequisites of a potential F1 race driver. - Loser: Anyone hoping Kimi Antonelli would switch off...For anyone unfamiliar with old English idioms, something ‘after the Lord Mayor’s Show’ is a classic expression to describe something mundane, or disappointment following something much grander – like, for instance, a bog-standard F1 Friday for Kimi Antonelli five days after winning the world championship!But anyone hoping Antonelli would be switching off with some kind of post-title hangover will be sorely disappointed by how he breezed through practice at Interlagos with all his rivals at arm’s length."It’s the next Lord Mayor’s show for him, not the after," said Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord."There’s two big things. We’ve got our constructors’ championship to win and a job to complete, and both drivers are really determined to do that, to translate and recognise the effort of everyone back in Brixworth and in Brackley."And then this is the start of 2027 for Kimi, and he’s determined to finish the season on a high, but take that momentum through into the winter."There is no hint of complacency, change in mindset, or relaxing off the gas for the new world champion. Without him, Mercedes would have looked right in the mix against McLaren and Red Bull, but nothing more. With Antonelli it heads into Saturday as the pole favourite - if the weather doesn’t change, of course. - Winner: Colton Herta (20th in FP1)It looks like Colton Herta has really, genuinely, finally done it – he qualifies for an F1 superlicence, in one of the most unnecessary and dragged-out driver eligibility storylines of all time.Herta needed to rack up 100km in FP1, and avoid any licence penalty points, to get the one bonus superlicence point required to finally hit the threshold he and Cadillac thought he’d reached a week ago in Mexico.That basically meant 23 laps of Interlagos. Herta’s credited with 31, which is well past the kilometre threshold – although, as Cadillac’s Marc Hynes mentioned, there’s a tiny degree of doubt whether you count only timed laps or just what’s logged in the session.By our count, Herta managed 23 timed laps that were not inlaps or outlaps, so we reckoned he should be safe. Hynes said 24 was the “sweet spot”, but this just means being absolutely 100% sure either way. And Herta avoided any sanction in-session that would deny him the bonus superlicence, after a near-miss not coming into the pits when the session was red flagged because he was too close to the pit entry to react when the panels lit up. Phew!The FIA subsequently confirmed that Herta’s now all good, so this is now something that everybody, especially him, can stop worrying about... - Winner: Gabriel Bortoleto’s Audi (8th)The one Audi that held together all day was rapid, leading the midfield by a couple of tenths and picking off Isack Hadjar’s underperforming Red Bull for good measure.“The track was quite grippy today, FP2 especially, so quite in a happy place,” reported Gabriel Bortoleto. “I think the car was behaving well, I was driving well today.”The key of course will be building on that encouraging start through Saturday, when conditions could change, and ensuring the car holds together well enough to avoid another scoring opportunity slipping through Audi’s fingers.“Honestly, my car has been working OK this weekend, and hopefully it can keep up like this,” Bortoleto added, “and hopefully they fix also Nico's car, because we had a good performance this weekend, I'm sure he can come strong as well.” - Loser: Nico Hulkenberg's Audi...There was a bad case of deja vu for Audi where one side of the garage was again beset by reliability trouble.In Mexico, Bortoleto logged no laps in FP1. In Brazil, it was Nico Hulkenberg’s turn – except he went one ‘better’, completing zero laps at all, all day.That’s because FP1 stand-in Freddie Slater took over Hulkenberg’s car in the opening session, but ground to a halt with what eventually turned out to be a gearbox problem.Not only did this ruin Slater’s outing one week after his Mexico FP1 debut was slightly limited by a different problem, it was so complicated to trace that by the time Audi had a handle on the issue it was too late to get everything ready for Hulkenberg to drive in FP2.Racing director Allan McNish couldn’t hide his frustration. The only silver lining was the seven laps Slater did, he enjoyed, and the team was impressed by, as the 18-year-old has made a good impact with his approach off-track and the quality of the work he’s started to do on it. - Winner: Haas (10th & 16th)Ollie Bearman was within two tenths of the lead of the midfield in practice two on Friday, a welcome distraction from Haas's dramatic off-track headline-making with Rafael Camara replacing Esteban Ocon this weekend.The usual practice caveats apply but 10th is a very handy place for Haas to end its day, although its lack of pace on the hard tyre and the reprimand Camara received for badly impeding Leclerc means this entry has its drawbacks.But quick on the softs, and with Camara doing "brilliantly" on his first day in the car, there's a silver lining to what was always going to be a tough weekend amid the current turmoil at this team. -

item.title: Doctors pull knife from man's eye that went through his brain—and he's fine now
item.author: Beth Mole
item.content:encoded: A man in his 20s showed up to a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife sticking out of his face. The 15 mm-wide blade hidden within went completely through his right eye and through his brain, with the tip of the blade hitting the top of his skull.Despite the ghastly injury, the man was alive and conscious when he arrived. He could still talk and move all four limbs. His doctors described him as being in a state of agitation. On the Glasgow Coma Scale, he scored a 12 (E3 V4 M5), indicating a "moderate" brain injury, just one point above "mild." He could open his left eye when told, but otherwise kept it closed (E3 score); he could talk and answer questions, but was confused (V4); and he intentionally moved away when pressure was applied to his body (M5).In a report published Friday in BMJ Case Report, his doctors said they were concerned that in his confused, agitated state he may try to pull the knife out on his own. So, they swiftly sedated and intubated him. They put him on prophylactic treatments for bacterial infections, including tetanus. Then they used images to see what was going on in his head.

The Elon Musk-owned company has already deployed thousands of direct-to-cell satellites, but its next big challenge is building out its 5G network here on Earth.SpaceX’s big plans have garnered some reactions in the telecom industry. Tim Höttges, the CEO of T-Mobile’s parent company Deutsche Telekom, said he takes SpaceX’s plans “super serious” but that it could cost Musk more than $200 billion to pull off.Follow along for the latest updates on Starlink’s major mobile carrier ambitions.

item.title: Ships loiter near subsea cables amid Iran's warnings to Trump
item.author: Jeremy Hsu
item.content:encoded: Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes.The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October, according to the Financial Times. Six active cables currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region.Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region's undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: ‘Dangerous’ but also ‘brilliant’ - Rafael Camara’s F1 debut
item.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
item.content:encoded: New Haas driver Rafa Camara received a reprimand on his Formula 1 debut for what was deemed “clearly dangerous” impeding of Charles Leclerc in Brazilian Grand Prix practice.Camara weaved and moved into the racing line as he prepared to start a push lap in FP2 at Interlagos just as Leclerc was coming by to complete a lap of his own.Though he was warned several times that Leclerc was approaching, Camara ended up squeezing the Ferrari towards the run-off at high speed “with a significantamount of the car off the track”, said the stewards, who upgraded the typical practice penalty for impeding from a warning to a formal reprimand.“The situation that was created was clearly dangerous and [Camara] should have taken more care to avoid impeding [Leclerc]."Camara’s incident with Leclerc was a blot on an otherwise solid and steadily improving first day in the car.He finished 0.86s slower than Ollie Bearman in FP1, and trimmed the gap to 0.57s in FP2, with the biggest part of his time lost in the middle sector - although he had been even closer on the initial hard-tyre push laps before switching to softs.There was a recurring problem under braking into Turn 1, where Camara had huge run-ending lock-ups in both FP1 and FP2, although several drivers had trouble here.And he was still trying to smoothen his throttle usage exiting Turns 2 and 12 by the end of Friday as well.But considering Camara has been thrown in at the deep end with a lot of procedural stuff to learn as well as getting on top of a 2026 car he is driving for the first time, Haas felt he had a “pretty strong day”, head of car engineering Hoagy Nidd said.“Obviously a massive learning curve today, it's pretty intimidating, but he did brilliantly,” said Nidd.“He built up steadily through FP1. He was sort of almost a bit reticent to give too much feedback from FP1 and obviously for FP2 he was improving all the time and building with his feedback and his driving, so a pretty strong day I would say.“Working on procedures, you probably saw us go out, do a few starts, things like that, just the normal bread and butter things that we almost take for granted with most drivers, so we're very pleased with him I think.”

item.title: Mariners hire Tanner Swanson away from Yankees
item.author: Madison Pavich
item.content:encoded: For the second time this week, the Yankees have lost a significant member of their coaching staff. Tanner Swanson, the organization’s director of catching since 2020, has been hired by the Seattle Mariners to join new manager Jason Kanzler as their bench coach according to the Joel Sherman. This comes on the heels of Triple-A manager Shelley Duncan defecting over to the Red Sox on Wednesday to join their staff, and now despite not making any firings of their own on the coaching staff the Yankees will have some holes to fill.Swanson was revolutionary in the organization for developing the team’s ability to frame pitches. Austin Wells has become the model for his work, becoming one of the best pitch framers in the game, and his development lined up directly with Swanson’s arrival in New York. The Yankees have been providing catchers to several teams over the years though, as they traded from their surplus of catchers sending Carlos Narváez over to Boston for Elmer Rodriguez, flipping Jose Trevino to Cincinnati for Fernando Cruz, and including Kyle Higashioka in the package to San Diego that netted Juan Soto.The loss of Swanson is a big one for the Yankees to swallow, but they’ve hopefully learned enough from his time here to continue the catching pipeline that has netted them so much value. For Swanson, the chance to coach in the major leagues is an opportunity that he couldn’t pass up on, and he’ll now get to work with a premier catcher in Cal Raleigh coming off what was a disappointing follow-up to his MVP runner-up 2025.

item.title: Yankees Mailbag: An early look at outfield options
item.author: Madison Pavich
item.content:encoded: Good afternoon everyone, it’s time to dive back into the mailbag and answer some of your questions. Remember to send in your questions for our bi-weekly call by e-mail to pinstripealleyblog [at] gmail [dot] com. If the CBA negotiations go really sideways is there a possibility we see replacement player games next year?Never say never, but I doubt the owners would want to go this route even if it’s looking like the season is completely lost. Recruiting scab players at this point in the league’s history would be a black eye on ownership and would completely kill any goodwill they could have with the public as these negotiations drag on, as the product on the field will be a clearly inferior copy that wouldn’t draw much interest while also making them look desperate to recoup on the broadcast deals they’ve negotiated. Speaking of those broadcasting rights, while the league is a much more regional product than the NFL or NBA and several teams were having trouble finding an actual partner for their TV audience, it’s my hope that the prospect of future negotiations with broadcasters is one of the pressure points pushing ownership to get to the table sooner rather than later resulting in an actual season being played out in 2027 — perhaps a bit too hopeful, considering the lines in the sand that have been drawn this time around, but a girl can dream.LocalBlueWhaleRuinsEverything asks:With the Yankees needing some offense, could they consider Arozarena or Suzuki? Theoretically, they could stick one in LF and have Cody move to CF. It’s not something I’d want them to do long term, but for one season I’d be interested. Stanton and Garcia should be gone after next season, so in the future you’d a spare DH spot to rotate them.Theoretically they could, but that takes a lot of the value that Bellinger provides away by moving his excellent left field defense over to center field, where he has been underwhelming at best since 2021. Arozarena and Suzuki are both quality offensive options that would improve the lineup tremendously, but the defensive setback that adding either would cause problems down the line. That being said, the free agent market for true center fielders is abysmal, so if they’re looking for an upgrade they’re going to have to get creative with trades to find it.It seems JD was overhyped for years by Cash. Does he have any real value?Jasson Domínguez’s career is looking like a relatively unremarkable one, which is what tends to happen to the majority of MLB players — but most players don’t get compared to Mickey Mantle when they were 17 years old. That unfair expectation has felt like a weight on Domínguez’s shoulders the entire time that he’s been in the organization, with every glimpse of a solid run down in the minors being heralded as the turning point where he was going to spark a path straight to the majors. However, Domínguez has now had two full seasons in proximity to the majors, and while he’s still very young entering his age-24 season in 2027 it just doesn’t seem like there’s much to work with in his game.Our own Andrés tackled the idea of whether the Yankees should move on from Domínguez the other day, and while his conclusion was that there’s no pressure to do so immediately time is running out for the former wonder prospect. He’s got one minor league option remaining meaning he’s likely to start the year in the minors, and while there’s some underlying promise in his peripherals the majority of his Savant page is disappointing. Domínguez’s defense has been atrocious to watch, and he’s alternated from being unable to hit lefties to being unable to hit righties. If there was just some consistency to his game he’d at least be able to stick around as a bench option in the majors, but as is he’s got to get consistent playing time to try and make something of himself and he isn’t going to find that in pinstripes at the moment.How reliable are Cole, Fried, and Rodón next year considering recent arm problems in the last 3 seasons and age? Any innings projections? Does Schlittler come back to earth in 2027?I don’t have many concerns about Max Fried at the moment — he’ll probably be good for one short-term IL stint but otherwise give the team 25-30 starts and has been lights out when he has been active. Likewise, while Gerrit Cole has missed significant time over the past couple of seasons the core issue has now been dealt with and he should be fully healthy entering 2027. It’s wild to think that we’re already seven years into the nine-year deal that Cole signed with the team, but there’s just two seasons left of his contract and if you told me back then that he’d have compiled three top five Cy Young finishes with one win up to this point, I’d be pretty content entering the final days of that deal. Carlos Rodón has salvaged his Yankees career quite well following his disastrous first year in pinstripes, but of the three his health still concerns me more going forward — not enough to panic, but enough to keep my eye on how he’s getting through each start even when he’s on. As for Cam Schlittler, the sky is the ceiling for the team’s newfound ace and while it would certainly be unrealistic to expect a 1.95 ERA as the standard going forward I think he’ll remain the team’s best pitcher next year as he comes into his own.

Both Chainalysis and publicsources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats.We regret to inform you...Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It's not clear why the company considered such information "non-sensitive."

item.title: Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity
item.author: Jacek Krywko
item.content:encoded: In the Grand Canyon, there is a line in the rock where time seems to have gone missing. Ancient crystalline rocks mark its bottom, while sandstones laid down as life started to diversify during the Cambrian explosion mark the top. “It’s called the Great Unconformity, and it’s a gap in the geologic record,” says Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, Australia. "This gap can be anywhere between 200 million years, which is not that impressive, to more than a billion years.”In a recent Nature study, Flament and his colleague Santosh Dhungana argue that this gap was carved with help from deep within the planet. According to their models, slow currents of hot rock in Earth's mantle pushed entire continents up for hundreds of millions of years, letting glaciers grind them down and then let them sink, allowing fresh sediments to bury the scar. The largest hole in the rock record might be a fingerprint of processes happening deep in the planet's interior.The oldest sediments resting on the Great Unconformity in North America are between 635 and 482 million years old. Geologists have traced it across most of North America and parts of northern Europe and northern China. “Something seems to have happened, in particular in North America,” Flament says.

item.title: Wolff backs MotoGP's handling of calendar dissent
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: Mercedes Formula 1 boss Toto Wolff has backed MotoGP's handling of its Qatar Grand Prix amid rider discontent, ahead of F1's own planned races in the region.While F1 has gathered at Interlagos for the Brazilian Grand Prix, MotoGP is competing at Qatar's Lusail circuit on the same weekend - with 16 of the 22 full-time riders (and two injury replacements) in action.This followed several secret and unofficial votes between the MotoGP riders, in which the majority had voted against holding a Qatar race due to fears of conflict escalation in the Middle East.In the end, though, only the Yamaha riders - those representing the factory team and the satellite team Pramac - are absent from the Qatar GP without replacement.Yamaha announced last Sunday that it "had not identified sufficient grounds to change its existing company-wide travel restrictions" to send its teams to Qatar, a decision that was met with "disappointment" and suggestion of "sporting consequences" from MotoGP. The series emphasised it did not "receive any information that would warrant a change to the current plans for the event" after consultation with Qatar, the track and "independent safety advisors".As for the riders present in Qatar, some have taken a more conciliatory stance over the handling of the event, but others have maintained a more confrontational tone.Notably, seven-time series champion Marc Marquez said in the pre-event press conference: "I would like to be in another place. For that reason I arrive on the latest flight possible, and I will leave on the earliest flight possible."F1 has two races scheduled in the region - November 29's Qatar GP, and December 6's Abu Dhabi GP.And when asked at Interlagos whether his understanding of the situation with those races was being informed with MotoGP racing at Qatar this weekend, Wolff offered an extensive answer that backed MotoGP's approach and questioned what the riders have shared publicly."Stefano [Domenicali, F1 boss] and Mohammed [Ben Sulayem, FIA president] have been pretty clear about the situation, that Formula 1 follows what the international guidelines are, whether there's travel restrictions, airlines not flying, any warnings in the region, the kind of feedback that local governments are making - so not only the promoters, but what the local governments are making. And this is what you need to rely on, in my opinion," Wolff said."And I'm fully with that. I think that if riders stand up, that geopolitically know nothing about what's going on but [they] have the audience that listens, I think that is something that creates media value [headlines] - but I would have done the same that MotoGP management has done."You want to ride, or drive, go. If you don't want to, don't go. As simple as that."And everybody can take their personal decisions on that, and I respect it. Of course, you've got to be wary of what's happening in the next few days, or few weeks."And Stefano has the finger on the pulse to monitor that. If things were to get more dangerous, then he's going to be the first one, together with Mohammed, to protect the people that were meant to travel. And so that's why I'm following the guidance of what I'm hearing."Internally it hasn't been raised, hasn't been a topic. But also there, if someone feels he or she doesn't feel comfortable in travelling, then it's something that I would always respect."And maybe that's an opportunity to give somebody else a chance."It wouldn't change anything for the relationship. I've always respected that, that some people didn't want to go to certain grands prix. And that's how I see it at the moment." Crunch time for F1 calendarWolff’s comments come ahead of a crunch week for Formula 1 when it comes to defining how the 2026 season will end.For a while now, Imola has been getting its venue ready as a fallback option in case the final Middle Eastern races cannot happen.However, it is now at the point where it needs to commit to the final major preparations or abandon its work because the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are happening.It is understood that F1 has set itself a deadline of next Tuesday (November 10) to make a final call on what to do with the Imola event.If by then it is satisfied that the Middle Eastern races are good to go, then Imola can be stood down.That call means, however, that if after that date tensions escalate in the Middle East and the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi have to be halted, then it means Imola will not be able to host any more – which means the season would finish in Las Vegas.While the situation in the Middle East remains unpredictable, F1 teams retain faith that no "risks" will be taken in the final call.Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack said that despite team personnel asking more questions about what was happening, there was confidence in F1’s senior management.Speaking on Thursday at Interlagos, Krack said: “Now, I discussed it at length with Andy [Stevenson, sporting director] this morning, and we think, we are really convinced, that F1 is not taking any unnecessary risk.“They are aware of the situation, they have much better information than we have. And I think if there is a serious risk, I think they will take the correct action.“I think at the moment they are still evaluating that situation, and I’m sure they have set themselves some deadlines, which we have not gone over yet. So, I think we need to give them the time to do that. But I would be really surprised if they take risks.”

item.title: What happened in F1 2026 Brazilian GP second practice
item.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
item.content:encoded: Kimi Antonelli showed no signs of becoming complacent after his recently-sealed 2026 Formula 1 title win as he completed his domination of Friday practice in Brazil.Antonelli topped FP2 with a comfortable 0.253s margin ahead of McLaren’s Lando Norris, who headed a gaggle of other cars.In fact, the gap the lead Mercedes had over a mixed-up cast of would-be contenders at Interlagos reflected how 2026 has tended to play out overall.Norris, Max Verstappen's Red Bull and George Russell's Mercedes were covered by just 0.020s, while Oscar Piastri was fifth in the second McLaren only half a tenth further back.Verstappen was once again displeased with some engine behaviour in this session - and his confusion over Red Bull’s slightly vague update on how it was "adapting" to him prompted an amusing radio exchange where Verstappen suggested he should start talking to the clutch directly.Less funny was the fact he ended the session early in the garage as a steering issue emerged that Red Bull could not quickly resolve.In performance terms, the outlier at the moment is Ferrari, which seems to be struggling on balance but also (as usual) with straightline speed.Lewis Hamilton led the team in sixth, nearly three tenths ahead of Charles Leclerc – who survived a high-speed near-miss when F1 debutant Rafa Camara’s Haas inadvertently squeezed him coming onto the start-finish straight.Camara, who ended his first day as an F1 driver 16th fastest and just over half a second slower than Haas team-mate Ollie Bearman, will be investigated after the session for the incident. He was preparing to start a lap when he squeezed Leclerc, who was finishing one, towards the run-off as they navigated the flat-out kink of Turn 15.Leclerc kept his foot in over the bumpy run-off and managed to finish the lap, losing a couple of tenths in the process, and expressed his irritation afterwards.These were Leclerc’s first laps of the weekend after Dino Beganovic drove his car in FP1. Early on Leclerc complained that the balance was too far to the rear, and at the end of the session he was asking about the engine.Towards the foot of the top 10, Gabriel Bortoleto was eighth in his Audi on home soil, just over a second off Antonelli but ahead of Isack Hadjar's Red Bull.Ollie Bearman's Haas completed the top 10 but there was just half a tenth covering him, Franco Colapinto's Alpine and the Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson.The only driver not to set a time was Nico Hulkenberg, who did not run at all after the issue that stopped Freddie Slater on track in FP1 could not be addressed by Audi in time, leaving Hulkenberg without a single lap in the car on Friday.For those who did drive, there was a recurring challenge for almost everybody: lock-ups into the first corner.At least half the field had a big moment under braking for the Senna S, struggling with the bumps as the track falls away, which could be a precursor to a defining performance differentiator come qualifying on Saturday.1 Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) 1m10.763s2 Lando Norris (McLaren) +0.253s3 Max Verstappen (Red Bull) +0.259s4 George Russell (Mercedes) +0.273s5 Oscar Piastri (McLaren) +0.321s6 Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) +0.450s7 Charles Leclerc (Ferrari) +0.720s8 Gabriel Bortoleto (Audi) +1.017s9 Isack Hadjar (Red Bull) +1.076s10 Ollie Bearman (Haas) +1.228s11 Franco Colapinto (Alpine) +1.233s12 Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls) +1.245s13 Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls) +1.279s14 Pierre Gasly (Alpine) +1.346s15 Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin) +1.775s16 Rafael Camara (Haas) +1.798s17 Carlos Sainz (Williams) +1.979s18 Lance Stroll (Aston Martin) +2.179s19 Alex Albon (Williams) +2.190s20 Sergio Perez (Cadillac) +2.553s21 Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac) +2.620s22 Nico Hulkenberg (Audi) no time

Nvidia hardware worth $11.4M vanished between Oakland and Texas
item.author: Nick Indge
item.content:encoded: A shipment of Nvidia hardware valued at $11.4 million vanished in transport between Oakland and Texas over the summer, and more than two months later, police have announced no arrests or recovery of the cargo.As reported by The Mercury News, six pallets of unknown Nvidia equipment left Oakland on August 29 on a truck bound for Fort Worth, Texas. The hardware was reportedly picked up as scheduled by a truck bearing the logo of a food transportation company before vanishing off the grid. The theft wasn't noticed until early September, when the buyers realized that the shipment had never been received. Police attempting to trace the truck's route found it had made several multi-hour stops after picking up the hardware before losing the truck somewhere in San Bernardino County, California.Oakland police confirmed that there was a grand theft report filed on September 13 and that the investigation remains ongoing. Authorities have not said what Nvidia hardware was stolen or exactly how the theft was carried out.

item.title: Shure’s popular podcasting and streaming mic is almost $50 off
item.author: Brad Bourque
item.content:encoded: While the is popular with streamers and podcasters, it’s equally good at impressing your friends and coworkers on meetings and Discord calls. It’s currently marked down to $255 at various retailers, including Amazon, Guitar Center, and directly from Shure. That’s almost $50 lower than its usual price, and just a few dollars off Amazon’s all-time low. If you don’t already have a stand, both Amazon and Shure are offering a bundle that includes the mic and a desktop stand for $269, and the white model is also discounted at Amazon. When our team shared some of our favorite audio gear in late 2024, we noted that the Mv7 Plus was the mic we send to podcast guests for remote interviews. It’s known for its crisp and clean audio quality, with auto-leveling and denoising, so you can use it without touching an equalizer.The MV7’s unique shape and sonic profile is inspired by the Shure SM7B (also discounted), a microphone that’s often used in professional recording. This version is meant as a more budget-friendly variant for content creators looking for a simpler setup, with both an XLR output and USB-C, letting you wire into an audio interface or directly to a computer.

item.title: What we learned about Ferrari's key Hamilton/Leclerc meeting
item.author: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded: Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur wasted little time following his arrival into Sao Paulo on Thursday night in getting his Formula 1 drivers together for their well-publicised Mexican Grand Prix postmortem.Fresh off his own arrival from Italy, and with Charles Leclerc having also flown in from Monaco where he had returned for the birth of his first child, the pair of them got together with Lewis Hamilton at their downtown hotel.Away from the prying eyes of journalists and photographs, the three of them ran through the events of that opening lap in Mexico, were Vasseur told them his views on events and then agreed a path going forward that it is hoped will avoid a repeat clash in the future.Speaking in the team principals' press conference on Friday, Vasseur adopting his usual tone of wanting to keep things "private" when he appeared in front of the media.His tone of answering throughout was very much of keeping details close to his chest for what he now considers a closed matter."It went well," he said about the meeting. "It was good to discuss, good to clarify my position and their position. It was good to do. Now we turn the page and we are focused on the next one."But while Vasseur was not expansive in terms of details from the meetings, there were still some clear hints about where the situation stands now after Mexico.The major one is that there has been no significant change of approach from Vasseur in terms of the capacity for both his drivers to race each other hard.Vasseur has long shied away from any desire to interfere in the on-track battles – which has sometimes been equally frustrating for one or both of his drivers.But Vasseur did state that the racing guidelines that his team operate to – even without formal rules of engagement – were unchanged."The guidelines are still the same," said Vasseur. "I think they accumulated perhaps a bit of frustration because they are starting each weekend side by side and you have a kind of accumulation of facts. But at the end of the day, the guidelines are always the same."Vasseur repeatedly referenced that key to the guidelines being followed was not letting personal interests overtake those of the team and that this "message was clear" for both Hamilton and Leclerc.Referencing this later he said: "They are working for the team and the team has to come first. In this situation, we failed collectively because we were 1-2 and we didn't win the race in the end. It's clear that we failed and we have to react."The conclusion of the meeting yesterday evening was clear. It was a clear reminder that Ferrari is coming first. It's coming first for the brand, for the employees, for the tifosi and this we have to keep in mind."Vasseur sat in the press conference alongside Mercedes boss Toto Wolff, who interrupted at one point to reference that what Ferrari was living through now felt like a repeat of the headaches he faced with Hamilton and Nico Rosberg during their title fight years of 2014 to 2016.Wolff suggested that difficult moments like Mexico for Ferrari were important in exposing weaknesses in the system, and, like the 2016 Spanish GP for Mercedes, often became a catalyst for allowing change to happen.He explained: "I think sometimes it needs the really tough ones, like the last one, to make a point."It was always when I was there with Nico and Lewis, when there was an accident, it was understood that that was now the limit and it wouldn't continue like this."That's why maybe it needed to escalate to the point, because it's a respect to the team and many, many thousand people, the brand, that work together and that's what they need to keep in their heads."But while Wolff was quite open during those years about how he was laying down the law with his drivers – which included him stating at one point that he would sack one of his drivers if they could not race each other cleanly - Vasseur’s approach is much more secretive."I'm not sure that Toto, 10 years ago, told you exactly the content of the discussion with Nico and Lewis and I will do exactly the same," said Vasseur, who perhaps had not recalled Wolff’s openness at the time."We had a discussion. It has to stay private, it's a matter of respect also for them and for the team. And once again the most important is the message."The message is that we are working for a brand, we are working for sponsors, we are working for, but I would say mainly also the employees of the team."Vasseur did not see any cause for alarm in how the relationship of his two drivers stands, but may have offered a hint that he was not impressed with how Hamilton had spoken strongly after Mexico.Asked about any concerns in Hamilton saying he would "not be silenced" based on what was said after Mexico, Vasseur said: "No, no – but this I was clear with Lewis and I will keep it between Lewis and me."Vasseur certainly countered Hamilton’s suggestion that Leclerc races the seven-time champion harder than any other drivers on the grid – citing his opening lap move on Max Verstappen in Austin as proof of him being super aggressive with other teams."If you have a look at what Charles did in Austin in the first section, everybody said that it was magic and the line is fine between the two," said Vasseur.However, he acknowledged that a rivalry between his drivers was to be expected and it was naïve to think the pair of them could battle like they did and be best buddies."I'm not asking them to be best friends," said Vasseur. "I think it would be even probably a bit negative. I'm just asking them to act and to work as professionals and this is it."Despite repeated questions over a topic that Vasseur would have loved not to have cropped up in the first place, he acknowledged that there were downsides to having two top line drivers battling each other in the same team.However, he felt that it would be hard to enjoy the benefits that come from having a pairing like Hamilton and Leclerc without expecting there to be any negatives."I think it’s probably the downside of the system is that we have two competitive guys starting each weekend next to each other," he explained."But I think if we are P2 [in the constructors’ championship] today, it’s also because we have two guys very, very close and we have to manage it. "But it’s a choice, it’s a choice in the line-up and I have the positive and the negative. I will deal with the negative."

item.title: Belgian champion leaves UAE Team Emirates-XRG for three-year deal with Movistar
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: This year, racing for UAE Team Emirates-XRG, the 28-year-old claimed the surprise national road race title from a large breakaway that escaped and foiled favourites like Jasper Philipsen on a mostly flat course around Antwerp in the absence of stars like Wout van Aert, Remco Evenepoel and defending champion Tim Wellens."I am really excited to join the team. From what I have seen so far, we are working in the right direction," Herregodts said in the press release. "I think the team is making a lot of progress in terms of performance and, for me, this is a good environment to show my quality, help the team and also have more opportunities in breakaways and Classics. I am really looking forward to next year and to having a great season together. I am convinced we will be successful."Herregodts will become the second Belgian racing for the Spanish WorldTour team, linking up with Cian Uijtdebroeks, who left Visma-Lease a Bike for Movistar after the 2025 season."I have spoken a little with Cian and also with the team to get to know the way they work," Herregodts added. "He was very enthusiastic, and that has strengthened my confidence that this is a good place to develop my career as a cyclist."After starting his elite career with the Flanders-Baloise team in 2021, with whom he won the Ronde van Drenthe and a stage of the Ruta del Sol, Herregodts joined the WorldTour with Intermarché in 2023, winning the ZLM Tour the next year.A strong breakaway rider and fast finisher from small groups, Herregodts' time with UAE Team Emirates was less fruitful, and the Belgian title was his singular victory for the team, albeit one of the biggest days of his career.Head of Sports Sebastián Unzué said, "Rune joins the team at a point of full maturity, with the experience and quality needed to contribute across different terrains. I am convinced that his arrival will bring great value to the group."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: FAA to finally ditch floppy disks in what it calls "historic" tech upgrade
item.author: Jon Brodkin
item.content:encoded: While you might be pondering whether to replace a smartphone with one that has a slightly better camera or a second screen, the Federal Aviation Administration is planning a much bigger leap in technology for the country's air traffic control system.The FAA said yesterday that it will stop using floppy disks as part of a long-awaited upgrade that will give air traffic controllers faster access to data needed for crucial safety alerts. The new Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) will be installed in 435 facilities, replacing several information display systems dating to the 1980s.The FAA "is continuing its historic modernization of America’s air traffic control system by replacing outdated floppy disks that contain vital weather and other critical information with a streamlined, 21st-century system," the agency said. E-IDS will be "deployed to operational control positions at more than 400 facilities across all air traffic control domains," and "provide operationally essential information for controlling aircraft," the FAA said.

item.title: Westchester Knicks 2026-27 Season Primer
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: New York’s G League affiliate opens its 2026-27 season tonight against the Maine Celtics in the Tip-Off Tournament. The roster features three players on two-way contracts, a returning fan favorite (hint: he’s great on toast), and a collection of prospects hoping to dribble their way up to an NBA court.With the Knicks operating near the second apron, Westchester provides a way to develop young players without committing additional standard roster spots. Two-way players can spend most of the season in White Plains while remaining available for NBA duty, subject to a limit of up to 50 games on the active roster. The G League has also given players like Deuce McBride and Tyler Kolek opportunities to get more work. Here’s a peek at the players worth watching.Dalton Knecht: A second chance in New YorkOf everyone on Westchester’s roster, Dalton Knecht has the clearest path to helping the big club this season. The 2024 first-round pick (17th overall) arrived after the Lakers waived him, with New York releasing Kevin McCullar Jr. to make room for Knecht on a two-way contract. This low-risk move could pay off if the former Tennessee star rediscovers his shooting touch and improves his court awareness, which was a criticism raised in the comments section at Silver Screen and Roll.The 25-year-old made a promising debut for the New York Knicks this week, scoring 10 points on efficient 4-of-6 shooting (including two threes) with seven boards, a dime, and a block in 16 minutes off the bench in a rout of the Bulls. Finding consistent playing time will be difficult, however. With Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby, Josh Hart, Landry Shamet, Pacôme Dadiet, and Mohamed Diawara competing for minutes on the wings, Knecht will probably need an injury or another opening to receive an extended look. (TBH, he already looks ahead of Dadiet.)Coach Mike Brown has said he’d rather see Knecht playing meaningful minutes in the G League than sitting on the NBA bench. Makes sense. Knecht needs opportunities to shoot, make decisions, and work through mistakes. He has shown he can score, but questions remain about his defense, shot selection, and ability to contribute consistently as a role player.If Knecht performs well enough, the organization could eventually consider converting him to a standard NBA contract, which would require sufficient roster and financial room. For now, he should get plenty of opportunities to let it fly against G League competition.Speaking of flamethrowers . . . Tyler “Silent K” Nickel might be the most straightforward fit for what the Knicks need. New York selected the Vanderbilt sharpshooter with the 47th pick in the 2026 NBA Draft after an impressive senior season. He followed that with a promising Summer League showing and signed a two-way contract.From what we’ve seen, Nickel moves well without the ball, finds open space, and punishes defenses for leaving him unattended. The big league Knicks have several players capable of creating offense, and a dependable perimeter shooter who doesn’t require many touches could fit nicely alongside them (see: Landry Shamet).His defense will help determine how quickly the 23-year-old advances. He needs to prove he can handle quicker, stronger NBA bodies while maintaining his shooting efficiency against more aggressive closeouts. Westchester should give him plenty of reps to work on both.Nickel doesn’t seem to have Knecht’s offensive versatility, but his shooting gives him a clearly defined role. If he can hold his own defensively, he could become a useful option for additional spacing. For the time being, Westchester might have its very own set of Splash Brothers to keep you entertained (at a reasonable price).Jaden Akins: Defense and versatilityJaden Akins took a less direct route to New York. Undrafted out of Michigan State in 2025, he spent last season with the Motor City Cruise after earning All-Big Ten third-team and All-Defensive recognition as a senior. His combination of scoring, secondary playmaking, and defense caught the Knicks’ attention. Westchester acquired his returning player rights in September, and he secured a two-way contract before the season.Akins faces considerable competition at the one- and two-guard spots. His best chance of separating himself is to use his time at Westchester to polish his defense and his work off the ball. Can he defend multiple positions, run an offense for stretches, and make open shots? Can he contribute consistently without committing unnecessary fouls or turnovers? Those qualities will probably matter more to New York than his individual scoring averages.Dink Pate: Back for another seasonThe fan favorite returns! Dink Pate returns to Westchester after a confusing offseason. The 6’8” wing, still only 20 years old, averaged approximately 16 points, seven rebounds, and four assists across 50 games with the club last season. He subsequently attempted to play college basketball at Providence, but that plan fell through amid questions about his NCAA eligibility. The Knicks signed and waived him on an Exhibit 10 contract, and he returned to Westchester, which already held his G League rights.Pate has length, can create his own offense, and contributes as a rebounder and passer. His combination of physical tools and professional experience makes him one of Westchester’s more interesting developmental players. Decision-making and efficiency are where he needs improvement.Unlike Knecht, Nickel, and Akins, Pate doesn’t have a two-way contract. He would need an available two-way or standard roster spot and a new NBA contract to join the big club. Westchester’s rights also don’t prevent another NBA team from signing him. Thus, his time in White Plains is a prove-it run for a broader audience—so we expect to see some inspired hooping from him this season.Frontcourt depth: Robbins, Dante, and MiličićWestchester’s frontcourt includes several players who could provide useful depth. , a seven-footer who went undrafted out of Vanderbilt in 2023, is probably the most recognizable. He showed some encouraging work around the iron during Summer League with the Knicks, and Westchester subsequently acquired his G League rights.Robbins brings size, rebounding, and shot-blocking ability. The big league club could use more reliable center depth behind Karl-Anthony Towns and Andre Drummond, with James Wiseman slow to make an impression. Robbins could use his time in White Plains to convince the team he deserves a look—perhaps before the front office starts eyeing its surplus of guards as trade bait., the 6-foot-11 former Oregon center, is working his way back from an ACL injury. His size and athleticism lift our eyebrows, but getting healthy and regaining his previous form will be the immediate priorities. , a 6-foot-10 forward out of Tennessee, brings international experience and positional versatility after spending time with the Delaware Blue Coats last season. Improving his outside shooting and defensive consistency would help him take the next step.The wings: Jourdain, Okani, and companyWestchester also has several forwards competing for rotation minutes. returns after averaging roughly eight points and more than five rebounds last season. The former Memphis forward provides rebounding, energy, and defensive effort. His journey from local tryout to returning player is a nice story, even if an NBA opportunity remains a longer shot., the former West Virginia wing, brings length and athleticism after spending time with multiple G League organizations. , an undrafted forward out of Duquesne, and are also trying to establish roles after joining the training camp group.The guards: Shooting potentialWestchester’s backcourt includes several capable players. is worth watching after arriving from the Stockton Kings. The 6’5” guard shot approximately 42% from downtown last season, giving Westchester another option to stretch the floor. returns as a scoring option at guard and on the wing, while joins the club after being selected 25th in the 2026 G League Draft. Spears brings extensive college experience, including a productive stint at UTSA, and spent last season playing professionally in Mexico.The three two-way players will receive the most attention this season, although we’ll also keep an eye on Pate (‘cuz he’s kinda electric). The rest of the roster will compete for minutes and try to establish themselves as dependable professional players. Westchester opens its Tip-Off Tournament schedule tonight at 7 p.m. against the Maine Celtics at the Portland Expo, then faces the same opponent at the same venue Sunday at 12:30 p.m. Both games will air on MSG Network.

item.title: World Champion Brandon McNulty to debut rainbow jersey on home soil at El Tour de Tucson - North American Roundup
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: World champion Brandon McNulty debuts his rainbow jersey on home soil on November 21 at El Tour de Tucson. A native of Phoenix, Arizona, McNulty will make his first appearance at the Tucson event, now in a 43rd edition that has grown in size to 12,000 participants across three routes, the longest 103 miles.A number of former pro athletes are also part of the front corral of starters including four-time triathlete world champion Leanda Cave and former Grand Tour riders George Hincapie, Bob Roll, Bobby Julich, and Frankie Andreu. All riders compete for prestige and bragging rights in a choice of three distances, as there is no prize money. El Tour de Tucson is the flagship event for El Tour America, a non-profit that produces cycling events and helps raise funds for more than 120 other non-profits. Many of the current and retired pros participating in the ride will also participate in The Prologue, an exclusive camp for limited attendees to raise additional funds.RNRNYC Racing p/b R1 will support former WorldTour rider Ide Schelling for a second season, this time with a focus on gravel racing, and will be the the new home for New Zealander Ethan Craine as the team grows their roster for 2027. RNRNYC, which takes their name from cycling apparel brand Rubber N' Road that has a design studio and manufacturing in New York City, launched last season as an elite club team. They promote inclusivity and give riders opportunities to develop and race at a high level alongside experienced pros.Schelling had a limited role with RNRNYC Racing last year, participating in a limited calendar of road and gravel, taking 10th place in The Gralloch. The Dutch rider retired from an 11-year pro road career in 2025, which included six years at the WorldTour level with Bora-Hansgrohe and XDS Astana. He will continue as a brand ambassador for RNRNYC and be supported as a privateer in gravel."Ide will be racing a lot more by himself, but remains part of the bigger ecosystem, the RNR and L1 racing family. Maybe he'll do a couple of races with the team, but really he will focus on doing gravel events, which are mostly in Europe. Maybe doing Big Sugar and a couple more in the US," Gil Lavi, co-founder of Rubber N' Road and RNRNYC Racing, told. Lavi said the cycling apparel brand benefits greatly from an international roster of riders, since the company has production facilities in three countries and customers around the globe. "Having Ethan [Craine] is huge. César Marte and Wiley Close are very talented racers, super young, super talented," Lavi said about some of the new riders that have been announced so far.Craine, 25, joins from five years with Project Echelon Racing, where he had stage wins in the Green Mountain Stage Race, Salt Lake Criterium and Chicago Grit. Close, 22, moves from ENVE MOG Squad's gravel team, where he finished eighth on the queen stage at Green Mountain Stage Race in his first road race in September. Marte, a sprinter from the Dominican Republic, earned top results in the US across multiple teams at the Tour of Somerville, Gateway Cup, and Tour of America’s Dairyland since 2022 and als has multiple stage wins at the Vuelta Independencia.The full roster will be disclosed in the coming weeks, with 12-15 riders expected to compete on a heavy road racing calendar, with a few gravel races mixed in.Retirement news is typically reserved for riders, but this time organisers for Crusher in the Tushar confirmed Thursday that the Utah gravel race would permanently close after 14 years. Taking its name from the Tushar mountains of central Utah, the highest range in the state, the Crusher was cancelled twice in the last three years due to impact from active wildfires in the area. Life Time purchased the event from founder and former road pro Burke Swindlehurst in 2019, and included the race as part of the Life Time Grand Prix series from 2022 to 2024, though the third instalment was not held due to the fires. Keegan Swenson won the two Grand Prix editions while Haley Smith and Sofia Gomez Villafañe split the wins for elite women."We made the decision to retire Crusher in the Tushar," Life Time posted Thursday on social channels and the web site for the event. "Since its founding, Crusher in the Tushar has played a pivotal role in shaping gravel cycling, challenging athletes on one of the sport's most demanding and memorable courses."We are deeply grateful to founder Burke Swindlehurst for his vision, the greater Beaver community for its incredible hospitality and partnership, and the athletes, volunteers and partners who have made Crusher such a special event over the years."Our thoughts remain with the Beaver and Piute County communities as they continue to recover and rebuild following this year's devastating wildfires and flooding."A total of 12 US teenagers will be part of EuroCrossAcademy's November block of training and racing, with the first competitions set for the Netherlands November 14-15 including Vam-Berg Cross in Wijster. The squad will have multiple skills training sessions in Alphen, Netherlands and Lichtaart, Belgium, with a focus on forest trails and sand, then complete the two-week trip with racing in Hilversum, Netherlands and Maldegem, Belgium.This is 24th year EuroCrossAcademy, led by Geoff Proctor, and a third consecutive year for a unique block for 15-16 year olds. The programme began in 2003 as EuroCross Camp to help athletes prepare for the Cyclo-cross World Championships. It has grown into a non-profit, EuroCrossAcademy (ECA), which now provides summer camps in Montana and Vermont as well as blocks of European racing experience in the development process for young US riders. The group of 15-16 year olds are the focus for November, with the 17-18 year old riders taking part in a separate experience in December. "The emphasis at the ECA November block is specifically on development, not results or outcomes. Are are they becoming better people by improving their character/continuing to find purpose?" Proctor told about what measuring success. He said ECA coaches measure success based on the level of "finding joy in a safe, kind, supportive environment" as well as learning life skills, not just riding skills, from their teammates, mechanics, support staff, and themselves. For both blocks of training and race, will provide coverage with rider dairies, the athletes providing first-person accounts of the 'character development' and competition.EuroCrossAcademy 2026 participantsThe road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down.
