item.title: TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: Which is the best app to support your structured training?
item.author: Paul Norman
item.content:encoded: TrainerRoad and TrainingPeaks offer an objective-driven approach to training, helping you to target specific events or develop a plan to cover your whole season. They also focus on offering more detailed analysis of your performance than other platforms, such as Zwift and MyWhoosh and are generally used by riders whose priority is training and data or who don't need an immersive virtual training world.They go about this in rather different ways, though. While TrainingPeaks delivers workouts via its TrainingPeaks Virtual app, TrainerRoad is more old-school, with a simpler ramp-based graph interface. Where TrainerRoad scores, though, is its AI-driven workout selection. It also caters for missed workouts and changed schedules via its Train Now functionality.TrainingPeaks was bought by Garmin in July 2026. It’s not clear how this will affect the app in future, but for the moment it continues to operate as normal.Garmin may be looking to strengthen its own indoor training offering, which is currently delivered via the niche Tacx app.TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: ApproachBoth TrainerRoad and TrainingPeaks are much more hardcore than apps such as Zwift and Rouvy. They aim to offer objective-driven, structured training based on goal setting and planned activities to meet your goals.TrainerRoad provides AI-driven training, with its app assessing your performance after each workout and tuning your future activity schedule based on this. The assessment is across multiple aspects of your fitness, not just FTP. This, it claims, gives a more precise assessment of your strengths and weaknesses and allows it to more accurately target its workouts.As well as structured, scheduled plans, there’s also the Train Now option, which allows you to fit in workouts around your other activities in a more flexible way.TrainingPeaks is more focused on its structured plans, which offer less flexibility than TrainerRoad. There’s a wide range of plans available, but these are extra-cost items on top of the basic access. TrainingPeaks doesn’t just work with cyclists; it offers training for other endurance sports and also strength training. There’s the option to work with in-person coaches to manage your training.TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: User interfaceTrainerRoad offers a fairly basic user interface while you work out, consisting of the classic ramp profiles on a black background, with stats on your performance. There’s no interactivity with other users. You do have the option to ride its workouts on other platforms, though – see below.TrainingPeaks offers a virtual world with a similar, although less finished, look to Zwift or MyWhoosh. This can be explored solo, but you can also join up with other riders, join group rides and chat in-app.Ride physics is simulated, so you’ll get a boost from drafting, and headwinds can slow you down. As with Zwift, there are virtual riders too, and you can upload your own GPX files to ride your own routes.There are the same ramps in intensity as with TrainerRoad, just presented in a more visually appealing way. If you want to, you can select Focus mode and switch off the virtual simulation, or Zen mode and ride alone in the virtual world.TrainingPeaks Virtual also offers a range of different races at different performance levels, adding an element of competition to your riding. TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: Workout alternatives Both TrainerRoad and TrainingPeaks allow you to work out on other platforms, although you will need a separate account for the second app.TrainingPeaks workouts can be ridden on Zwift, which offers a greater depth of immersion than its TrainingPeaks Virtual environment and all the Zwift add-ons such as power-ups, as well as a larger user base to ride with or race against. You’ll need both a TrainingPeaks and a Zwift account, but then workouts in your TrainingPeaks calendar will appear in your Zwift workout schedule and, once you’ve completed a workout, it will automatically be synced back to TrainingPeaks for analysis and progress tracking. TrainerRoad offers a feed out to Zwift too, so that scheduled TrainerRoad workouts appear in your Zwift account and you can ride them there, with data then transferred back to TrainerRoad for progression tracking and analysis.TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: PricingA TrainerRoad annual membership is priced in US dollars and annually works out at $17.45 monthly equivalent, but you can also pay monthly, which costs $21.99 per month. TrainerRoad offers a 30-day money-back period.TrainingPeaks costs the equivalent of $11.25 per month if you pay for a year’s Premium access. You can also pay quarterly, which increases the price to $16.33 per month equivalent, while paying month-by-month costs $19.95. Again, there’s a 30-day money-back period.But with TrainingPeaks, you also need to factor in the price of its training plans, which are not included in the basic price. Its 12-week Base and FTP Development plan, for example, costs $5, while the VO2max Booster costs $20. Other plans can cost as much as $500.TrainingPeaks has the option to work with a live coach to develop a custom training plan. Three tiers of interactivity range in price from $149 per month to $359 per month. The lowest-priced option puts limits on your communication with your coach, while the most expensive option offers unlimited interactions and feedback on every workout.TrainerRoad vs TrainingPeaks: Which should you choose?TrainerRoad’s adaptive training and its sophisticated metrics will be attractive to cyclists wanting some flexibility in their objective-driven training. It’s a solitary experience, though, and it takes a certain mental outlook to follow a plan when the workouts are presented as ramp charts only; although riding on another platform does offer a more interesting alternative, it has to be said.There’s more opportunity for interactivity with other users and with coaches in TrainingPeaks, which some may find more engaging. This does increase the cost of access, though, so TrainingPeaks is likely to be more expensive to use. Its analysis is also less sophisticated than that of TrainerRoad, but it does cover a wider range of sports.

item.title: 'Tom's pace is pretty mind-blowing' – Tom Pidcock swaps two wheels for four to tackle fearsome Nürburgring Nordschleife race track in Porsche 911
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: With the cycling off-season in full swing, Tom Pidcock has swapped two wheels for four, taking to the German motor racing circuit Nürburgring Nordschleife in a Porsche 911 GT3 RS.The Briton has won world and Olympic titles on cyclo-cross and mountain bikes, but he's no slouch in the race car, either, joining Porsche brand ambassador Jörg Bergmeister for a track day at the legendary circuit in Germany's Eifel mountains.Pidcock has previously recorded a 6:52.37 lap time around the fearsome 20.832km former Formula 1 circuit, which features 73 corners, leaving him just 27 seconds off the all-time lap record, set by Stefan Bellof in 1983.The 27-year-old, who this year won Milano-Torino and finished ninth at the Tour de France, will soon be gearing up for his third season at Pinarello-Q36.5, where he'll be joined by new arrivals Giulio Ciccone, Mauro Schmid, and Ethan Hayter, among others. However, he took time away from the bike to explore the track with Manthey Kit on Wednesday."The organisation of the race team and where all the parts are feels very similar to how we have our service course in the cycling team. The parts storage, the packing lists – it's a similar world," Pidcock said of the company's headquarters, located near the famous 2km straight of the circuit."What I've learned from Manthey is that, if you're developing a car at the Nürburgring, the data doesn't tell you everything. You have to use feeling."And personally, I think feeling is even more valuable than data when I'm trying to develop a bike. The Nordschleife is such an unpredictable place, and Porsche and Manthey manage to make the cars feel as predictable as possible for the people driving them."This time around, Pidcock took on the challenging circuit in wetter conditions, and Bergmeister said that Pidcock's pace is particularly impressive given he isn't a regular at the track."I know a couple of pro and ex-pro cyclists, and the line and flow that it takes to do a smooth, quick lap comes naturally to these guys. Tom gets in and knows exactly what he's doing and has great feel for the car – and also no fear," he said."For someone who isn't here regularly, Tom's pace is pretty mind-blowing. There are people on the Ring every day who go slower. The advice I could give him is to simply focus on hitting the marks: braking points, turn-in points."But you can see it all comes naturally. I guess there's a reason why he's so good on the descents in cycle racing!"Pidcock explained what drew him to the track and racing high-performance cars, such as the powerful Porsche 911 GT3 RS."I guess it's because it's about 'high performance', just like cycling is for me. It's the same mindset," he said."Driving, in general, is a pursuit of improvement, which is constant in what I do daily. But here there's no pressure – I can also enjoy the fact that I don't need to push it to the extreme limit. When I'm competing [in my career], there's always so much pressure, so on track it's nice that I can simply just compete with myself."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: How to turn an AI into your personal coach: Goal-specific prompts and setup instructions
item.author: Tim Perkin
item.content:encoded: The world of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is moving so fast that even WorldTour cycling teams are now using it to help understand and interpret riders' data to aid with training and racing.AI use is commonplace now, and cyclists are using it to their advantage. Following suit, I decided to see what AI could do for me.My end goal was for AI to generate a bespoke training plan that could return me to my peak level of fitness, whatever that was. Simple, or so I thought. I wanted to learn about customising an AI training plan based on my own historical data, and improve my skills along the way.The first challenge was choosing a platform. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Microsoft Copilot were all AI assistants that I investigated.Some AI engines or apps are free, some aren't. Free versions limit what you can do and, in this case, how many files you can upload to be analysed. I paid a subscription fee as I was always going to need to use my full training history. After researching the different platforms, I settled on Claude because it could read and analyse my CSV files directly.With Claude chosen, I paid for a subscription and began to see what it could do.I decided to ask it to build me a 12-week indoor training plan using this simple prompt: "Build me a 12-week indoor cycling training plan of between 7 and 10 hours a week. I can ride 5 times a week, but not on Thursday."Claude then produced the plan below for me:FTP test in Week 1, then sweet spot and tempoThreshold and over under intervalsV02 Max intervals with some threshholdThe plan is perfectly acceptable, but it's limited. It offers nothing beyond what you can find in cycling training manuals or on hundreds of websites online.The plan falls short because it is not based on my own data. Without access to my training data, asking AI to build me a plan will always result in something this generic. Granted, you can input parameters such as how many rides you intend to do each week, how many hours you have available for training, and which days suit you best, but beyond that, the output will always be limited.To create a bespoke plan and something tailored to my requirements, I realised that I needed to provide AI with my training data. Only with this could AI produce a bespoke plan. And for that, I knew where to go:My Strava account held almost all my training data, and with the functionality to download it, I could then take the relevant files and have AI analyse them and utilise my training and riding history. [Ed. Since undertaking this project, but prior to publishing, Strava launched its MCP connector, allowing direct plugin to AI assistants, enabling the sharing of historic datam, plus future data in perpetuity].However, I had to undertake a slight side quest first. Strava did not have all my data. My early years of training results were held on spreadsheets, so I had to get these uploaded into Strava using a third-party app.I reformatted the spreadsheets got the data uploaded into Strava, using a third-party go between. I then requested my complete set of training data from Strava. An email link soon arrived with a 1.7 GB archive, though I only needed one file from it.The summary file was called "activities.csv" and contained enough data to enable AI to produce a tailored plan for me.To download your own data in Strava, go to Settings > My Account > Download or Delete Your Account, then select Request Your Archive. Strava then emails you a link to the data.Only activities.csv is needed, so there's no need to upload the whole thing. If you have many years of riding and the file is too large to upload, delete the oldest rows, but keep your best season so the AI can compare against it.A word of caution: activities.csv includes heart-rate data, which is personal health information. I recommend checking your AI platform's privacy and data settings before you upload it.Power figures only appear in activities.csv files for rides recorded with a power meter or smart trainer. Without them, the AI's FTP estimates and power targets will be much less reliable, so bear this in mind too. The next challenge was writing the correct prompts to finesse my training programme. My first attempt was too simple. After some research, I learned that a good prompt needs four key components.The first component is the persona, which assigns the AI a specific role, for example: "You are an elite cycling WorldTour coach."The second component is the specific task, such as "Using my uploaded data, analyse and assess my current level and create me a 12-week training plan that gets me to and surpasses my previous best cycling fitness levels."The third component is the context: including any important details, which in this case were the days I could train and for how many hours.The fourth and final component is the format, or how I would like the answer to look.The prompt I decided to use to build my specific training plan was as follows:"You are an elite cycling WorldTour coach. Using my uploaded data in the spreadsheet only, analyse and assess my current level and create a 12-week training plan that gets me to and surpasses my previous best cycling fitness levels.""I have 10 hours per week for training and can ride 5 times a week, with the exception of Thursday.""Sessions in the week must not last longer than 90 minutes. I would like a detailed session plan, detailing how long each session should last, power output and heart rate."I also find that going to a separate Claude chat window and asking it to suggest its own prompt is a good way to learn the phrasing and terminology that Claude itself understands. You can iterate on its suggestion more easily than create your own from scratch, and the wording is often less vague than anything I would generate myself. I later refined these prompts into a shorter version that you can reuse:"You are an elite WorldTour cycling coach. Using only the rides in my attached Strava activities.csv, assess my current level against my all-time best (estimated FTP, and best 20-minute and 60-minute power), then create a 12-week plan starting [date] to beat it.""I have 10 hours a week over 5 rides. I can't ride on Thursday or [second rest day], and weekday rides must be 90 minutes or less. Give me my power and heart-rate zones, then a table for each week showing day, duration, session, target watts, and target heart rate. Include recovery weeks and FTP tests in weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12, and be honest about how realistic the goal is."Before building the plan, the AI assessed my data. It estimated that my FTP had fallen from about 325–329 watts at my peak (December 2021 to February 2022) to about 260 watts, a drop of around 20%, and that my weekly riding had halved from 8–10 hours to about 4.5 hours. That told me straight away that this plan would be built around me, not a textbook.The output, generated by the first of the two prompts above, was a very detailed plan with tailored power and heart-rate targets. The table below shows Week 1; the other 11 weeks are just as detailed.The plan is not fixed. After each FTP test, I can give the AI the result and ask it to recalculate my zones and update the remaining weeks, so the plan keeps pace with my fitness. With the newly added MCP Connector, this could even be automated. Example Block 1: Rebuild (FTP 260 W) Week 1 (26th Oct), 8 hours, approx 430 TSS20-min FTP test. 15 min Z2, 3 × 1 min at 290 W(1 min easy), 5 min easy, 20 min max effort (start at 265 W, build). FTP = 0.95 × 20-min averageEasy, with 4 × 30 s spin-ups at 110–120 rpmEndurance, last hour includes 2 × 10 min tempo (5 min easy between)Prompts you may find useful This prompt gets the AI to act as your personal cycling coach and build a 12-week plan that fits around your life and moves you towards a goal, such as beating your best FTP. It is a fuller version of the short prompt above, giving you more control over the output."You are an elite WorldTour cycling coach who builds periodised, power-based plans for time-limited amateurs. Using the 'Ride' and 'Virtual Ride' activities in my attached Strava activities.csv, create a progressive 12-week plan to [goal, e.g., beat my previous best FTP]. I have [X] hours a week across [X] rides; I can't ride on [days], and weekday sessions are capped at [X] minutes.Remember to be specific in your demands; a degree of nuance and experience is needed here, and if you choose to experiment, the more you do, the better you will get.I asked the AI to give me:An assessment of my current level against my all-time best, with key numbers. Estimate FTP from Weighted Average Power in 20–60-minute rides, and include weekly hours, load, and consistency over the last 12 weeks.A zones table: % of FTP, watts, and heart rate.One table per week: day, duration, session (with intervals and recoveries), target watts, target heart rate, and weekly total hours. Include recovery weeks and FTP tests in weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12, with week 12 a taper that ends in the final test.Up to five rules on fuelling, adjusting when fatigued, and updating zones after each test.Be realistic about what 12 weeks can achieve.This prompt uses your data to check whether you've been riding too hard too often over the past month without enough easy days or rest between hard rides. The aim is to catch fatigue before it leads to poor performance, illness, or burnout."You are a cycling physiologist specialising in recovery and fatigue monitoring. Using the 'Ride' and 'Virtual Ride' activities in my attached Strava activities.csv file from the last 30 days, find the days where my recovery was probably not enough. My FTP is [X] W, and my threshold heart rate is [X] bpm. Classify each ride as hard (above 85% of FTP), moderate, or easy (below 70% of FTP), using Weighted Average Power, Relative Effort, and heart rate, and treat a heart rate of 0 as not recorded. Flag hard days back-to-back, more than three hard rides in any seven days, and heart rate out of line with power." I also asked my AI coach to give me:A 30-day calendar table: date, ride, duration, Weighted Average Power, and Hard/Moderate/Easy/Rest.Each day where recovery was not enough, with a one-line reason.My hard-to-easy ratio compared with 80/20.Three changes to my weekly structure.This prompt checks whether your recent riding has prepared you for a specific event, such as a sportive, road race, or time trial, and tells you what to work on in the four weeks before it."You are an experienced cycling coach who prepares riders for races and sportives. Look at my rides from the last 12 weeks in the attached Strava activities.csv file. I'm riding [event, e.g., a 120 km sportive with 2,000 m of climbing] on [date]; my goal is [goal, e.g., finish under 4 hours], and my FTP is about [X] W. Tell me whether my training so far has prepared me for this event.I also asked my AI coach to give me:A short summary of how fit I am now, in three or four sentences.A table of my last 12 weeks: hours ridden, longest ride, total climbing, and number of hard sessions (Weighted Average Power above 85% of FTP) each week.What's missing. Check whether I've done enough long rides, enough climbing, enough long steady, hard efforts, and enough short bursts for attacks. For each gap, show the evidence from my data and why it matters for this event.A four-week plan to fix those gaps, with the key sessions, the long ride for each week, and power and heart-rate targets.An honest one-line answer on whether my goal is realistic.Rather than building all of the above as a self-serve chat-based coach that you ask questions of and manually prompt when you want it to adjust or analyse your work, it could even be built agentically. An overarching AI Agent could be given the primary prompt, the database of Strava workouts uploaded as resources alongside your preferences, and improvements to your power duration curve or your FTP can be its reward signal. The trio of prompts above - alongside others - could then be created as 'skills' - essentially tools that the LLM can call upon, and automations can be built to check your progress periodically, update the plan in real time, and flag whenever you're off track. If you wanted, you could even connect it to your Whoop (if you use one), and your Calendar app of choice to slot the workout into your day. There's a lot of potential here, and although the build essentially seeks to mimic much of what's already been achieved by TrainerRoad, Zwift Plus, Vekta, FasCat, Xert et al, there's a certain enjoyment and pride in building it yourself (even if Claude is doing the hard yards), and being able to tweak it to your liking. AI can be a valuable tool for cyclists to understand their training and improve performance, and many are already experimenting with ways to use AI to improve their training. The results are going to depend on the input. While generating a basic training plan is easy, creating a genuinely bespoke one is harder.The real insights come when AI accesses your historical training data. It analyses past performances, assesses your current state, and builds a plan around your ambitions, time, and individual needs. This results in a more detailed and personalised approach.For the plans and outputs to be relevant, the data must be accurate, prompts carefully constructed, and output critically evaluated. Training recommendations are only as useful as their underlying information and assumptions. AI should not replace professional coaching or understanding your body's response to training.There's also a cost, both for AI platform subscriptions and the time to organise data and refine prompts. Yet, for cyclists willing to invest the initial effort, the reward is a plan built around their own numbers rather than a generic one.I aimed to see if AI could help me regain peak fitness. I now have a structured, data-driven 12-week plan designed to do just that. Its success will ultimately be determined on the bike in the coming weeks.

item.title: Russell to take grid penalty at F1's Brazilian GP
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: George Russell will take a five-place grid penalty for this weekend's Formula 1 Brazilian Grand Prix for a new internal combustion engine, his second grid drop in four races.Russell had a 60-place grid penalty for a suite of power unit component changes in Singapore last month, a necessity after he retired with a power unit failure in Malaysia the week before.He knew then that he would have to take another grid penalty before the end of the year, and Mercedes has chosen Brazil to do so at Interlagos this weekend, with Russell confirming the decision on Mercedes' Instagram account."We always had to take a grid penalty at some point between Singapore and the end of the season," Russell explained."We felt like this was a good place to take it. Lewis [Hamilton] had a big grid penalty here a number of years ago [in 2021] and did pretty well."Five places doesn't seem that bad and we’ll try to come back through."Driving for Mercedes in 2021, Hamilton was disqualified after topping sprint qualifying for a technical non-conformity (a misaligned DRS), yet charged from 20th to fifth in the sprint.Back then, the sprint result dictated your start position for the grand prix but, after taking a new internal combustion engine, Hamilton was dropped back to 10th on the grid.He still comfortably won the grand prix from there.So Brazil is a logical choice for Russell to take the engine penalty, one that was originally going to coincide with the debut of Mercedes' Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities-assisted (ADUO) engine.But the debut of that ADUO engine is uncertain, and there's no guarantee it will appear before the end of the season, with a maximum of three races remaining after Brazil.Mercedes does not want to rush its introduction and will only introduce it when it is sure it is ready, with the drivers' championship already sealed and the constructors' championship all but guaranteed.

item.title: Ferrari set for crunch meeting as Hamilton and Leclerc tension reaches Brazil
'I felt quite lost and desperate' – How Ashleigh Moolman Pasio re-wrote the ending of her 17-year career, and how she's re-writing the future for African cyclists
item.author: Dan Challis
item.content:encoded: Ashleigh Moolman Pasio's career could have ended very differently had she given in to a drawn-out and frustrating recovery to a fractured vertebrae. She considered hanging up her race bike during the 2025 season, a year earlier than planned, her confidence weakened after 18 months of trying to find form due to a crash at the 2024 Volta a Catalunya. However, the South African was determined to write a different final chapter to her 17-year professional career, and saddled up for one last campaign. Speaking to Moolman Pasio over a video call from her home on the outskirts of Girona, it's clear that this conversation would have been very different had it occurred twelve months earlier. The AG Insurance-Soudal rider is leaving the peloton satisfied to have bowed out on her own terms and in good shape, rather than being forced out through injury. I didn't finish because I wasn't good enough any longer. I finished because I've decided it's time to put my focus into other things."At the end of 2025 I actually didn't know who I was as an athlete any longer. It was such a disconnect from the athlete I was in training and who I knew I was in terms of the power and the performance I could produce," Moolman Pasio tells a few days after her final bow at the gravel worlds. "I felt quite lost and desperate. It did cross my mind to retire sooner than planned."Alongside her T10 vertebra fracture, Moolman Pasio also discovered at that time that she was suffering from high insulin sensitivity, causing her muscles to flush out glucose from her bloodstream; a physiological concept known as the 'athlete paradox'. After adjusting her diet, she got back in shape for the 2026 season."I decided that I wanted to finish my career on my terms and managed to get back to a level that I was very happy with," she says, having finished fourth at April's Brabantse Pijl among several other strong results in her final year. "I finished on my terms and I finished the athlete that I know I should be. Whereas if I had finished last year having had all those performance issues I would have felt like I was forced to retire because I'm not good enough any longer. Now, I actually could continue… I still am at the level that I could hugely contribute to a team.""I didn't finish because I wasn't good enough any longer. I finished because I've decided it's time to put my focus into other things," she adds.Moolman Pasio was pleased with her final road worlds performance, finishing in the top-20 on a tough course in Montréal. Things didn't go quite as smoothly on the gravel two weeks later, however, as she endured a cold in the days before and ended her final race early due to a crash.No "fairytale ending," she says, but turning 41 in December, Moolman Pasio is now taking time to reflect on almost two decades in Europe that have themselves had the twists and turns of a good novel. An outsider infiltrating a European sportNo African woman precedes Moolman Pasio for her longevity and achievements in professional cycling. After qualifying as a chemical engineer at Stellenbosch University, the Pretorian discovered her talent for cycling later than most, encouraged and supported by her husband, Carl.Moolman Pasio began racing on the South African scene while at university. She soon signed for one of the country's big teams, Cyclelab-Toyota, which in 2008 enabled her to race in Europe for the first time at the Tour Feminin de l'Ardèche. She finished the six-stage race in 39th, doing enough to convince Lotto Ladies to hand her a life-changing contract."The Tour of Ardèche was a big big eye-opener. [I was] totally out of my depth at that point in time; crashing, punctures, all sorts of nonsense. But thankfully I made contact with Lotto. We managed to negotiate this ride for a couple of members of the local team on the Lotto set-up. [It was] for free. We just got our bikes and support," she explains. "It took determination, it took guts. I had to be really brave to make this all happen. It also took the support around me which I was very lucky to have."Moolman Pasio describes racing a 'double season' in her first couple of years; competing in Europe during the northern hemisphere summer with Lotto, and then again throughout the summer months in South Africa. She survived on the small amount of pay from racing in South Africa as well as some personal endorsement deals from South African companies. She says her first "proper contract" came along in 2014 when she joined the Norwegian Hitec Products team after a season in which she finished on the podium at La Fléche Wallonne. However, throughout all this time, she and Carl had been struggling with visa restrictions due to their South African passports. Utilising his Italian heritage, Moolman Pasio's husband managed to get Italian passports for both of them, solving their visa restriction woes.Moolman Pasio went on to take a total of 49 UCI victories throughout her career. She became the first African woman to win a WorldTour stage race in 2022 at the Tour de Romandie, won the UCI eSports World Championships in 2020 and was twice overall runner-up at the Giro d'Italia Women. For much of that time, Moolman Pasio has been the only African rider at the top level of women's cycling, something which she plans to change in the next phase of her life. 'The hunger in their eyes' – Paying it forward with Team AmaniMoolman Pasio's career has not only been characterised by what she has achieved on the bike, but also her activities off it. She set up Rocacorba Cycling in 2021 alongside her husband, a boutique cycling hotel in a restored 17th century estate, nestled in the mountains near Girona and named after one of the local climbs. Alongside the hotel, Moolman Pasio established the Rocacorba Collective, a thriving indoor cycling community with a particular mission to uplift and bring women together. In a sport that has become more insular, with riders able to focus on little else aside from their performance, Moolman Pasio has always ridden with a wider set of goals in mind. In 2023, during the middle of her Classics campaign, she travelled back to South Africa to support women from Khaltsha Cycling, a cycling project partnered with Rocacorba Collective in the country's largest township, to ride the Cape Town Cycle Tour. "I've always been driven by impact, purpose, paying it forward, deeper than winning bike races," she says. "Yes, performing at bike races motivated me, obviously, to keep always giving my best, but my real inspiration as an athlete was so much more than winning bike races." Now that she has hung up her wheels for good, Moolman Pasio will plough her full focus into her new role as general manager of Team Amani. She will guide the East African cycling project's women's Continental team, which aims to enable African women to race at the very top levels. The ultimate and immediate goal is to race the 2028 Tour de France Femmes. Moolman Pasio's original plan in the latter stages of her career was to set up her own cycling team, linked in with the Rocacorba community. However, after speaking with Ethiopian former men's WorldTour rider Tsgabu Grmay, she recognised a synergy between her ideas and what Amani was already putting in place. Instead of competing with Amani, Moolman Pasio was invited to join the team staff, and has even spent time supporting its riders this season, hosting a small group at Rocacorba and spending a day coaching them in descending. Instantly, Moolman Pasio was gripped by the potential of the riders from Ethiopia, Rwanda and elsewhere in East Africa."It was actually quite mind-blowing really," she recalls of her day coaching the riders in June. "We went out for a session on Rocacorba to do some downhilling skills and it still gives me goosebumps to think of that day because it was just so high impact… The hunger in their eyes, that's something that really stands out to me with these girls. They have so many challenges back home, especially the Ethiopians with war that's looming [In October, fighting resumed in the Tigray region, where Amani's Ethiopian riders are from, following the 2020-2022 Tigray War between the Ethiopian Armed Forces and the Tigray People's Liberation Front – Ed.]. "Two of them have young children and their families are there, but the hunger and just how they were soaking up everything that I was showing them, everything I was saying to them. I could just see their eyes, I could see the sparkle, I could see the switch flick in their brains."Days later, Moolman Pasio raced with her AG Insurance-Soudal team against Team Amani at the Volta a Catalunya, finishing 12th. Amani's best finisher was Ethiopian Eyerusalem Haftu Reda in 20th overall. "Seeing how [Eyerusalem Haftu Reda] moved in the peloton, how she was fighting for her place. She transformed her descending just from spending a few hours with me. I was just blown away by it and that's when I was like these girls have it, you know." "It's now moved from 'I want to pay forward, I want to help Africans, I want to give them opportunity', to saying 'We can get to the Tour de France, we can compete at the highest level'. If this is how quickly they can turn things around, imagine if they have a full season. They can do it." "It didn't change my motivation, I was always motivated, but it just amplified everything. We need to make this happen. So that's when we really started talking quite aggressively. We want to be at the start line of the Tour de France in 2028 and we really do believe we can do that. So now it's about putting everything possible in place to make that happen."The loss of Moolman Pasio's presence in the WorldTour peloton will be felt in 2027. This driven rider, with her punchy style and consistency, has been a constant figure in the bunch for 17 seasons. However, speaking with this giant of African cycling, you get the sense that she is just getting started. The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.content:encoded: We’ve made it to the weekend, and now that we’re a full week into November the holiday season is fast approaching. I’m personally brushing up on some fun fall recipes to have on hand for a Friendsgiving later in the month, which is how you know we’re fully into offseason mode when baking is the lede we’re going with. To be fair, it’s not like we’re anticipating much of a hot stove in the baseball sense with the lockout about to freeze transactions once the calendar turns over to December. The league is still rolling out award nominations, with the Silver Sluggers the most recent batch to be announced, and we’ve got a few weeks to go until we know who will be tendered a contract among arbitration-eligible players and who will accept their qualifying offers.It’ll be a quiet day as we get your morning started. Jonathan looks back at Fernando Cruz’s season and hands out our next report card, and then John takes us through James Paxton’s career on his 38th birthday. Later on in the afternoon, I’ll return to answer your latest questions from the mailbag.1. item.title: Low pressure in US midwest brings unseasonable heat to New York and Boston
item.author: Ollie Lewis for MetDesk
item.content:encoded: Further south this week, severe thunderstorms affected midterms voting in Florida, Oklahoma and ColoradoDespite the rapid descent into autumn in the northern hemisphere, parts of eastern North America have experienced an exceptionally late taste of summer in recent days. Temperatures approached 23C (73F) in New York and Boston, about 7-10C above what is expected in early November. The unseasonable warmth spilled into parts of eastern Canada, with temperatures exceeding 20C, about 10-15C above normal for the time of year. The balmy conditions were caused by an area of low pressure in the US midwest, dragging up exceptionally warm air from the Gulf of Mexico along its eastern flank. This area of low pressure will gradually drift eastwards, allowing temperatures to fall closer to the average.Further south, severe thunderstorms have resulted in numerous flood warnings and evacuation warnings being issued this week across many states, with disruptive weather affecting polling stations in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado. The powerful thunderstorms even resulted in a tornado touching down in Keyes, Oklahoma, forcing the relocation of a polling station. The tornado caused extensive damage, although no causalities have been reported. Officials across many states have requested federal funding assistance after the extreme weather resulted in widespread damage to homes and infrastructure.Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Every day, someone loses a hand or a leg’: the brutal reality of India’s textile recycling industry
item.author: Anuj Behal in Panipat. Photographs by Elke Scholiers
item.content:encoded: In Panipat, 1m tons of used clothing a year are turned into products for global brands, but dangerous machinery and few safeguards mean life-changing injuries are commonFor three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.Continue reading...

item.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.One connection, works every time, needs no retriesThere are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.

item.title: NASA unveils mysterious X-70 experimental aircraft using AI-generated image
item.author: Jeremy Hsu
item.content:encoded: NASA has announced a new experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, that will supposedly feature reconfigurable flight-control technology and a modular design for swapping in different payloads. But much remains unknown about the aircraft’s design and development timeline, even as NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said the X-plane could take flight within two years.The mystery surrounding NASA’s newest X-plane was exemplified by the agency’s press release, including an apparently AI-generated image of the X-70, showing a dark silhouette vaguely resembling a military fighter jet obscured by smoke. The news was announced by Isaacman during the UP.Summit held at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on November 4.“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” Isaacman said. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next.”

item.title: Outshining established players, mid-season promotions and Grand Tour victories – Taking a closer look at 10 stand-out neo-pros of 2026
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: The first year as a professional cyclist is often one of finding a footing in the intensely competitive pelotons, where the dream of being paid to race a bike can become a brutal reality. There are some, however, that do just more than learn and survive in that first year – they step up to the challenge and thrive.Some neo-pros entered the 2026 season with the weight of expectation already on their shoulders, such as Jarno Widar and Jakob Omrzel after steadily laying foundations and building blocks via years of racing in Europe through the junior and U23 ranks, accumulating results that put them in the spotlight along the way. Others took a more unconventional path, such as Sandrine Tas, Lennart Jasch and Lauren Dickson, starting out in another sport and then discovering a talent for cycling later on. Then there are those, like Jasch and Talia Appleton, who at the start of the season were actually not yet even neo-pros but made such a splash in the development teams that a mid-season promotion to the next tier came early.From the surprise breakthroughs to the long watched new stars of the professional peloton, we take a look at the achievements and path of 10 riders who have made such a big mark in their first season as a professional that it seems likely you'll be hearing about them on an increasingly regular basis through coming seasons.This German rider wasn't on anyone's radar as one of the neo-pro's to watch at the start of this year for one simple reason, at that point he was still listed on the Tudor Pro Cycling development team roster. Lennart Jasch came to cycling late, coming from speedskating, but has been quick to make a big impression since he signed up with a regional cycling team in 2024. After a year with the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe Rookies in 2025, Jasch made his potential crystal clear at the 2.Pro ranked Tour of the Alps when, having stepped up to take on an event with the senior team, he claimed victory on stage 4 from among a field packed with WorldTour riders. Not surprisingly after that he was quickly bumped up to that squad for the rest of the season. That, however, is not where his winning run ended with a stage win at Il Giro d'Abruzzo to prove his early season efforts were no fluke. That left him heading into his final stage race of the season with what he said was 'absolutely no pressure' but undoubtedly a big opportunity. The newcomer to the world of cycling who had only just stepped up into the ProTeam level was being given a chance to take on a general classification tilt as team leader at Le Tour de Langkawi with the pre-race objective outlined as his team being a top five overall. He well and truly overshot that goal.After the very first climbing challenge to Gunung Jerai on stage 2, Jasch was already in the overall lead with a 20 second margin, though other teams had multiple options lining up behind. There were no shortage of attempts to find ways to wear down the leader, but even as the temperature of the competition and environment continued to rise, Jasch kept a cool head. He displayed the patience and composure that many far more experienced players often find it hard to muster. Plus, while he was prepared to rely on his team, Jasch was also ready to take responsibility for jumping on a dangerous move and could also finish off the team effort in a way that meant he could not only hold onto, but also add to, his leading margin. It was a race that Jasch said would provide a 'first answer' as to how he may fare as a GC rider and that first answer is one that is bound to make his rivals sit up and take notice.Sticking to the theme of skaters turned cyclists, let's take a look at Sandrine Tas. The 31-year-old this year turned a childhood passion and one time training tool into a profession this year. Tas switched from the ice to the road with her debut at this year's La Flèche Wallonne just months after competing in the speedskating at the Winter Olympics. She had already made her cycling capabilities clear, coming eighth in the elite women's road race at the Belgian National Championships in 2025 and also winning two national level races. However, the first real test was launching into the professional peloton in the tough and talent packed one-day Women's WorldTour race, and Tas came through it with flying colours. She finished 57th, 3:35 off the winning time of Demi Vollering in a showing that clearly demonstrated an ability to manage the chaos of a top-tier peloton.What's more, on just her sixth race day in the professional peloton the first win came on stage 1 of the Bretagne Ladies Tour. Then she followed it up with another on stage 3 which landed her in second overall at the three day 2.1 tour. A win, let alone two in a first season as a professional, is an impressive beginning, though more podium appearances and a Tour de France Femmes start were yet to come. In fact Tas even managed another top step before the season was over, with victory ahead of Charlotte Kool on stage 1 of the Eneco Tour to round out one extremely successful first year.Australian rider Luke Tuckwell certainly wasn't heading into his first year as a professional without eyes on him, his second place overall at the Giro d'Italia Next Gen and top 10 at Tour de l'Avenir in 2025 made sure of that. He started the year at home at the Santos Tour Down Under, where he came fourth in the youth classification, and then as the season built so did the results. At the Tour de Romandie, Tuckwell delivered his first WorldTour overall top 10, taking sixth among a strong field led by none other than Tadej Pogačar. That was impressive by itself, but it also opened up another opportunity, as it led to the decision to send the Australian to the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes. That's when an already great season as a first year professional turned into a phenomenal one. After a solid start to the race, stage 6 delivered an opportunity that Tuckwell wasn't going to let slip through his fingers. A huge break got away, with Tuckwell part of it, and while he helped his teammate Maxim Van Gils claim the stage win the Australian also finished third with a margin that comfortably shifted the rider up from twelfth overall to the very top spot.It was a step up from the UAE Development Team for Federica Venturelli in 2026 straight into the world's top team, and while track was still a focus – which delivered plenty of success – there was no hiding in the peloton on the road. The Italian's very first race of the season was the 1.Pro Clásica de Almeria in late February and she went straight to the top step of the podium with a winning sprint from a reduced group of six.There was then another victory at Dwars door de Westhoek in June, quickly followed by a second place in the opening stage of the Tour Féminin International des Pyrénées. At the end of three stages of racing she also walked away with the points classification. It's an impressive tally from just 16 days of racing as a professional and bodes well for what's to come when the all-rounder adds some more in 2027, particularly if the 2025 U23 European time trial champion manages to add some more races against the clock into the mix.It was Jakob Omrzel who beat Luke Tuckwell to the top spot at the Giro d'Italia Next Gen in 2025 and the 20-year-old also delivered strong GC results as he stepped into the a new tier. That began with sixth overall at the Tour of the Alps in April, a top 10 at the Tour de Hongrie, third at Tour of Slovenia.Then in the second half of the season it was time for the rider from Slovenia to take on his first Grand Tour, as the youngest rider at the Vuelta a España,and he did way more than just survive it. First there was a fourth place on the challenging uphill finish of stage 7. Then on stage 12 Omrzel got into a 30-man breakaway and then also rode away from it to cross the line solo and claim his first WorldTour win, and at a Grand Tour no less. In doing so he became the youngest Slovenian to win a Grand Tour stage, no small feat given this his compatriots in the peloton include Tadej Pogačar and Primož Roglič. Also in that moment he became the second youngest ever stage winner at the Vuelta, after Celestino Prieto who took his win in 1981. The rider who is signed with Bahrain Victorious through till the end of 2029 also walked away from the Spanish tour with second in the youth classification and seventh overall. Though, perhaps, more importantly he left his first Grand Tour having gathered experience and tested his limits, which look set to stretch to considerable heights through the years ahead.For Liv AlUla Jayco, there is plenty of pride wrapped up in the Australian summer, as it is the one time of the year when the nation's only Women's WorldTour Team gets to perform at home. There, too, is plenty of effort put into making the team is also taking the green and gold stripes of the national champions jersey back to Europe. Ruby Roseman-Gannon may have been the favourite from the squad to do just that, but Mackenzie Coupland, who had just stepped up from the Liv AlUla Jayco development squad at the start of the year turned out to be the one to claim the jersey after making a late move that stuck.That meant a neo-pro year in the distinctive national champions kit for the first year professional, a big enough achievement on its own delivered in one of her very first races with the Women's WorldTour team. She was also the squad's top finisher at the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race later that month, narrowly missing the podium with fourth and then in March, joined the development squad for a race and claimed a stage and the overall victory at Vuelta a Extremadura Femenina. A third place at La Périgord Ladies when then followed up with a spot on the Tour de France Femmes squad and a strong fourth at Chrono Féminin de Gatineau to help round out a first year in the professional peloton for the 21 year old. After starting with such a strong opening round in Australia in 2026, there is no doubt there will be plenty of eyes on her to see what she can deliver in round two in 2027.There was no shortage of focus on Jarno Widar in 2026 as he stepped up to the Lotto Intermarché WorldTour team from the development squad, having won the Kristallen Fiets young talent of the year award for a second year running plus delivered results that included victory at Liège–Bastogne–Liège U23, stage wins in the Giro NextGen and the Tour de l’Avenir as well as the European U23 road race title. It was a results list that meant he was ushered into the team with considerable fanfare, with the expectation that he would be doing far more than learning the ropes but would be supported to chase key results, in fact the 20-year-old even entered his first Grand Tour, the Vuelta a España, as team leader.The first half of the season had its challenges, with illness and lingering knee injury keeping him away from racing for 16 weeks, though he made a solid mark soon after his return with fourth on the final stage of Tour de Suisse. He then upped the ante in his Vuelta debut, coming second on stage 4 behind Tadej Pogačar. There was also a fourth on stage 13 of the Spanish Grand Tour.It was, however, the closing month of 2026 when Widar stepped up to deliver on the promise and to the top step, with a win Tre Valli Varesine and then his first WorldTour stage victory in the final day of racing at the Tour of Guangxi, which also clinched him the overall win. Those strong closing weeks are bound to help make the challenges of the early season feel like a distant memory and set the rider up as a focal point for the team in 2027, a year where the squad will be losing its former great hope, Arnaud De Lie.Lauren Dickson is another of the later entries to cycling, initially finding her way into the sport via triathlons but only a couple of years after her first race finding a spot on one of the world's top teams, FDJ United-Suez. It may have been a fast progression but there could be little doubting that the British rider who turned 26 this year was ready for it.Less than three months into her professional racing career and she already managed to find her way onto the podium the Spanish 2.1 ranked race, the Vuelta a Extremadura Femenina, when Dickson snared second behind new Australian champion Mackenzie Coupland on stage 3 and also second overall. Impressively she then also followed that up with podiums in the Women's WorldTour race of Itzulia Women, where her third place on stage 3 once again also secured her the final spot on the overall podium. Then it was fourth at Durango-Durango Emakumeen Saria and 11th overall at the Giro d'Italia. There was another second on stage 1 of the Tour de Suisse Women, though her run was halted by a broken collarbone later in the race. Still the momentum was recaptured later in the season and she moved up to the top step at the Faun Tour. The late season win will make sure that even though she may be a new rider at one of the world's top teams, there will be no disappearing into the background when plans for 2027 are being formulated. Brady Gilmore succinctly summed up his year at the top level of the sport in a social media post as "a season I'll never forget" with "a lot to be proud of". He may not have entered his neo-pro season with quite the same fanfare as some of the others on the list but with multiple wins while racing with the development team, including two Volta a Portugal em Bicicleta stage victories and a Circuit des Ardennes stage and overall win, there was plenty of reason for optimism that he could make some kind of impression in his first season with the NSN Cycling WorldTour squad. There was certainly no waiting around, as he did just that in his very first races with the squad, twice missing the podium by just one spot on stage 4 and stage 5 of the Tour Down Under and then landing on it with a third at the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race. It wasn't long then until he found the top step, beating Dorian Godon and Remco Evenepoel over the line in a reduced group sprint on the final stage of Volta a Catalunya. From there the top tens continued to roll in through the season. Given the home performance at the start of 2026 as Gilmore was just integrating with the team, it will be intriguing to see just what the 25-year-old can deliver if we see him on the start line again for the Australian summer season in 2027. Talia Appleton had well and truly proven her ability in Australia and beyond in 2025, claiming a number of victories across the top-tier domestic series, the ProVelo Super League and also coming second overall, plus also stepping up to the podium on three stages and in the overall of the Tour de l'Avenir. It was a season that earnt the rider a place in the Liv AlUla Jayco development squad for 2026, but she quickly proved that she was capable of even more. An early season run of results that saw her take seventh at both the GP de Chambéry and the Clásica de Almería as well as third overall at Vuelta a Extremadura meant by May she had been promoted to the WorldTour team. Once there the solid results continued to flow, with the 20-year-old consistently near the front section of the field despite the then 20-year-old rider's very recent introduction to it. Regularly a top five performer in the youth classification, and also finishing 14th overall at the Tour de Suisse, Appleton also broke through with her first professional win in June, making the most of her climbing strength to claim the 1.1 ranked Alpes Gresivaudan Classic. With that win and a results list through the season that paints a picture of consistency and strength, the rider from Victoria not only clearly justified the fast track to the Women's WorldTour team, but delivered more than a small hint of her GC potential.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: 'I felt the bone snap' - Hannah Otto survives 40% gradients, snowy summit and fracture to set epic one-day Kilimanjaro summit record
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Hannah Otto (Scott Sports) added another endurance record to her resume on Wednesday, this one to an elevation of 19,300 feet above sea level. On November 4, she completed a Fastest Known Time (FKT) with Beyond the Summit: Kilimanjaro for World Bike Relief, becoming the first woman to use a mountain bike to summit Mount Kilimanjaro and descend in one day. Her effort on the highest mountain in Africa almost came to an abrupt end with two miles to go, when she slipped in some mud and broke her tibia. She was able to remount her bike and pedal with one leg to complete the journey, a film crew nearby capturing the effort for a future film, though she refused assistance so the record would count, recorded as 'one day' for the FKT since it was a mark."Kilimanjaro FKT!! Mission accomplished! Dream come true! The first known woman to climb and descend Kilimanjaro in one day by bicycle," she posted to Instagram one day ago."From the dark hours of the early morning and listening to the monkeys scream at me in the rainforest to steep pitches over 40% gradients, to scrambling over rocks with a bike on my back, to a 19,300-foot [5895 metre] summit covered in snow this was the best experience of my entire life and also the hardest thing I’ve ever done. "As if it wasn’t hard enough, with two miles to go I had a small crash. It was simple, just sliding out in some mud. But my foot got caught and I felt the bone snap. I laid in the mud feeling my dreams slip away, and that felt more painful than any broken bone. I crawled to my bike, used it as a crutch, and finished the final two miles pedaling with one leg to the finish. "X-rays show a broken tibia. I think this shows that a dream may just be the most powerful thing in the world."After an assessment at hospital in Tanzania, Otto told that she travel back to the US immediately for medical attention to repair a proximal tibia fracture."I was advised to fly home for further care and examination. I’m heading home from Africa today [Friday]. I have a consult with a surgeon on Tuesday and I’ll have more information then."The Utah-based mountain bike specialist completed her fifth season as part of the Life Time Grand Prix two weeks before making the trip to Africa. She ended her run of four consecutive seasons in the top 10, missing the mark by just three points for 11th overall. Her best race finishes in the series this year were third at Little Sugar MTB and eighth at Leadville Trail 100 MTB, a race she won in 2022.Otto has accumulated an eye-popping collection of FKTs, which she also uses as training for her endurance off-road racing. Last fall she set a new FKT for women on Mauna Kea, riding the 55-mile (88.5km) mountain road with 13,700 feet (4,175 metres) of climbing in Hawaii in 5 hours, 43 minutes and 50 seconds. She also has a trio of FKT records in high terrain US desert routes - Kokopelli Train, White Rim and Whole Enchilada.While only 26.5 miles in distance (42.6km) in Tanzania, the main obstacle was elevation gain across the dormant volcano. The summit is just above 19,300 feet (5,895 metres) with five climate zones crossed from top to bottom. Several days prior to her solo FKT, Otto made an initial ascent with a group and local crew, including a lead guide who had summited Kilimanjaro over 180 times. The 'first' summit was made on November 1."The entire crew made it to the top to celebrate this momentous moment together. Now we descend all the way back to the bottom and I’ll attempt to summit in just one day on November 3rd," she wrote on her social diary."After seeing this whole mountain piece by piece, it scares me. Things can change in an instant and the only constant is inconsistency. But that’s the entire point. I’m diving into the fear, I’m believing despite not knowing. I hope what anyone takes away from this attempt is the bravery to try without promise. We’re almost at $60K raised for World Bicycle Relief via The Intrepid Foundation!"She said she realised her power on the bike would drop at the higher altitude, so she was keeping a close watch on her heart rate. "Instead of tracking miles I'm tracking elevation climbed."Clad in a heavy coat, lined gloves and her helmet, Otto smiled for a photo when she was able to dismount and sit on the rock wall at the top of the mountain with a bright blue sky shining above. "This film will be absolutely epic; that I’m sure of," Otto posted. The date of the film release is yet to be announced.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Superprestige Middelkerke: Joran Wysure steals the win as Michael Vanthourenhout has heated run-in with Cameron Mason
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: Joran Wysure (Corendon-Crelan) claimed the victory in the nighttime Superprestige Middelkerke, overcoming a series of mishaps to take the high-speed race ahead of series leader Michael Vanthourenhout (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw). Kevin Kuhn (Heizomat Cube) finished a close third.The race wasn't without drama, as Cameron Mason (777tv) had a late run-in with Vanthourenhout and endured an earful from the Belgian after the race.On lap eight of 10, Vanthourenhout tried to keep Mason from passing in a turn before the sand pit, bumping Mason in the shoulder. But he paid for his aggression, losing his balance in the off-camber and losing a few positions. The incident hardly affected the results.The nighttime Superprestige Middelkerke started with a full field under the lights with Maes Hendrikx (Bomba Join) getting the quickest start when the lights turned green, but he was tailed closely by Vanthourenhout heading into the first corner.Now the series leader, Vanthourenhout is a top contender for the European championships and was keen to get a top result, but held back in the early laps to save his energy for Sunday.A crash disrupted the back of the field but at the front, it was Vanthourenhout's teammate Gerben Kuypers who took charge of setting the pace in the first laps. The pace and the numerous short, sharp climbs and technical turns steadily whittled down the number of riders in the leading group, even though there were no major attacks.Mason took the lead heading into the fifth lap, and his pace made Kuypers suffer. Vanthourenhout took to the front on lap six to let his teammate rejoin, but a surge from Wysure broke things up again but a mistake in the barriers knocked him out of the lead group.On lap eight, Wysure was still pushing the pace when Vanthourenhout ran into Mason and lost touch with the leading group briefly. Then, it was Mason's turn to tumble on the barriers, but he was quickly back up and riding, and on Vanthourenhout's wheel.Wysure led at the start of the penultimate lap, with Kuhn, and Jente Michels (Alpecin-Premier Tech) in pursuit. Vanthourenhout found Kuypers again and latched onto Michels' wheel with Mason just behind.The evening dew caused mayhem again as Wysure slid out in a greasy turn and his spill allowed Kuhn to join him, and it wasn't long before the rest of the chasers were in contact. Kuhn surged into the lead, gaining a second over Wysure who was rattled by the barriers. Kuhn crossed the line at the bell with Wysure and Vanthourenhout on his wheel.The Corendon-Crelan rider managed to get to the lead, wanting the freedom to pick his own lines and set the pace. He used the downhill sections to gain a few seconds, but Vanthourenhout was on the hunt. Wysure overcame his mental block and cleared the barriers cleanly, he passed the greasy corner without slipping and went into the final stretch with enough of a lead to win the race without a challenge.Joran Wyseure (Bel) Crelan - CorendonMichael Vanthourenhout (Bel) Pauwels Sauzen - Altez IndustriebouwKevin Kuhn (Swi) Heizomat - CubeCameron Mason (GBr) 777TV CX TeamJente Michels (Bel) Alpecin - Premier TechGerben Kuypers (Bel) Pauwels Sauzen - Altez IndustriebouwNiels Vandeputte (Bel) Alpecin - Premier TechVictor Van De Putte (Bel) Charles Liégeois CX TeamMees Hendrikx (Ned) Team Bomba JOINJarno Bellens (Bel) Baloise Verzekeringen - Het Poetsbureau LionsLaurens Sweeck (Bel) Crelan - CorendonToon Vandebosch (Bel) Crelan - CorendonAnton Ferdinande (Bel) Pauwels Sauzen - Altez IndustriebouwArne Baers (Bel) Baloise Verzekeringen - Het Poetsbureau LionsKay De Bruyckere (Bel) Pauwels Sauzen - Altez IndustriebouwUgo Ananie (Fra) Team CX TPMLoic Vanlaere (Bel) Pauwels Sauzen - Altez IndustriebouwLukas Herrmann (Ger) Heizomat - CubeTibo Vancompernolle (Bel)Lorenzo Marasco (Fra) Sebmotobikes CX TeamDeclan Oldham (GBr) Hope Factory RacingMartynas Medelinskas (Ltu)

item.title: Hamilton backs claims Leclerc races him harder than F1 rivals
Superprestige Middelkerke: Aniek van Alphen puts in dominant performance ahead of European Championships
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: Aniek van Alphen (777tv) pulled off her first victory of the season in the nighttime Superprestige in Middelkerke, soloing away from the field on the second lap and maintaining a strong advantage to the finish. The result signalled she will be a strong competitor at the upcoming European Championships in Zeddam on Saturday.Defending European champion Inge van der Heijden (Crelan-Corendon) couldn't chip away at Van Alphen's lead after missing the attack as she was caught in traffic in the early laps. However, she held on for second place, conserving her energy after distancing Denise Betsema (De Ceuster Bouwkranen), who bobbled in the final lap and had to settle for third.The nighttime round of the Superprestige had a small women's field with the European Championships just two days away. While the race was missing top rider Lucinda Brand, 27 women toed the line under the bright lights in Middelkerke.After following closely as Hélène Clauzel (777tv) took the hole shot, Defending champion Amandine Fouquenet (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw) remained at the head of the race for the first lap.But on the next one, she bobbled on one of the many short, steep climbs and had to chase Van Alphen, who opened up a lead of six seconds at the start of lap three.Fouquenet continued to fade as European champion Van der Heijden caught Clauzel and set off in pursuit of Van Alphen. Betsema latched on during the fourth lap to form a three-rider chase.Clauzel began to struggle, losing touch with Van der Heijden and Betsema, and by the end of lap four, the European champion was 10 seconds behind, with Betsema just ahead of Clauzel at 15 seconds by the start of the fifth lap.It was Van der Heijden and Betsema chasing together with two laps to go, with a 14-second deficit to Van Alphen, with Clauzel and Fouquenet further behind.Betsema surged on lap six, bringing the gap to the leader down to ten seconds but Van Alphen matched her acceleration and extended her lead on the sinuous second half of the circuit and started the final lap with 16 seconds over the two chasers.Aniek Van Alphen (Ned) 777TV CX TeamInge Van Der Heijden (Ned) Crelan - CorendonDenise Betsema De Ceuster BouwkranenHélène Clauzel (Fra) 777TV CX TeamAmandine Fouquenet Pauwels Sauzen - Altez IndustriebouwLeonie Bentveld (Ned) Pauwels Sauzen - Altez IndustriebouwRebecca Gariboldi De Ceuster BouwkranenJulie Brouwers (Bel) Charles Liégeois CX TeamAnnemarie Worst Baloise Verzekeringen - Het Poetsbureau LionsPuck Langenbarg (Ned) Fenix - Premier TechLauren Molengraaf (Ned) 777TV CX Team

item.title: Israel’s Herzog yet to decide on who should form government as Eisenkot secures significant backing
item.author: Jason Burke International security correspondent and agencies
item.content:encoded: President says he will make a decision on Sunday about who should try to build a government as Netanyahu rival is endorsed by 67 lawmakers Gadi Eisenkot, the main rival to Benjamin Netanyahu, secured endorsements on Thursday from a majority of lawmakers to try to form a government but Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was still unclear who could break the deadlock and that he would decide on Sunday which of the two men should try first.Of the Knesset’s 120 elected lawmakers, 67 had ​endorsed Eisenkot through several days of talks with Herzog, while 46 endorsed Netanyahu. Herzog said on Thursday that while the “results ‌of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the ‌best shot to form a government.Continue reading...

item.title: 'Purely from results, I'd say it definitely wasn't good'– Geraint Thomas admits challenging season for Netcompany Ineos
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: In a partial review of Netcompany Ineos' season, team Director of Racing Geraint Thomas conceded that 2026 "definitely wasn't good" from a results standpoint, although he did point out several positive aspects of the year.Speaking with Decathlon CMA CGM Directeur Sportif Luke Rowe on the podcast, Thomas accepted that the team was a long way from where it once was when he, Chris Froome, and Bradley Wiggins were dominating Grand Tours. However, he pointed out several of the team's successes as they look to progress to their former dominant position."People have kind of said, 'oh, you know, you can say was our season good or bad?' And purely from results, I'd say it definitely wasn't good," Thomas said."I feel like Dorian [Godon], Oscar [Onley], and Kévin [Vauquelin] are all new to the team and that takes a bit of gelling. I think the fact that they executed is a big plus. I think they all learned then the next phase of that plan. And I think they'll all take that forward, and it's part of that growing."The three new additions were among Netcompany Ineos' highest performers in 2026. Godon was the team's top rider, winning seven times, including five stages across Paris-Nice, Volta a Catalunya, and Tour de Romandie.Vauquelin, meanwhile, won the Giro d'Abruzzo and took fourth at Paris-Nice, and Onley took a stage win and second overall at the Vuelta a Burgos before taking sixth overall and best young rider at the Vuelta a España. Thomas said the team was making progress, having "gone up the ladder a couple of steps" with their standout results."I think it's all learning and stuff as well, and even though results weren't particularly sensational, we had a lot of wins, but they were like smaller wins. It wasn't like any big wins, really," he said."It's all about that progression, and it's where you're starting from as well. This might be a headline now, but let's just say we're at 20% of what we used to be, to pick a number – you can't just go from 20 to 80 straight away."It's like climbing a ladder, isn't it? It's the same thing with a team, and I think we've gone up the ladder a couple of steps, for sure. We slipped a few times as well, but that's all part of it."Other standout performances of Ineos' season included Filippo Ganna's Dwars door Vlaanderen triumph and Thymen Arensman's ride to fourth place at the Giro d'Italia, his best-ever Grand Tour result."Great to see Pippo win Dwar Doors, the rest pretty flat, really. But it's kind of like that's what's always kind of been with our team as well, isn't it?" Thomas said, summing up the Classics season."[The Giro] was a bit more of a traditional sort of Grand Tour, wasn't it? Jonas was the outstanding favourite, but the way Visma rode was a bit more old school – controlling the harder days, and there was the race for the podium behind. Out of the three, it was a bit more kind of what you're used to."Thymen was 30, 40 seconds off the podium. I think it was a massive step forward if you just take him in isolation, from previous years. Just psychologically, a lot more consistent."He's done a lot of work with Steve Peters this year, and I think it definitely paid off, and the combination with his coach worked really well. It's the best Grand Tour result he's ever had. He was super consistent, there were no big standout mistakes, and I think that's a big positive for him."The team was set for something of an overhaul for the 2027 season, with Ganna among the notable names on the outgoing list as several promising younger riders come on board.Leading the list is the highly-rated junior world champion Benjamín Noval, who joins alongside fellow Spaniard Markel Beloki and former Tour de l'Avenir champion Joseph Blackmore. With 22 riders confirmed for 2027, there'll be more to come from Ineos in the transfer market before next season gets underway at the Tour Down Under.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Riders play nice at controversial MotoGP Qatar GP: 'Everything feels normal'
'It's about time' - BMC enter women's peloton with Basque Laboral Kutxa team partnership
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Swiss bike brand BMC are set to make their first foray into the women’s peloton for many years, partnering with a Spanish ProTeam, Laboral Kutxa-Fundación Euskadi.The deal, which is with the team’s Basque Country parent organisation Fundación Euskadi, will see the team not only riding their Teammachine SLR 01 frame sets, but also using their cockpits and wheels.BMC have been a presence in the men’s peloton for some years, and currently provide bikes to the Tudor Pro Cycling Team. Before that, they worked with AG2R Citroën, Dimension Data, CCC and, obviously BMC Racing. However, they have not worked with a women’s team since at least the creation of the UCI Women’s WorldTour in 2016.The company recently teased the partnership with a press release, saying "it’s about time we saw BMC bikes in both the men’s and Women’s Grand Tours," and the partnership has now been announced. As Laboral are one of the sport’s second-tier ProTeams, they have realised their desire to be present at the biggest women’s stage races."This partnership represents an exciting new chapter for BMC," said BMC’s head of marketing, David Heine. "As one of the brands that supported women's cycling early on, we are proud to return to the highest level of the sport with Laboral Kutxa-Fundación Euskadi. "Women’s racing is thrilling, inspiring, dynamic, and growing rapidly worldwide. We look forward to supporting the team with our performance-driven bikes and proudly cheering for the riders throughout the season."Laboral Kutxa have been riding at UCI level since 2020, starting life as Continental level team before moving up to ProTeam in 2025. During the 2026 season they rode Chinese XDS bikes and Shimano groupsets, it is not yet known whether Shimano will remain on board. The president of Fundación Euskadi, Iñaki Isasi, is rightfully pleased with the partnership. "Their technical standards and culture of performance correspond to the ambitions of Laboral Kutxa-Fundación Euskadi. This support allows us to approach the season with confidence and continue to grow our women's team at the highest level."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down.
