item.title: Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro review: A modern aero package but it badly needs a change of seatpost
item.author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
item.content:encoded: 7.3kg(cages, no pedals or computer mount) SRAM Red, Shimano Dura-Ace, Ultegra Scope x Atten Artech 6.A+We first saw the new Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro back in August 2025 for a wind tunnel test when we had a paintless, lacquerless, menacing looking thing that seemed fresh off the factory floor. It was somewhat overshadowed that day by us also having a prototype version of the Factor ONE in the tunnel (yes, we were very smug), but nevertheless it caused enough of a stir at the time and hence to have at least piqued my interest. Fastforward a year, and in order to review it properly, I took it on an extended trip home to Cornwall to see my family, where I sniffed out some familiar roads to calm my soul on the clifftops, and a few fresh sections to hunt out rare flat roads, where it does tend to shine. It is a fabulous place to ride, but absolutely murderous if you want an easy day out. Reviewing it as I did straight after hopping off the fabulous Look 795 Blade RS - to be published in the coming days - left it with a tough act to follow, and one it didn’t quite manage to live up to. It certainly isn’t without merit though, and while I don’t necessarily think it’s quite up there with the absolute cream of the best road bikes (or indeed the best aero road bikes), it is certainly a good bicycle, and may well suit your tastes more than it does mine. Ultimately the front end felt a little languid for my tastes, but more presingly the combination of a slack-ish seat tube angle and a 20mm setback seat post stuck me in what felt like a rather old school position out of step with the modern era. As always, let's tackle the subjective subject of how the thing looks first; I’m a fan. It manages to toe the line of looking hyper-modern without going absolutely bananas like the Factor ONE, with clear cues from TT bike design. Those hefty, extremely dropped seat stays would be just at home on the brand’s triathlon machines. Ridley also helped everyone out by normalising massive headtubes with the Noah Fast 3.0, something the Nitrogen Pro has up front to go with a relatively wide-set fork that’ll handle 34mm as measured tyres, which is a capacity matched at the back end. While it can handle a 34 it comes with 30c Vittoria Corsa Pros on Scope Artech 6.A wheels, but not the standard set that I had the pleasure of riding on the Look Blade; these are a collaboration with Scope and Atten, Argon’s in-house componentry brand, and the extremely fast wheels have been reshaped to better suit the 30mm tyres and to better interact with the frameset, all while keeping the Scope hubs and that eye-catching fish scale texture. In reality they feel no different to the standard Artechs, but it is heartening to know they’ve at least been optimised to this machine in particular. Back up front and you get the same CHB-01 cockpit as is found on the brand’s Anti Matter aero gravel bike that my colleague Tom loved so much. This you can spec when you buy it in either a 36cm or a 38cm width, and with a choice of stem lengths from 80-130mm at no extra charge. What you cannot do is spec a zero offset seatpost, which is something I believe you should not only to do but also something you do. I’ll go into the why in a sec, but if you do want to do this it’ll cost you a cool £225.Geometrically I do want to start at the back end. The seat post is pretty set back; 1 full degree slacker than the Look Blade. This is compounded by having a full 20mm setback seatpost, rather than a 13mm on the Look. It is the same as on a Tarmac however, though again with a less severe seatpost setback from Specialized. Without boring you too much with maths, for my saddle height a 1 degree change in seat tube angle (STA) equates to roughly 13mm of increased saddle setback. Add in the 7mm differential in the seat posts and the Argon puts me a full 20mm further behind the BB; potentially manageable if you run your saddle in the middle of the rails but as someone who has theirs slammed forwards I would have needed a costly swap. This is all compared to somewhat ‘normal’ geometry bikes. The seat tube angle is 1.5 degrees slacker than a progressive Ridley Noah, and a full three degrees slacker than the Factor ONE, though these are a lot more radical and not everyday machines. Before I jump two-footed into the aerodynamics, it’s worth remembering the Nitrogen comes in two guises; the Pro, which I have with a lighter, stiffer carbon layup and more pricey build options, and the standard model with lower tier components and carbon, but ultimately the same aerodynamic shape. With a rider on, at the time of testing it proved to be reasonably fast. Since then, though, we have been fortunate enough to test a load of other new releases, and it isn’t quite as fast as many of them, now sitting around ⅔ of the way down our power rankings of road bikes. While you should obviously read all of our wind tunnel content, and the one pertaining to the test in which the Nitrogen Pro was included, it’s worth bearing in mind that while ‘bottom third’ sounds bad, it is only shipping 7.5 watts to a Cervélo S5 in reality. If you need every watt then this may be of concern to you, but it’s perfectly plausible you could make this up elsewhere, though you could also make up that deficit elsewhere have a faster bike. It’s easy to perhaps look at ‘bottom third in the wind tunnel rankings’ and conclude that this is a slow bike, but it isn’t really. Seven and a half watts is measurable, though only barely perceptible, and on the flats the Nitrogen Pro feels very much at home once you settle into a decent position, though as with so much of the performance of the machine the thing that seems to be holding it back is mostly down to the position it puts you in. Having a relatively slack seat tube angle combined with a 20mm setback post means you do feel like you’re hanging off the back of the bike. On the flats, while the bike is certainly aero enough, it lacks that feeling of efficiency that comes with being more over the front of the bike. My hips felt impinged, and more than anything else it just felt quite old school. On the flat it lacked that feeling of biomechanical efficiency (though it felt aerodynamically so), and on the climbs where your weight is naturally going to be further back I felt I had to spend more time on the tops than in the hoods just because that’s where my weight fell. When out of the saddle, either on climbs or in a sprint, these problems dissipated immediately, but that isn’t a sustainable solution. A shorter stem may have helped a touch, but only in terms of the overall reach and not what’s going on at the hips. Basically it needs a zero offset seatpost, and I think you should factor it into the cost of the machine. I don’t think I’m alone; I did a basic straw poll (Instagram stalk) of Argon sponsored athletes. Chris Hall, Rasmus Bøgh Wallin, Linus Østdal, and the riders from Team Cranks appear to be on zero setback posts. It isn’t exclusive, and some other athletes weren’t, but from what I can see from a brief search it seems the majority are opting for the option to get them over the front of the bike. Up front I found the fact my weight was off the back more than I’d like, combined with a slacker head tube angle (0.8º slacker than Tarmac, for example) meant the front end felt a little more languid and slow than I’d like, particularly at slow speeds. Moreover, being over the back means less weight over the front wheel, meaning reduced front end grip. This is, again, solvable with a costly seatpost swap, though only to a point; the head angle ain’t going to change. That being said, if you want a road bike that errs towards stability rather than waspish agility then this could well be a machine for you. On the twisty lanes of Cornwall I often found myself wishing I was on something a little more reactive, but on the flip side if you relish longer, steadier efforts on flat or rolling terrain (once you lock the position in) I think this would be a very decent machine. At 7.5kg in this spec it’s not a superlight hillclimb machine but there’s a lot of carbon in the frame, forks and in those deep Scope wheels. It doesn’t have the immediacy of acceleration on steeper gradients that you get with bikes around the UCI weight limit (or below), but it’s also not absolutely leaden either. Certainly one more for fast, rolling terrain but if anyone tells me they can’t bear to ride a 7.5kg machine in the mountains I will tell them to go and touch some grass. Sprints… now we’re talking. That super-compact rear triangle with large, boxy stays in combination with a bottom bracket shell that’s tall enough to sit proud of the outer front chainring just gobble up high wattage efforts and there’s no concerning play in the cockpit at all. I’d have like the tops to sweep forward a little sooner; the right angle transition is quite sharp and can sometimes leave your forearms contacting the bars when you're sprinting in the drops, particularly uphill, but it’s a minor quibble, and not something I cared too much about while bagging a few local, extremely low hanging ego-massaging KOMs.The Nitrogen Pro, in this spec at least, is a funny old beast from a value perspective and is a little like the Force-equipped Factor Elara I reviewed recently. Everything besides the groupset is top drawer and as you would get on the best-of-the-best model, so you can look at it two ways: either you’re getting basically the performance of a £12,500 bike for £9,500 ($10,499), where a saving of three thousand pounds to Dura-Ace is significant, or you can look at it as £9.5k being a lot for an Ultegra-spec bike. An Ultegra Specialized Tarmac (not the S-Works, which this ‘Pro’ Nitrogen is more akin to) is £3.5k cheaper, but has less fizzy wheels, a separate cockpit, and it doesn’t say S-Works on the downtube. Personally I actually like this new trend of top tier bikes but with a downrated groupset. Aside from weight, Ultegra is basically indistinguishable from Dura-Ace and Force is essentially the same as Red so it saves a huge wad of cash for a negligible performance hit. Setback seatpost aside, as this is a problem that I think can be alleviated at a small cost, I think it accounts for itself reasonably well. Extremely fast wheels tuned to the frame and tyres, which themselves are a modern 30c width and not a cheaper option to bring the price down. A decent cockpit, and a stiff package that is pretty aerodynamic in the grand scheme of things, even if it isn’t world beating. As tested I think there’s a lot to be positive about with the Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro. It’s stiff, an excellent sprinter, and while the handling isn’t lively enough for my liking it is certainly acceptable if you prefer something a little more stable and forgiving rather than hair raising and spicy. I think it’s a bike that, with a change of seatpost that I think is more of a necessity than an option despite the added cost, would be a fine mile munching fast bike for rolling and flat terrain. I think if you’re looking for something of a do-it-all fast bike then you will perhaps have a better time with something with more of an all-rounder feel.Looks good. Under the space age looks there isn't a great deal groundbreaking going on however, but neither is there anything crazy and superfluous. Just a groupset away from top spec. Own brand Scopes are fun, that's for sure. Perfectly acceptable for a chunky aero bike with big wheels.The aero is decent in the grand scheme of things, though not world beating, but the geometry has too many implications for me to have truly fallen in love with the thing. Top tier but with a step down in groupset can be viewed a couple of ways. I think it's a good entry point into superbike performance, but it's not an absolute bargain. Also you have to buy a new seatpost if you want an inline.

item.title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections

item.content:encoded: Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cutsThe African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. item.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I’m a little excited that we’re struggling’
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: New York hosts the 1-6 Bulls tonight for their second game in a week after beating them last Wednesday.Chicago is not a team the Knicks should be too worried about, but hey, this is a matchup between sub-.500 teams, so who knows what will happen then and there.Here’s some of what we heard from the Knicks heading into today’s game.On a mediocre start to the season:“Everything can get better… I’m not pissed about the start or upset about the start. There’s a part of me… I’m a little excited that we’re struggling. I want to see if we, right now, can figure it out.“When you go through the offseason that we went through, everybody celebrates you the way that this lovely city did and the fans of the New York Knicks did, you want to be shaken and brought back to earth right away when the season starts because that grounds you.“Right now, because we’re not playing our best basketball, we’re seeing some of the challenges that we need to work on. Right now we could be winning games, but it could be false reality.”On Jalen Brunson’s early-season shooting struggles:“He’s taking the same shots as in the past. In my opinion, he’s just missing shots. He’s taking the right shots. I think all our guys are, for the most part, taking the right shots. Right now, they’re not going in. And that can be for this reason, that reason, I don’t know, and I’m not going to try to overanalyze it. As long as they keep taking the right shots, keep working on the shots, I think eventually they’re gonna fall sooner than later.”On the NBA’s best shooters’ slumps:“It happens. It happens to the best of them because everybody is definitely human and every human has their ups and their downs when it comes to shooting. That’s why we have to keep embracing the little things, because they’re not gonna always fall.”On Landry Shamet’s natural ability to create opportunities through off-ball movement:“You could drill it, and guys will pick up on it, but you can tell (Shamet) is a natural with it.”On the explanation for his unusually poor shooting percentages to start the season:“Missing shots. I normally make.”On whether his offseason wrist surgery has affected his shooting:On Landry Shamet’s ability to create defensive closeouts:“He creates great closeouts, whether he’s shooting or catching. He has a good knack for it.“It’s just how he operates. He just finds the right windows, whether it’s benefiting him or someone else.”On Jordan Clarkson’s role:“He has a professionalism about it. For a person who is willing to do that — he makes our team better. Great person, great teammate. Off the court, he’s a great dude and someone I enjoy being around.”On why the Knicks’ defense has been ahead of their offense early in the season:“We have great coaches. [Brendan O’Connor] and [Darren Erman], they do a great job indicating to us what we need to be doing on the court, and then guys are executing defensively and we’re getting stops. That’s always our goal.“We don’t think about it. Even when you said that, I didn’t think about it. There’s always room for improvement though, so always striving for better.”On the Knicks finally increasing their pace:“We finally played fast. We’ve been playing very slow, very stagnant. We finally got out, we ran.”On the champion Knicks remaining a work in progress:“It’s early in the season. I think everything’s a work in progress. Last year, I feel like we probably hit our best stride in the playoffs. So we were a work in progress the whole year. That’s the nature of the NBA season. You gotta keep getting better each and every day, each and every game, and be ready to go.”On the Knicks’ dissatisfaction with their start to the season:“I just think we’ve got to win, and I think it’s still early in the season, and I don’t think anybody in this locker room is satisfied with where we’re at. Happy to be in the win column tonight, but, you know, to point to 10 things offensively and defensively that we need to improve on. So the good news is there’s no panic there. Some nights right now, it might be the offense ahead of the defense and vice versa. We’ve had a hard time making shots so far early in the season. Tonight a few went in, but then we had some slippage defensively. So, a little give and take, but luckily that’s not the point. The point is for us to continue to get better and we’ll continue to do that.”On Mike Brown holding the Knicks accountable and not allowing the Nets win to disguise their problems:“We have to be real with ourselves. And Mike’s great with that, assesses things in film, calls it as it is. Our group’s great with that. We all understand that by no means — we’re not taking this as any potential fool’s gold. The whole goal right now is to continue to get better, and we want to do that. So that’s the thought process.”On learning to move without the basketball by playing three-on-three without dribbling as a child:“I remember growing up playing full-court three-on-three with no dribble, so you just learn how to move without the ball. I’m lucky I had that implemented for me at a young age. I wish more kids and hope more kids would do that moving forward in today’s game. I think it really helps you learn how to play and understand how to move and get open. So, it’s kinda always been something I’ve tried to continue to get better at.”

item.title: Tadej Pogačar's race-ridden Colnago and Brandon McNulty's rainbow jersey up for grabs in auction raising funds for US cyclists ahead of LA 2028 Olympics
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: The USA Cycling Foundation's annual auction goes live on Wednesday, with Tadej Pogačar's race-ridden Colnago, signed rainbow jerseys, and and rides with pros amongst the items up for sale to raise money for American cyclists.Now in its fifth year, the online auction – which is open to anyone around the world – raises money to support US Olympic and Paralympic cyclists, with the upcoming Olympic Games in Los Angeles in 2028 making fundraising especially important this year. In the US, Olympic athletes do not receive any government funding.The first items will go live on Wednesday, November 4 with the auction running through to Monday, November 9, and 99 items up for auction in total.Topping the list in terms of value and intrigue is undoubtedly Tadej Pogačar's world champion edition Colnago V5Rs which he rode to victory at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2025. Donated by Colnago, the bike is valued at $80,000 and will go live on Friday with a starting bid of $25,000. There's plenty of other pro memorabilia up for grabs, including signed rainbow jerseys from Brandon McNulty and Ashlin Barry, Tejay Van Garderen's white jersey from the 2012 Tour de France, and more from Demi Vollering, Enric Mas and Kate Courtney. There are a number of money-can't-buy experiences included in the auction, such as rides with Keegan Swenson, Christopher Blevins and Alexey Vermeulen, plus several bikes, kit, helmets, and gift cards, as well as guaranteed entries to many of the biggest US gravel events, and even an entry to the Étape du Tour in 2027.Supporters can also bid on plenty of non-cycling items, including sports and concert tickets, holidays and hotel stays, and food and drink. Starting bids start at as little as a dollar with hopes of raising potentially hundreds of thousands of dollars for US cyclists. "Our athletes are proof of what private support can do," said Molly Pickall, the USA Cycling Foundation's executive director. "In Paris, American women won every one of Team USA's Olympic cycling medals. LA28 is the first Summer Games on home soil since 1996, and we want to arrive with the strongest team we've ever fielded. This auction gives every fan, anywhere in the country, a way to be part of the Foundation that supports USA Cycling."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: The Giro d'Italia's most feared climb – A closer look at the mighty Monte Zoncolan ahead of its return in 2027
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: A modern icon of the Giro d'Italia will return for the 2027 race after six years out of the action: the Monte Zoncolan. The brute of the Carnic Alps, one of Italy's most fearsome climbs, and on its eighth appearance at the men's Giro, it will serve as the grand finale to the race for the maglia rosa on stage 20.It will be approached from the traditional Ovaro side in Friuli-Venezia Giulia, roughly 120km northwest of where the 110th Giro starts in Trieste, offering up an average gradient of 11.9% across the 10.1km to the summit as one of the sport's most savage double-digit beasts.Even worse than the average gradient, though, is what is hidden underneath the profile on paper – the steepest sections exceed 20%, where even the most elite climbers in the world can be made to look ordinary as they battle to survive, and the suffering barely repents as the road up to 1,750m ticks by. After an eye-opening 1.65 km at 9.1%, the riders are lulled into a false sense of security as they hit a tiny flat section between Liariis Piazza and Inizia Strada Zoncolan, but they will all know the worst is still to come, and this only brings the climb into the most difficult sector. The subsequent 4km are raced at a vicious average gradient of 15.3%, and it's here where the steepest pinches will be found, upwards of 22%, and the group will start to thin at a rapid rate as those unable to live with the tempo are forced to fight for cadence and position on the mountain. With several important mountain days already in the legs, whoever is in pink before Zoncolan will be hoping their gap is all but out of sight by this point, but race organisers RCS have opened the door to late drama as an off day could cause total capitulation.Anyone could falter on the section after the village in Liariis, but it doesn't get much easier from thereon out, with the next 3km still averaging 13.9% gradient, and the final 2km to the line – where the legs will already be empty and screaming – are taken on at 7.1% and 8.9% respectively. The riders will traverse through tunnels marking the final kilometre, having almost completed the narrow, often snow-lined in May and exposed roads overlooking the Gorto valley, arriving at the foot via 120km of mostly flat roads, and then two late warm-up ascents up the Passo Duron and Sella Valcalda.All the way up will be massive crowds roaring on the GC favourites and pushing those in the grupetto to survive the climb, which vies for the top spot when it comes to professional cycling's most difficult ascent alongside the Alto de l'Angliru and Passo del Mortirolo – which, in the 2027 Giro, the riders will have already tackled twice in the same day on stage 16. Emerging from the tunnels, the strongest competitors will still have a steep final run to the line to contend with, but by this point, it will be clear who is going to add their name to the short list of iconic winners atop the Zoncolan, and it will also be certain on stage 20 that the holder of the pink jersey after its 10.1km is completed will be the champion in Rome a day later. Lacking the same history as fellow Giro icons such as the Passo dello Stelvio and Blockhaus, the Zoncolan has established itself as a modern icon, with the list of winners in the men's race including Gilberto Simoni (twice, in 2003 and 2007), Ivan Basso (2010), Igor Anton (2011), Michael Rogers (2014), Chris Froome (2018), and most recently Lorenzo Fortunato (2021).The Zoncolan was first introduced to the Giro on stage 10 of the women's race in 1997, where Fabiana Luperini took victory. A legend of the Giro and the holder of the most titles in what was then called the Giro d'Italia Femminile, Luperini said there was "a lot of fear of a climb like the Zoncolan" and that "To win on a climb like the Monte Zoncolan is a great thing, so I feel proud of my victory there." Victory there propelled her towards the third of her five eventual titles.Six years later, it made its maiden appearance in the men's race, where Gilberto Simoni conquered the steep slopes en route to his second maglia rosa triumph in '03.However, on both occasions, the riders started the climb from the less steep and steadier side in Sutrio. It was from this side, too, that the Zoncolan last featured in the Giro in 2021, with Lorenzo Fortunato taking a stunning breakaway win in the fog and cold, as Egan Bernal extended his overall lead. Bernal's impressive performance saw him break Simoni's record from the Sutrio side by more than a minute, but it's the Ovaro side the Giro peloton will be concerned with in 2027, and it's here that the Italian still holds the record from his 2007 victory. Four years after its maiden ascent, the organisers introduced the steeper and now more traditional side to the Grand Tour, but it was Simoni who still emerged on top. By this point, he was 35 and sat fourth in GC, but alongside teammate Leonardo Piepoli and Andy Schleck, still had the climbing power to distance maglia rosa Danilo Di Luca on the steepest sections. Crossing the line alongside his fellow Saunier Duval teammate, Simoni and Piepoli hold the climbing record from Ovaro to Zoncolan to this day at 39:03.The stage profile for the 2027 race is similar to that from the 2010 edition, when Ivan Basso dropped everyone on the steep slopes and defeated World Champion Cadel Evans in the rainbow bands by more than a minute. Having started the day 7:43 off the lead, it served as a major gain in Basso's GC fightback against David Arroyo, taking back 3:50. He went on to complete the pursuit of pink four days later as he left Arroyo behind on the Mortirolo alongside teammate Vincenzo Nibali and Michele Scarponi en route to Aprica, where the latter won the stage, but Basso took hold of the maglia rosa. Returning a year later, the Zoncolan stage was marked by controversy and shortened, with the removal of the brutal Monte Crostis climb being announced to fans' disappointment the night before the race. A replacement climb was inserted up the Tualis, but the race route was eventually diverted to avoid the village where the volunteers protested against the judges’ decision.The drama didn't stop when the rider finally reached the Zoncolan either. Anton won the stage solo, attacking in the steepest sections, but the most important battle was happening around 30 seconds behind him between Alberto Contador and crowd favourite Vincenzo Nibali.Contador was booed by the vociferous fans, accusing him of playing a role in the Crostis' removal, and after he waited in Nibali's wheel and eventually dropped him in the final 500 metres, a move which the Italian described as showing "a lack of respect from him". Neither would end up as the overall winner of the 2011 Giro, though, despite Contador originally triumphing in pink, as he was stripped of his title in February 2012 for doping and Michele Scarponi was named the champion. When the Zoncolan returned in 2014, the stage was taken by the breakaway instead of the GC favourites, but this didn't mean it was without more controversy.On paper, it points to Michael Rogers riding away solo from the remnants of the early 20-man move, but he was actually locked into a close battle with Francesco Manuel Bongiorno until the final 3km. As Rogers took his hands off the bars several times to part the crazed fans in their thousands, it was the Italian rider who actually came undone by the actions of a supporter; a fan in a rainbow jersey's decision to try and push him forward in excitement led to the Bardiani rider unclipping and putting a foot down as Rogers powered away to the win. By this point on stage 20, Nairo Quintana already had the GC sewn up, comfortably defending his lead up the steep slopes of the Zoncolan. With it, he became the first Colombian to win the Giro d'Italia, and the first South American Grand Tour winner since compatriot Luis Herrera at the 1987 Vuelta. The most recent ascent up Zoncolan from Ovaro dates back to the 2018 race, when eventual winner Chris Froome attacked away 4.3km from the summit and held off a late charge from maglia rosa Simon Yates in the final few hundred metres. After a slow start at the Giro, Froome had started the day way down in 12th overall, jumping up seven spots to fifth with his exhibition on Zoncolan. Way down on his best, it looked somewhat like a consolation prize for the four-time Tour de France champion, but his best trick was still to come on the Colle delle Finestre four stages later, where Yates completely capitulated, and Froome's audacious 80km attack saw him move into pink at the last gasp with a second stage win.In the same season, Annemiek van Vleuten became the first and to date only woman to win a professional race atop Monte Zoncolan starting from the Ovaro side. Taking victory ahead of Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio, the Dutch star claimed the summit with a dominant solo victory en route to the first of her four pink jersey Giro titles.Who will join the list of winners in 2027, and what drama will come on the brutal steeps of the Monte Zoncolan? That will have to wait until stage 20 in May, but if history is anything to go by, the modern icon of the Giro d'Italia is just awaiting its next chapter. The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Turned up to 11 – The 2027 Giro d’Italia Women route is tough, but it risks producing a race without crucial jeopardy
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: The route of the 2027 Giro d’Italia Women was revealed on Tuesday and presents the peloton with a tough nine days of racing. With four mountain days, including an uphill time trial, and five flatter stages, it will be interesting, but it seems a little like an enhanced version of the 2026 race, won so brilliantly by Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ), with everything turned up to 11.Since taking over the organisation of the women’s Giro in 2024, RCS, which organises the men’s event, has done a good job in modernising and increasing the visibility of what remains the second biggest race in the women’s calendar. Of course, visibility was helped this year by the date change, which the previous organisation requested, but with the power of RCS behind it, the race has been to places and climbs it would otherwise have been unable to reach.However, despite that obvious progression, the 2027 race route is not a step forward, just much, much more of the same. The race has been made punishingly difficult, thus reducing the number of riders able to compete for the podium, and it could either be won on the first mountain top finish on stage 4, or we may be faced with a desultory stand-off, riders waiting for the final day. The 2027 Giro is, in fact, shorter than this year's edition, though not by much. Organisers have slated 1,132km, as opposed to last year’s 1,151, which was reduced from the original distance after the Colle delle Finestre stage was truncated for safety reasons.However, next year’s race includes a whopping 17,450m of vertical ascent, more than 5,000m more than 2026. And we all know by now that harder is not necessarily more entertaining.Of course, we don’t yet know whether Vollering will defend her title next year, but she has developed into the most outstanding stage racer of her generation, able to climb better than almost everyone, with the punch to create gaps and the engine to maintain them. With more climbing and the retention of the mountain TT from the 2026 race, the route plays into her hands, reducing, rather than increasing jeopardy.But it’s not about whether Vollering wins or not; whether the race was harder or easier she would probably still win, such is her class and strength and that of her French team. It’s about entertainment and engagement, getting eyes on the sport and keeping them there, and for that, as in all sports, there needs to be jeopardy.Jeopardy is why the 2026 Giro was so brilliant. With 40km of the final stage left to ride all three places on the general classification podium were up for grabs until Vollering played her card, eventually winning the GC by 30 seconds with a jaw-dropping ride. I was on my feet from the moment she attacked until she triumphantly crossed the line, awestruck by her performance while simultaneously feeling for Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime) as her grasp on the pink jersey slipped away. The day had everything I wanted from sport.And all that happened on a stage with only 2,100m of vertical ascent, just a bump in comparison to next year’s trio of Alpine stages. Let’s start with the mountain time trial. It’s the second consecutive edition with such a stage, and last year the TT set up that thrilling final, Van der Breggen’s win startling her rivals as she moved into pink. But such a stage influences the GC hugely, and to include a near facsimile the following year is too much. In a race of only nine stages, to have such a similar defining stage each year lacks imagination.Like the entire race, this year’s TT is shorter than in 2026, but unlike last year, it’s unrelentingly uphill and will produce some notable time gaps. Better might have been a more sporting time trial, flatter, allowing those specialists who are slightly less capable in the mountains to stay in touch with the overall lead and add some of that crucial jeopardy into the final day.Don’t get me wrong, of course there is a place for brutal TTs, but we had one last year, so why do it again so soon? Even in a nine-day race there’s also a place for stages with 3,500m climbing, we had one last year, after all, but three in one week? Add in that TT, and we have four stages in the mountains likely to produce sizeable time gaps, especially when two of them are mountain top finishes. Perversely, those mountain top finishes could be the saving grace, allowing the real lightweight climbers like Petra Stiasny (Human Powered Health) and especially Sarah Gigante (AG Insurance-Soudal), who came close to winning the 2025 race, to challenge. For them descending is the problem and without that to challenge them they could challenge Vollering.The first of those 3,500m days comes on stage 4 with the final climb to the Passo della Presolana, if that doesn’t decide the final podium, stage 6 will, with even more vertical ascent over two climbs of almost 20km. The one saving grace about the three Alpine stages is that they get progressively harder, but we really could see the GC all but decided on day four, and if it’s not we could have three days of pure grinding stalemate, the favourites waiting for the final day to make their bid for glory. On the other hand, RCS has provided some real interest for the five flatter days, even if they do all contribute to the total amount of climbing metres. Last season the same sprinter won each of the three opening stages, Elisa Balsamo (Lidl-Trek) eventually taking four victories in total. This year there’s less for the fast women, with each of the opening three days covering much more climbing than last year’s corresponding stages, the second stage has as much as 2,100m of climbing, though the run into Genoa is relatively flat before an uphill kick to the line. Perversely, this could be very good for Balsamo, who deals with punchy climbs brilliantly, but it doesn’t matter who wins, it matters that the race interesting and entertaining, and stages like these invite attacks, uncertainty and miscalculation in the chasing bunch. It doesn’t even matter if they all end up in bunch sprints with the same rider winning, provided there is some of the crucial sporting ingredient: jeopardy.While it won’t affect the racing, the location of the route also fails to show off what is arguably the most beautiful country in the world. When we first saw the overview map of the nine stages the first thing we noticed was a huge expanse of empty space – where is the race? It seems as though the entire event has been geographically swept into the top left-hand corner.Of course, nine stages limit where the race can go, and long transfers are hard on riders and race staff alike, but with its diversity and distinct regions, it’s a shame we won’t see more of Italy.The Giro is always a great race, and since RCS has been in charge it’s far better organised and executed, with better coverage and more fans at the roadside. That is to be applauded, what is not is constantly making races harder but not more interesting, and we should hope for a more even parcours in future years.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Could Spain's hardest climb be getting even tougher? Vuelta organisers receive proposal to add gravel sector to Alto de l'Angliru
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: According to a report, a former local mayor has proposed the addition to the Vuelta race director, Javier Guillén, who is set to consider it.José Antonio Muñiz, the former mayor of Riosa, a municipality local to the 12.4km 9.7% climb, reportedly outlined two options for adding gravel sectors to the Angliru in future."The ascent of the Angliru is bordering on extreme difficulty, with large crowds of spectators. We are open to studying its feasibility as long as it increases the interest and spectacle of the stage without overloading the riders or compromising safety. We listen to all ideas, although only some can be put into practice," Guillén said at a ceremony at the climb where La Vuelta Femenina was awarded a gold badge by the 'Association of the Friends of the Angliru', led by Muñiz, this week.Guillén had previously not been a fan of gravel sectors before the addition of a sector on the final climb of stage 6 at the men's Vuelta this year. The gravel sector was a success, as eventual champion Enric Mas chased down Tadej Pogačar, and Guillén conceded later that gravel will have a place in future editions, too.Any possible addition of a gravel sector to the climb would come in the first 5km of the ascent, before the road reaches a false flat at Viapará.The route would then rejoin the usual road for the final 6km and the climb's toughest section, where the gradients reach double digits, including the famous La Cueña les Cabres section, where gradients reach up to 23% in places.Local newspaper explained the options laid out by Muñiz: "One of the options to include some gravel sections in the ascent to Angliru would be to ascend from the town of Muriellos along a track of about 4km, which combines concrete and dirt, until linking up at the Llagos curve with the traditional climb from Viapará."The other option would involve taking the road from Ablaneo to El Cabornín and then ascending a track that would also connect at the Llagos bend, before La Cueña les Cabres."Both options combine gravel with concrete on the steepest slopes and would make the legendary Angliru climb even tougher, although they would shorten some of the current 12km from La Vega to the Angliru"It remains to be seen whether Guillén accepts the proposal for future editions of the men's and women's Vuelta.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Manchester United’s wild win against Roma showed angry fans we care, says Dalot
item.author: David Hytner
item.content:encoded: Full-back believes 3-2 win can transform seasonUnited were booed off by supporters at half-timeThe Glazer family, who have owned United since 2005 and loaded £1.2bn of debt on to the club, continue to be the focus for fan anger and there was yet another protest against them before kick-off at Old Trafford, with thousands of green-and-gold balloons released from the Stretford End. The home crowd sang anti-Glazer songs and threw tennis balls on to the pitch when the clock showed 20 minutes and five seconds, to symbolise the year 2005. The team have seven points from their opening nine games of the Premier League season, their worst start since 1987-88.Continue reading...

item.title: Vincenzo Nibali praises 'innovative' 2027 Giro d'Italia route and says Paul Seixas 'would do well to participate'
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: Former Giro d'Italia winner Vincenzo Nibali has said that next year's route is one where Tadej Pogačar would be "the clear favourite" but that Paul Seixas is also ready to fight for the pink jersey.The 2027 Giro route, which was unveiled on Tuesday, packs in the climbing and an uphill time trial on a difficult course that organisers RCS will hope can attract some of the peloton's top GC riders.Giving his assessment to Nibali – who won the pink jersey twice in 2013 and 2016 – praised the route and the slight changes made for 2027."It's a modern Giro, one that continues to innovate while not losing its ties to tradition," he said. "I spoke about it with [new race director] Luca Guercilena, maybe there's no longer a hat-trick of horrible stages, but the difficulties are more evenly distributed, and that's certainly a good thing."The question of how the race plays out, however, will also be largely down to who decides to race, which we don't know much about just yet, but Nibali thinks the route would be perfect for the sport's biggest stars."Pogačar, if he came, would be the clear favorite. I think the route is very suitable for [Jonas] Vingegaard, too. It would be a good challenge for [Remco] Evenepoel," he said."And Seixas, after finishing fourth in the Tour on his debut, would do well to participate. I saw him in person at Il Lombardia and he impressed me, I think he's ready to fight for the win. He climbs very quickly and is no slouch in the time trials, far from it... I read that he's interested in coming, and it's no coincidence."As defending champion, Vingegaard could well opt to return and chase another pink jersey, whilst there are plenty of reasons why Paul Seixas might, surprisingly, opt for the Giro over the Tour next year.The hope of attracting international stars may be big, but the Giro can also count on a talented crop of home riders to battle for success in the race that no Italian has won since Nibali himself 10 years ago."[Giulio] Pellizzari, [Davide] Piganzoli, [Giulio] Ciccone: in a Giro like this, they'll have plenty of room to express themselves," Nibali said. Pellizzari has plenty of time to fix some lapses, Piganzoli is growing rapidly, and Ciccone will find further motivation from the change of team. They need to believe in it."And in terms of the decisive stages, the monstrous stages 16 and 20 are of course at the top of Nibali's list, but he predicts the race would be open until the very end, such is the balanced design of the route."The Valtellina stage [16] is brutal. There's 5,700 metres of elevation gain, so even the thought of climbing it is difficult," he said. "And it's historic, because the Gavia Pass, in the middle of a double Mortirolo, on the toughest side, has never been seen before. A brutal, potentially decisive day. "And then before the Zoncolan, I wouldn't underestimate the Madonna di Campiglio climb [on stage 18]. In short, you can't make a mistake in the final week. And with the Zoncolan on the penultimate day, the race could remain open until the end. Maybe someone could ride a bit 'conservatively', relatively speaking, and go all out on the Zoncolan."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Hunt 5AM Limitless wheels review: How do the fastest wheels in the wind tunnel fare in the real world?
item.author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
item.content:encoded: Hunt has been pushing the boundaries of the best road bike wheels for a while now. I remember kicking about on a set of Limitless wheels a few years ago, before wide road tyres had really taken off, and marvelling at how when I looked down I could see more rim than tyre. Wind on a couple of years and now it has come out with the 5AM Limitless wheelset, with the ‘5’ roughly denoting the depth and the ‘AM’ definitely not standing for ‘Aero Mullet’, but rather ‘Aero Maximised’. Like it or not, the road mullet trend is here to stay, and this is another new wheelset with a deeper front wheel than rear. Hunt makes some bold claims, but we can park them for a second as the 5AM Limitless Ti-UD Carbon Spoke Disc (to give it its full title) came out as the fastest road bike wheels in our recent wind tunnel test. Wind tunnel numbers can only tell you so much, so I slapped ‘em on a Dura-Ace equipped Look Blade 795 RS, in place of the Scope Artech 6.A wheels it came with (I know, this job is hard and miserable and awful) and gave them a good seeing to. The short version is they back up on the road what they promised in the tunnel. Well behaved, lithe and responsive, without that nagging feeling of fragility I sort of felt under me with the Scopes. 1,229g (measured) Dark grey £1,999 / $2,599 (£2,489 / $3,199 with ceramic bearings)Shimano, SRAM, Campagnolo F58mm / R55mm 23mmF34.5mm / R30mmLet’s start with the aesthetics before we move onto the design; these are good looking wheels. Maybe you don’t agree, but you’re not the one writing this review. The vast majority of road and gravel wheels now are matter black hoops with a white logo. Not only are these not black, but a lovely almost steel blue-grey, but they’re gloss. Long have I craved for gloss carbon to make a comeback, because it’s so much easier to live with. Moreover the logos are applied under the lacquer, which makes them look and feel more premium. I always find it incredibly frustrating when the logos start chipping off a set of Scope Artechs relatively swiftly, or even more so how a set of £4k Enve wheels just have vinyl stickers slapped on ‘em; it feels cheap. The vaguely '80s vibe of the grey continues to the hubs, which also look very smart with the colour matched disc rotor lockrings. I know aesthetics don’t actually make any difference to performance, but I think if we’re all honest with ourselves we all want a set of wheels that .The rim dimensions are pushing the limits of what a ‘5’ designation can comfortably cover, with a 58mm deep front and a 55mm deep rear. While this is technically road mullet, in practice not even my beady eyes can perceive a 3mm difference in rim depth unless the bike is up against a wall and I’m thinking about it intently. Width-wise, the front and rear differ slightly, too, with a 34.5mm external width up front for a claimed greater stability in the wind, and a 30mm at the rear, which I assume is also a play to keep the weight down as a system. Both rims have a 23mm internal width, and are hooked. This perhaps isn’t as wide as you’d like if you’re pushing the limits of road tyre widths, but if you’re cutting about on something 28-32mm it’s just right, and I suspect most of you considering buying these probably are. The system weight is a claimed 1,212g (574g front, 638g rear). On our scales they weighed in at 1,229g, which is certainly acceptably close to the claim. It also makes them 78g lighter than a set of Scope Artech 6.A wheels, which have for some time been a personal benchmark for being both extremely aerodynamic and very lightweight. Part of this weight saving is down to the low spoke counts; just 15 at the front, with a scant 5 on the non-disc side. At the rear you get a mere 18, with a 2:1 ratio on the driveside vs rotor side. In this guise the spokes are bladed carbon with Ti hardware at the hub end and hidden alloy nipples at the rim for another aero boost. The hubs can be upgraded from steel bearings to ceramic from Ceramicspeed, but come with low contact seals in either case. I tested the steel versions.I shan’t spoil all the aero details, but if you are a real watt watcher and want to deep dive into just how these wheels performed then I implore you to go and read Josh’s incredibly detailed writeup of our latest wheels wind tunnel test. The short digest for the purposes of the review is that with a 28mm tyre fitted these Hunts were the fastest on test. The margins are small over the competition, but that’s how the data falls. I’ve ridden a fair few very good wheelsets in my time, and while Hunt has been making fast wheels for some time it hasn’t necessarily had something in the category until now; something to challenge the Scopes of this world. Perhaps this is also because it does such a good job at disseminating its budget friendly wheels about the place that it slightly diminishes its more premium offerings, but here, with the 5AM Limitless, it has a superwheel that’s absolutely up there with the best wheels on the market. I’m not going to claim I can feel the difference in aerodynamics between these and a set of Artechs; I can’t, and you wouldn’t believe me if said I could anyway, but from a performance standpoint these are the fastest by the tunnel data, and when paired with a bike of the calibre of the Look Blade 795 RS they absolutely flew along. The aero is a given, but they’re so good in so many other ways that I find them so hard to overlook in the ‘best road wheels on the market’ conversation. First of all they’re hooked. Say what you like about hookless being fine if you do everything right, and I have never had an incident with hookless wheels (because I’ve done everything right) but I’d just rather have hooked road wheels and have one less thing to worry about. They’re also wider internally than the new Roval Rapide CLX III, which my colleague Tom noted made them perhaps a little dated already. They’re also just about the lightest wheels we tested, besides the CRW Works Ultimo 6060. Weight isn’t everything, but to be the most aero and near as dammit the lightest too is quite something, and out on the road they feel much like the Scopes did when I had them fitted to a Pinarello Dogma F; fast on the flat, and then this feeling that they just keep being fast on whatever gradient you like. Flat blasts are a joy, and while they aren’t as stable in the wind as the delightfully placid Reserves that I rode on the Cervélo S5, they’re extremely well behaved, but they also feel incredible if you like hitting out on punchy climbs. I matched my best ever time up my local test, a 200m all-out sprint at 12% average, maxing out at 17% in places. Close your eyes and you have a shallow, hyper-responsive climbing wheel.I was a little worried the low spoke count might make them feel a little less stiff. They don’t feel as stiff as a set of Artechs, but this may also be a perception thing as I mostly just felt like I felt less road buzz and chatter through them, which to my eyes is a good thing. They’re more than stiff enough for all-out sprints, and feel great in cornering without being overly jittery. They’re quiet, too. I have had a set of Hunt hubs in the past that were so loud they made a toddler cry as I rode past. The Scopes are louder even than those, but the Chase SLC hubs here are only moderately loud. If I had my way they’d be silent, but that’s not how ratchets work. The 7.5º engagement angle is sufficient for road, and I never felt like I was caught floating between teeth.I also am pleased to say I accidentally tested the durability of these wheels. After a Wednesday night hill sprint session, followed by a couple of beers, I went to get some delicious takeaway Szechuan hot pot. So distracted was I by the promise of a warming, savoury, numbing broth (and absolutely nothing to do with the beers on an empty stomach after exercise) that I rode straight into a curb head on. It wasn’t overly fast, but it was hard, and I am pleased to say I neither dropped my soup nor broke the front wheel. More aero than anything else we tested. Lighter than all but one of the cohorts we tested, with performance on the road that backs up the lab testing numbers, combined with good looks, and all for a price that’s cheaper than the equivalent from Reserve, Parcours, DT Swiss, Roval, Scope, Vision, and Syncros. The only cheaper wheels we tested were Chinese brands, and they didn’t perform all that well in aero terms. Even with the ceramic bearing upgrade they’re still cheaper than most in this performance bracket, so it’s hard to not give them full marks for value. I am writing this assuming of course that you’re after or indeed . There’s every chance you perhaps budgeted a lot less that £2k and found your mind wandering, and in broad terms the differences are tangible but small to cheaper wheels. While we haven’t directly compared, the wattage gulf will be one that is easily traversed, perhaps a couple of watts in it really, and a small gram penalty too thanks to the law of diminishing returns. Despite this it’s hard to not see these as exceptionally good value wheels given how well they perform against far more premium competition. I think these might be the best road wheels on the market right now. Maybe Hunt doesn’t have the brand cachet of Reserve, Roval, or Vision, but it’s created a set of wheels that rides fantastically on all terrain, with sensational aero and weight figures that beat the competition in almost all circumstances, and all for a price that’s lower than almost all the mainstream competition too. My caveat to this is that, for example, if you were building up an S-Works Tarmac SL9, then a set of Rovals will have been designed to work with that frame in a way that may surpass what these are capable of. Likewise the Reserves in the Cervélo S5, but even then the price differential is such that I could look past it, as there’s almost £1,000 between these and a set of Rovals. Modern width, good looks, good shapes, classy hubs and finishing bits. All good things. For an aero wheel the weight is maddeningly low. Segment-topping aero backed up by real-world performance whatever the (paved) terrain. Tubeless compatibility and setupI had no issues at all, and they're hooked, which helps the tyre selection worries.They're still expensive wheels, especially with ceramic bearings, but compared to those from big brands they're a steal for what they're offering

item.title: 'Tadej Pogačar is more than welcome' says Giro d'Italia director, but Slovenian stages not designed to lure the five-time Tour de France champion
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: The director of the Giro d'Italia has stated the somewhat obvious in saying that Tadej Pogačar would be very welcome at next year’s race, but insisted that the route's incursion into Slovenia is not designed as a bid to tempt the world's best rider onto the start line. Pogačar has enjoyed taking the opportunity to race on home soil in the past, as evidenced by his two titles at the Tour of Slovenia and his huge disappointment at having to miss this year's European Championships in Ljubljana.The route for the 2027 Giro d'Italia, unveiled on Tuesday, features two stages on Slovenian soil, with the opening stage crossing the border between the start and finish in Trieste, and the second stager taking place entirely in Slovenia, between Ljubljana and Koper. This has widely been viewed as an attempt to lure Pogačar to the Giro for only the second time in his career, three years on from his dominant victory in 2024, but this notion was played down by the new Director of Cycling at race organiser RCS Sport, Luca Guercilena. "Tadej is clearly the man of the moment, so he would be more than welcome at the Giro d'Italia, absolutely," Guercilena said in a video interview published by following the route presentation in Rome. "The stages in Slovenia are made primarily for the Slovenian fans. Given the proximity of Slovenia to Italy – and specifically to the Friuli Venezia Giulia region – which plays a key role in this Giro, it felt like the right thing to do. "From a purely cycling perspective, Slovenia is currently producing a great number of champions for our beloved sport, so it felt only fitting to pass through Slovenian territory. If Pogačar were to come, he would certainly be welcome."'The goal is to attract top-tier riders'The Giro, by contrast, has 57km against the clock, but 19km of that is in an uphill time trial, while there are seven summit finishes and key climbing tests even before we reach the brutal final week with a monster queen stage 16 and the final act atop the Zoncolan on stage 20."I believe this Giro is well-balanced. While the mountain stages are truly significant and demanding, the race’s defining characteristic is the alternation between these tough stages, easier ones, and time trials. This gives all athletes, regardless of their individual strengths, a chance to shine," Guercilena said. "The goal is to attract top-tier riders, who will surely recognise that an iconic stage like the one to Aprica, featuring two ascents of the Mortirolo and the Gavia, is a gift to the fans, as well as a chance for riders to add a legendary, high-profile stage win to their palmarès."Pogačar tempted but unlikely to attendAs for whether Pogačar will be attracted, it seems unlikely at this point, even with the Slovenian stages. The five-time Tour de France champion has already indicated his preference for combining the Tour with the Vuelta a España, where he has unfinished business after crashing out while in the lead this year. A Vuelta title would round out Pogačar’s palmarès as a winner of all three Grand Tours, and would leave more space in the Spring to target the Classics, with Paris-Roubaix similarly the final Monument on his checklist. "Even though I'd rather ride the Giro, I'll have to tick off the Vuelta at some point too. I think that will be the goal for next year," he said recently. "I think I still need some time to really analyse what I really want for next year. And I think the final decision will be done in December, where we have another training camp."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. 'This was definitely the place that I wanted to be' – 21-year-old British rider Tomos Pattinson steps up to WorldTour with EF Education-EasyPost
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: After winning Liège-Bastogne-Liège Juniors and then spending three years of his time in the U23 ranks across two development squads, Tomos Pattinson is now ready to step up to the WorldTour in 2027 with EF Education-EasyPost.The 21-year-old British rider started out with the Team Visma-Lease a Bike Development team through 2024 and 2025, though he had triggered the interest of EF Education before that point.“Tomos is a really interesting rider. We looked at him as a junior, but we didn’t have a development team at that point. He signed for another team, and he stood out at all levels, but from what I’ve seen and what I believe, he’s a rider with enormous talent,” said head of scouting Sebastin Langeveld.“We got in touch again in 2025, and he had a really good meeting. This season, he came back from a small injury, but when he’s going well, he’s a super strong addition for the team. I think we can develop a lot of his skills over the coming years, and he can go long in breaks and be a strong all-rounder who can help the team. "We’re really pleased to have him on board for the future. We’ve not seen the best of him yet, so it’s a really exciting move for him and the team.”Pattinson swapped over to EF Education-Aevolo at the start of this season and was quick to jump into the WorldTour team for some races during the year as well, racing Tour de la Provence, Settimana Internazionale Coppi e Bartali and Tour of Austria with the team. Results while riding with the development team this season also included a sixth at the Visit South Aegean GP, eighth overall at the Circuit des Ardennes and sixth at Coppa Città di San Daniele, his season closing race.“I’ve had a good season, and I’ve learned a lot from the experiences," said Pattinson in a team statement. "I’ve raced a lot with the WorldTour team throughout the year, so I’ve gained a lot from that and become more mature. I’m happy with my results in races like the Ardennes and in Greece at the start of the year."The season ahead, however, is one where the rider from Dudley hopes to deliver even more with the aim being to improve in "as many areas as possible".“Of course, I’m excited. This is a dream, and it’s something that I’ve wanted to do since the start of my U23 career,” said Pattinson.“I’m looking forward to getting started with EF Education-EasyPost next season. Since I was a kid, I’ve been watching cycling, and being a pro cyclist, being able to call yourself a pro cyclist, is really cool. I like the Cannondale bikes, too. I’ve raced on them when I was a junior, and this was definitely the place that I wanted to be when it came to joining the WorldTour."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Game Preview: Knicks vs. Bulls, November 4, 2026
item.author: Moritz Wollert
item.content:encoded: One of the most dreaded speeches a head basketball coach has to make is the one where he talks up an obviously overmatched opponent. He knows the other squad will have plenty of trouble hanging with his ball club even on a good night. On a regular night, his troops would trash the opposition worse than the Globetrotters ever did the Washington Generals. Yet he also knows that complacency can ruin the best game plan and that arrogance has led many teams down the road to hell. Luckily for Mike Brown, he has recent history on his side for his pep talk about the Chicago Bulls.Those very ballers nearly pulled off the upset against your world champions Knicks last week. Although it came on a second night of a back-to-back and in the not-so-friendly confines of the United Center, the warning should still resonate with the Bockers before they host one of the league’s worst teams. Even if you could argue there isn’t anybody worse than Thiago Splitter’s young group so far this year.Sitting at the bottom of the league at 1–6, the Bulls have already lost games by 19, 35, and 43 points and sport the worst point differential in the NBA. Yes, even the Sacramento Acuffs have Chicago beat in that regard. While the offense at times actually looks serviceable, the defense has been nothing short of abysmal. They allow 128.8 points per contest, and games against them regularly turn into a shootaround for the opposition. Defending downtown has been especially tough, with teams nailing almost 40 percent of their long-range shots against Chicago. Yes, they’ve faced some stiff competition, but come on.Bulls come to MSG on a 5-game losing streakPeople in the Windy City are fairly relaxed, though. With a new coach and a young star in the fold, 2026–27 was always going to be a rebuilding year, one they sorely needed after what felt like a decade of drowning in mediocrity. Caleb Wilson, the fourth overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft, has been as good as advertised early on and finally gives Chicago fans something to look forward to. The former UNC highflyer is hardly efficient yet, makes plenty of rookie mistakes, and at times doesn’t really know what this basketball thing is that he’s doing out there. But man, does his game look promising.Wilson is an ultra-modern combo forward with world-class athleticism and a good, determined head on his shoulders. He plays extremely hard, looks to be enjoying himself a ton out there, and seems to possess a drive you usually find only in the cream of the NBA’s crop. If he adds a few pounds and works on his jumper, it’s easy to see the 20-year-old becoming the centerpiece of whatever the Bulls envision for their future.The same can’t be said for Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis, also two promising young players who have struggled under new head coach Thiago Splitter. Giddey’s scoring has dropped from 17 points per game last season to just nine this year, and he’s shooting south of 37 percent from the field. Rumor has it a wrist injury is hampering the Australian, and it might be a problem all year.Plenty of young Bulls are strugglingBuzelis’ excuse is that he’s struggled out of the gate before. But even with a world of athletic talent and plenty of promise, he sometimes looks like one of those players who will never really put it all together. It’s still way too early to give up on a 22-year-old as gifted as the former G League Ignite hooper. At some point, though, those gifts have to show up night in and night out on the NBA hardwood, well after the layup line.Chicago’s most accomplished veteran, Norman Powell, should help in that regard, but how much he can do is debatable. He probably hasn’t even unpacked his suitcase yet, and he’ll most likely be shipped out to a wannabe contender by the trade deadline. Is someone like that really going to change your culture? Powell has played very good ball for years, but can he be the guy who turns things around in Chicago? Your guess is as good as mine.Even if Powell is exactly the vet presence Bulls ownership envisions, Splitter is still fighting an uphill battle. The roster is extremely young and short on inside brawn (sorry, Stix Smith, Zach Collins, and Nic “I can’t lose to the Knicks” Claxton), reliable outside shooting, and any sort of cohesiveness. The losses should pile up pretty quickly. The Knicks should help their former rivals along and get back to .500 in this one. Anything else would be unacceptable.But I’m sure Mike Brown will remind his team of that in his pregame speech.Who: New York Knicks (3-4) vs Chicago Bulls (1-6)Date: Wednesday, November 4, 2026Place: Madison Square Garden, NYCFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

item.author: Nick Ames at Old Trafford
item.content:encoded: There were protests at Old Trafford and even though two academy products stood out, Michael Carrick’s future is far from safeGreen and yellow balloons bobbed around the Stretford End. Tennis balls rained down on the pitch in protest at the chronic, enduringly cinematic decline presided over by Manchester United’s ownership. Then came a reminder of the humble football’s extraordinary power to bend history, minds and wills. United’s players departed victorious having somehow won the game within the game, separating themselves from the fog of unhappy context swirling on all sides and turning the second half into its own soaring, ripping story for the ages.Will it be enough to save Michael Carrick, who was once again serenaded when minds wandered from the joint scourges of the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe? If Aston Villa defend a shade more competently than Roma on Sunday then perhaps not. United have led their supporters, remarkable in their tenor of backing for players and head coach here, up more than enough false peaks over the past 13 years. Arguably, that is one reason for Carrick being given the job on a permanent basis.Continue reading...

item.title: Player Grades: Knicks 103, Nets 90
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: For three quarters Monday night, the Knicks looked like they might actually lose to the Nets. The Nets? The last place Nets? While we might get apoplectic, the champs seemed unconcerned about falling behind. When they finally flipped the switch, they turned a 79–75 deficit into a 103–90 win, outscoring Brooklyn 28–11 in the fourth at the Garden. That’s 15 straight wins against the neighbors. Landry Shamet did a lot of the work to make it so.22 points (6–8 FG, 4–6 3PT, 6–6 FT), 1 rebound, 1 assist in 30 minutesOn a night when the starters happily hurled threes like pre-teens playing Pop Shot, Shamet sank a steady four of six, plus every free throw he took. His season-high 22 kept the Knicks in it long enough for the rest of them to wake up.While the Knicks spun their wheels in third-quarter mud, Josh Hart collected his fourth foul with a lotta game remaining. Shamet replaced him at 8:44 and scored six points on perfect shooting from downtown. The first, at 2:26, cut Brooklyn’s lead to a single point; the second, with a minute left, made it 77-75. According to Basketball Reference, he had a team-high game score of 19.4. Pretty good for a sub.8 points (3–6 FG, 2–5 3PT), 6 rebounds, 7 assists, 3 steals in 27 minutes (+22)Hart had a crooked finger in just about everything that made the fourth quarter exciting. In that final frame, he hit a Kolek-assisted three to pull the Knicks within one, then assisted on back-to-back Anunoby threes and a Kolek layup (everybody seems to enjoy playing with Tyler, don’t they?). Josh intercepted a Julius Randle pass and took it the other way for a layup. His grade suffers for taking just six shots and collecting six fouls, but maybe he deserves a little more love for being a team high +22?18 points (4–10 FG, 3–7 3PT, 7–8 FT), 4 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 steals in 38 minutesOG played 38 minutes, got to the line eight times, and hit back-to-back threes in the fourth when the Knicks finally started to put Brooklyn away. Seven free throws will do a lot for a night when only four shots fall from the floor. Give credit to his stamina: after bumping bodies with that bull Julius Randle all night, he still had gas in the tank to help his team in the fourth. He hit the go-ahead three at 10:29 and another bomb 28 seconds later to make it 84–79. He also set up Clarkson’s transition three. Loses points for still struggling to finish at the rim.11 points (4–11 FG, 1–4 3PT), 16 rebounds, 5 assists in 35 minutesA weird game for Karl-Anthony. He had double-digit rebounds in the first half, but zero points. After intermission, he scraped together 11 points with much more aggressive drives to the rim. As New York rallied in the fourth, he banked in a short fadeaway, grabbed three defensive boards, and found Landry Shamet for the Knicks’ final basket. His back up, Andre Drummond, grabbed nine boards in his 13 minutes, but dividing the workload between the pair is unsustainable. James Wiseman is glued to the bench. Leon, what’s your move?19 points (6–16 FG, 4–11 3PT, 3–6 FT), 2 rebounds, 6 assists in 33.5 minutesFour threes and six assists are dandy, but missing half his free-throws and ten field goal attempts had us a little worried. He’s been mostly automatic since coming to New York, so forgive us for jumping to conclusions like: maybe he should spend less time doing extracurricular activities and more in the gym? He started off the game great, making 3-of-4 from deep, but then disappeared for a while. 7 points (3–5 FG, 1–2 3PT) in 11 minutes (+17)Some guys can do a lot in 11 minutes. Clarkson squeezed seven points into his sliver of time (entirely in the second half) and was still a +17. As the fourth quarter started, a game that had been a nuisance all night was finally starting to break open. Jordan blocked Nolan Traoré’s layup and hit a transition three seven seconds later to push the lead to 10. He added a floater at 4:00 to keep the momentum going. He loses a point for collecting two fouls and a technical foul in the span of a minute during the third period, which didn’t help matters while the team was flailing.After the game, coach Mike Brown offered high praise for the vet. “I’ve been around some good teammates when it comes to players. He’s gotta be the best. He’s the definition of ultimate pro,” he said. “You have a veteran that’s been there, done that, and he’s willing to accept the role that most guys wouldn’t accept […]. And he’s willing to accept it… and still try to uplift everybody and connect everybody while he’s going through what he’s going through. That’s the ultimate team player.”6 points (2–4 FG, 2–4 3PT), 1 rebound, 2 assists in 16.5 minutesDeuce hit two of four from deep and added a couple of assists. A decent shift on a night when the Knicks could’ve used a few more of those. Two steals is great. Four shots in almost 17 minutes seems insufficient, however.6 points (1–7 FG, 0–2 3PT, 4–4 FT), 2 rebounds in 16 minutes (−11)Hoo boy. Bridges made one shot from the floor and did little on defense to make up for it. The Knicks lost his 16 minutes by 11 points, the worst mark in the rotation. At least he got to the foul line for the first time after six games. It’s perhaps too soon to sound the panic alarm, but he has shot 16 of 52 for the season. Mike Brown has taken notice. He ended Kal’s night after just a few minutes into the third quarter, and when he sent the starters back at the end of the game, Shamet took Bridges’ spot. The Knicks got away with three quarters of sleepwalking because Shamet kept them close and Hart, OG, and the bench gave them life in the fourth. Next up are the Bulls on Wednesday. In their first meeting of the season, last week, the Knicks won but needed 48 points from the bench to bail them out. Do we see a trend emerging?

item.title: Eric Brunner finds his groove and 'a little bit of an adrenaline rush' with pair of wins ahead of Pan-American Cyclo-cross Championships
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: A total of 46 weeks have passed since Eric Brunner won his third US elite men's cyclo-cross championship, and only once, at the UCI World Cup in Benidorm, has he worn the stars-and-stripes jersey. The 27-year-old focused on road racing this summer which delayed his return to cyclo-cross, but he made an emphatic arrival with back-to-back wins in UCI C2 races in Massachusetts over the weekend.Brunner overcame crashes and flat tyres to win both rounds of the 35th Cycle-Smart Northampton Cyclocross, joined on Saturday's opener by his Competitive Edge Racing teammates on the podium - reigning Pan-Am champion Andrew Strohmeyer in second and Dylan Zakrajsek in third - who both have two months of racing in their legs.The US champion said both days he used time trial mode - a discipline where he was best in stages at the Tucson Bicycle Classic, Redlands Bicycle Classic, third in Tour of the Gila, and sixth at the US Pro Road Nationals."This is my first race of the season, so I wanted to take it out a little conservatively and just see how I felt. Oftentimes, when I start going this hard for the first time, I get a little bit of an adrenaline rush and just feel a little weird. So, I just got in the group and found my groove, and found I felt pretty good," Brunner told organisers at the finish."It was more about just not making mistakes and capitalising if somebody else did. But, I bobbled one time and went down one time. I was just on my own for the last couple laps, and it was just a time trial to the finish. "On Sunday, on a dry but technical Look Park course, Brunner recovered from two flat tyres, the second on the final lap, and held off Aidan Vollmuth (Donovan Racing) by 12 seconds for the victory. Luke Walter (CXD Trek Bikes) took third another 31 seconds back. Zakrajsek finished fourth while Strohmeyer had some challenges in a wooded section of the course to finish seventh."I got away early, but had a flat. There were a lot of roots and rocks out there, and I think I may have hit something. I hit my rims all day. I had another flat on the last lap, but thankfully by then I had enough of a gap it didn't matter that much," he said after Sunday's race, noting when he hit the front with four laps to go before drilling the pace solo.In the elite women's races, New England native Lizzy Gunsalus (VIA LLP p/b Van Rysel) carried the Pan American champion's jersey to double victories at Northampton. The 23-year-old, who has been racing NoHo CX since she was 12 years old, won by two minutes on Saturday over Emma Betuel (DRRT) in second and third-placed Bridget Wilson another 24 seconds down. On Sunday, she led start to finish with clean lines and a clean white Pan Am kit but had to hold off 19-year-old Lidia Cusack (CXD Trek Bikes), who finished 16 seconds back. The rest of the field was more than 2:45 back, with Daniela Bronk third and Ellen Noble fourth. Like Brunner, Gunsalus filled her summer with road racing, competing for a fourth season with CCB p/b Levine Law Group, and earning a podium at Green Mountain stage race and the gold medal in the team time trial at the US Collegiate Road Nationals. Among her seven 'cross wins last year were championship titles in elite categories at Pan Ams and US nationals."Excited to have taken back to back wins at NoHo CX. Everything is dialed in and carrying good momentum into next weekend to try to defend my Pan-Am title," she wrote on Instagram.The next races on the North American calendar are Pan-American Championships, taking place Saturday in Washington, D.C., for a second consecutive year at the Armed Forces Retirement Home. Gunsalus faces stiff competition with three former elite winners in the field - Lauren Zoerner, Sidney McGill and Raylyn Nuss. And the entire podium from the U23 race are registered for the elite race this year - winner Mia Aseltine, Alyssa Sarkisov and Lidia Cusack.The elite men's field at Pan Ams will most likely be a back-and-forth engagement between Brunner and Strohmeyer, who now ride for the same Comp Edge team. Brunner won the men's elite title at Pan Ams four consecutive times before being supplanted by Andrew Strohmeyer last year. However, neither was providing tips on how they would work together on Saturday."I couldn't ask for a better start to the season here. Usually the first race takes me a little bit to get going, so I'm really looking forward to Pan Ams," Brunner told organisers after his win on Sunday."I've just got a little bit of training this week but a lot of rest and I'll give it my best at Pan Ams."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down.
