item.title: Giro d'Italia boss says motor-racing circuit sprints will improve safety, but recent Tour de France evidence suggests otherwise
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: One of them, the iconic Monza track, will host the start of the all-important stage 15 time trial, but the other two – the Marco Simoncelli circuit on stage 4 and the Mugello circuit on stage 11 – are set to play host to big bunch sprint finishes. This, said Guercilena, who took up his role as cycling director of RCS Sports following his departure as Lidl-Trek team manager this summer, was a deliberate ploy in the ever-more-urgent push for rider safety. "The initiative stems from listening to athletes and teams regarding the need for safe finishes," he said on stage during the presentation of the route on Tuesday."This ties into the broader requirement for environments where even children can train securely. We believe that the Giro d’Italia, which also has a role in fostering cycling culture, can promote the use of motor racing circuits as new hubs for youth teams, allowing young riders to train in a safe setting. This offers families peace of mind, knowing their children can cycle in a secure environment. "From a competitive standpoint, it also ensures that athletes have a very wide finish area, enabling them to perform at their best, and, above all, safely," he added.The use of motor racing circuits, which have wide tracks and smooth surfaces, would intuitively appear to make sense when it comes to safety, avoiding the road furniture and pinch points associated with city-centre finishes on public roads. However, the evidence – admittedly very limited – is not so supportive, with the last Grand Tour sprint finish on a motor track resulting in a slew of crashes and several riders airing safety concerns. The 2023 Tour de France exampleThe first crash occurred on one of the straights with 1.7km to go, with a bump of shoulders sending multiple riders to the ground, including a stage favourite, Fabio Jakobsen. A second crash through a left-hand bend inside the final kilometre sent more sprawling and further fragmented the bunch, leaving only around 25 riders to play out the sprint. Another crash against the barriers in the full swing of the sprint capped off a finale that was remembered more for the spills and less for the thrills. The crashes were not all necessarily linked to the fact this finale was taking place on a motor racing track, but there were interesting comments from several riders suggesting this might indeed have had something to do with it. "A circuit is not safer than a road to finish, I can tell you this,” said Mathieu van der Poel, who provided the lead-out for the day’s winner, Jasper Philipsen. "It was really fast and the corners are quite difficult to judge in the bunch and you also have nowhere to go so I'm really happy I managed to stay upright.""None of us are used to finishing on such a wide course, the entrance which is pretty small, then big lanes again. These kind of corners, everybody can keep pedalling and you can just take them 10 next to each other. In the end it’s like having a long straight but even more dangerous," he said. "Sometimes people think the wider we make the roads and the more we go on circuits and whatever, the safer it becomes. But today we see the opposite. I think sometimes what makes it more safe is when you stretch out the bunch, like yesterday for example with the U-turn. Then the bunch gets stretched out, and from there on everybody keeps his position or kind of keeps his position, and then you get safer sprints."It remains to be seen which exact sections of the two circuits are used at next year's Giro d'Italia, and crucially how many corners are involved, while various other factors naturally come into play as well – it's worth pointing out that some of that Tour de France chaos was attributed to the relative freshness after a very slow day until that finale.But until everyone arrives safely and securely on stages 4 and 11, there might still be some holding of breath and some reserving of judgement when it comes to the suitability of motor tracks for cycling sprint finales. The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: 'Too ambitious in too many segments' – Bianchi to renegotiate debt repayments amid financial woes
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Italian bike manufacturer Bianchi has until late May to renegotiate payments of its debts amid a structural reorganisation after the company accrued huge debts. According to a report by Bianchi has entered into 'Composizione Negoziata della Crisi' (CNC) on September 30, a court-backed status in Italy which means the company can delay paying its debts for a limited period and is intended to help businesses navigate financial problems.This status applies to the brand's holding company, FIVE Bianchi SpA, from September 30 and lasts for four months from the date it was granted, though it an be extended to 240 days, which would give Bianchi until May 28 to renegotiate payments. According to the report, Bianchi's most recent published accounts, released in late 2024, show that the brand owed €100 million, a large proportion of that to banks. Should a solution to the company's crisis not be found by May, insolvency proceedings could then follow.Since 1997 Bianchi has been owned by Swedish company Grimaldi Industri, which saw the company through the cycling boom which accompanied the Covid-19 pandemic. As the market contracted afterwards, however, the company continued to invest, introducing new bikes and opening a new factory outside Milan, which it hoped would build up to 1,000 bikes a day. This investment in a shrinking market saw it move inexorably from profit to loss.This aggressive policy was accompanied by a flurry of Chief Executive Officers, with four joining the company since 2021. The latest of those is Tony Grimaldi, son of the parent company’s owner Salvatore Grimaldi, who was appointed in early summer as part of the restructuring plan."We were investing a lot in too many areas at the same time. We have been too ambitious in too many segments, and the bicycle industry is so tough," Grimaldi told . "You cannot do everything everywhere, especially when we know that the market is oversupplied."It's a structured way to be transparent that you are reorganising and restructuring," Grimaldi said, adding that the company is already in constructive talks with the banks.Bianchi is one of the world’s oldest bicycle makers, opening for business in Milan in 1885 and with its trademark celeste colour scheme has become one of the sport’s most storied brands, sponsoring WorldTour teams until as recently as this year. However, last week WorldTour team Bahrain Victorious announced an end to their partnership with Bianchi, the team moving to Factor Bikes from next season. has approached Bianchi for comment.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Giro d'Italia 2027 route – A comprehensive guide to all 21 stages
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: : 3,418.9 kilometres: May 8, 2027 - May 30, 2027With seven summit finishes, plenty of punchy terrain, and some brutal high-mountain stages particularly in the final week, not to mention one of the race's two time trials being uphill, the 2027 Giro certainly leans towards the climbing specialists. It all kicks off on Trieste on May 8, 2027, and finishes in Rome on May 30, covering 3,418.9 kilometres and taking in 50,250 metres of elevation gain in total. Here, we go through the route stage-by-stage to see what's in store for the pink jersey hopefuls next May.The first pink jersey looks to be going the way of a puncheur, with an opening stage that ventures over the Slovenian border and features three short climbs in the final 40km, plus a downhill run to the line. It should be an explosive and exciting start to the race. After the stage 1 foray, stage 2 takes place entirely in Slovenia, and it's another punchy one, with a short sharp climb topping out just 3km from the line and followed by a fast dip down into Koper. Attacks will fly.A third successive stage that suits puncheurs and aggressive riders, with two modest categorised climbs and a false flat drag towards the finish another chance for the attackers to get rid of the sprinters. The pure sprinters finally get their chance on stage 4, with very few complications on the run from Argenta towards the Marco Simoncelli motor racing track, where the sprint will be contested.The proper climbing action comes early, with a first summit finish on stage 5. The organisers have only given this a three-star difficulty rating but the final climb to Sarnano-Sasotetto measures 13.1km at an average gradient of 7.4% and maximum pitches of 14%. It's a rude awakening and will provide an early indication of who's where in the fight for pink.Stage 6 is another stage that could see a sprint, or could something a bit more dramatic, with 1,700 metres of elevation gain on a route that climbs steadily for the final 10km.The second big general classification test of the 2027 Giro comes with the first of the two time trials, this measuring 19.6km but crucially heading uphill for pretty much the whole thing. The categorised part of the climb to Campo di Giove measures 12.5km at a modest average gradient of 4.4% but there are pitches of up to 9%. It's not quite a pure mountain time trial but it's far from a flat one and should provide an interesting test between the pure time trial specialists and the climbers.Napoli is most openly associated with sprints, and we should see another one again here, though the undulating terrain in the finale and the rise to the line make it one for the lighter and more versatile of fast men.An action-packed opening week closes with a second summit finish and third obvious GC flashpoint. The final climb of Monte Livata measures 13.9km at an average of 6.9%. Bigger mountain stages follow later in the race but by this point, after the time trial, things will be taking some sort of shape, and the favourites will surely hit out against each other towards the top of the climb.The second week opens with an interesting stage that features a tricky pair of climbs in the finale and a fast descent to the finish in Norcia. It looks like prime terrain for a breakaway.Another sprint stage with a complication. Some teams may look to use that late climb of Vetta Le Croci to drop the pure sprinters, but they have just under 30km to get back in to try and contest the victory, on another motor racing circuit.Our third summit finish of the Giro takes us up the Passo Due Santi, a short one at 8.7km but viciously steep at an average of 8.7% with pitches well in the double digits. We're not expecting huge gaps but it's an important test where any weakness can actually be punished heavily.There's still a climb in there, but finally, something pretty much nailed on for the pure sprinters, so expect a drag race in Reggio Emilia. We've already had plenty of summit finishes but stage 14 marks the heaviest climbing stage so far, with 4,900 metres of elevation in this route that sets out from the Lombardy region and heads over the Madonna del Ghisallo climb used in Il Lombardia. Three further ascents follow before the final climb up the Piani di Bobbio, which measures 10.1km at an average of 9%. That's brutal, and coming at the end of a heavy climbing day, it's a huge day for the general classification contenders.The second week closes with another huge test for the pink jersey hopefuls, in the form of the race's second time trial. Unlike the first, this is pan-flat, from Monza to Milan, and pretty long at 37.3km. It's one for the pure TT specialists, and one where the weaker of the GC contenders against the clock could take some pretty heavy blows from a time-loss point of view.The final week opens with one of the hardest Grand Tour stages we've ever seen. There are 5,700 metres of elevation on this brute, which is extraordinary. What we have is a sandwich of Giro icons, with a double ascent of the mighty Mortirolo either side of a first trip up the Gavia since 2014. The Mortirolo has seen some historic Giro moments over the decades, with savage gradients, while the Gavia takes the riders up into the snowline at 2,600 metres of altitude – it's the 'Cima Coppi' as the highest point of the Giro. The final climb to Aprica is more of a drag but by that point the race will be in pieces and riders will be only be dragging their weary bodies towards the line. A monstrous day.After that mountain monster, we pick up the theme of the opening days with a largely flat stage that throws a couple of short climbs into the finale – perfect launchpads for late attacks.The second of three big mountain stages in the final week, this one features 4,500 metres of elevation over the course of five big climbs. The final climb to Madonna di Campiglio, at 12.5km and 5.7%, is not super difficult, but it's what comes before that matters, and that will drain the legs well in advance. This looks like one of those classic Giro mountain stages where there's a huge fight for the breakaway and chaos ensues for basically the whole day.Another interruption to the climbing-fest in the form of yet another largely flat but still punchy day of racing. At this point, how many sprint teams will be left, and how much strength will be left? Stages like these so late in a Grand Tour are often ripe for breakaway action. The Giro d'Italia will be decided at the summit of the Zoncolan, a beastly climb measuring 10.1km at a barely believable average gradient of 11.9%. It's fairly new to the Giro, with no visits before the 21st century, but it's becoming one of the race's icons, and is certainly in a bracket with the Angliru as one of the hardest climbs in professional cycling. With 3,600 metres of elevation, this stage is the lightest of the final week's mountains stages on paper, but this final climb overcomes those statistics on its own, to make this a pivotal – and final – juncture in the battle for the pink jersey.The 2027 Giro concludes with a short stage in Rome made up of laps of a circuit through the Italian capital. Whatever sprinters are still standing will have the chance to fight for the final stage win before the overall champion is crowned.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Giro d'Italia 2027 route revealed – A climber's paradise with double Mortirolo ascent and return to iconic Monte Zoncolan and Passo Gavia
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: The route for the 2027 Giro d'Italia has been revealed as a climber's paradise, with three of Italy's most difficult and iconic ascents set to feature as the highlights in May next year: Passo del Mortirolo (twice), Passo Gavia, and Monte Zoncolan. At the presentation in Rome on Tuesday, race organisers RCS unveiled the 3,418km route from Trieste, near the Slovenian border, to Rome, with a major focus on the north of Italy, two individual time trials, and some days on offer for the sprinters and breakaway experts.After two years of foreign starts, the returning to Italy will see racing kick off on Saturday, May 8, with two rest days breaking up the 21 stages and 50,250m of elevation gain before the finale on Sunday, May 30. The real showpieces of the route will be the mountain stages, with the first return to the 2,600m-high Gavia since 2014 being sandwiched between a double ascent of the brutal Mortirolo on the queen stage 16, finishing in Aprica.There are seven summit finishes in total, ranging in difficulty across the Apennines and Alps, with the GC also set to be shaken up by two time trials – one being a mountain race against the clock to Campo di Giove, and the other taking in the Monza motor racing circuit on a flatter test.10 years on from Tom Dumoulin's maiden Grand Tour triumph at the Giro, this opens the door to a time trial specialist potentially dominating the road to Rome, though those aforementioned mountains will bring only the most complete riders to the fore in contention for the . With the duo of time trials, RCS will be hoping to attract the likes of Remco Evenepoel as the leading star, with defending champion Jonas Vingegaard not expected to return, and 2024 winner Tadej Pogačar likely to opt for the Tour de France and Vuelta a España in 2027. Though the Belgian is all but certain to return to the Tour, a combination may not fit with his team's plans, so the organisers may have to look elsewhere for their headline name on the start list. For those not chasing the iconic pink jersey, there will be between six and eight possible opportunities, though the pure sprinters see their chances squeezed as several uphill kicks and stages featuring late climbs offer up ground for opportunistic attackers or breakaway hunters to make their moves. All in all, it's a typical Giro route with something for everyone, albeit the first one not designed by Mauro Vegni – the previous race director who retired last year. In an ideal world, organisers RCS would have hoped that a Grande Partenza in Trieste and early foray across the Slovenian border would've attracted the likes of 2023 winner Primož Roglič and 2024 champion Pogačar. However, with the former still having not signed for a new team for 2027 and the latter wanting to complete the Grand Tour set with the Vuelta, neither look like probable starters for May. That being said, several of the world's best riders will descend on the northeast corner of Italy in Friuli-Venezia Giulia for the first Grand Tour of 2027, where the chaos, unpredictable weather, and brutal climbing of the Giro will be back at its best for the 110th edition.The first pink jersey will be decided in Trieste on a punchy , where three short hills in the final 30km should pit the top puncheurs against the versatile sprinters, with the GC favourites just trying to stay out of trouble and potentially fight out a small group sprint. will be battled out entirely in Slovenia from the capital city in Ljubljana to Koper, with another undulating route opening the door to the same types of riders who starred on stage 1. The same can be said of , when racing returns fully to Italy for a gradually rising uphill run to the line in Possagno in the Veneto region – again the puncheurs should have their day.Following a longer transfer down to Argenta in Emilia-Romagna, the sprinters will have their first guaranteed opportunity of the 2027 Giro on , finishing at the MotoGP circuit, Autodromo Marco Simoncelli in Misano, near the Adriatic coast.The first mountain top finish of the race arrives a day later on stage 5 to Sarnano Sassotetto, where the initial movements in the GC race will be made on the 13.1km ascent which averages 7.4% gradient. Only ranked with three stars of difficulty by the organisers, it's more of a GC loosener than a decisive day, with significantly easier climbs approaching the finale in the Marche region, but it will indicate who has survived the initial salvoes best in the fight for pink. fits into the same category as the opening three days of racing, where a breakaway could easily jump up the road to fight it out on the east coast from Alba Adriatica to Lanciano, where undulating and dragging roads will lead to the finish. The GC favourites will be looking to survive that ahead of the first really crucial day in the overall race. On , the action is the mountain individual time trial from Sulmona to Campo di Giove, where19.6km of racing and a testing 12.5km should completely reshuffle the standings and potentially the pink jersey holder. It's the first mountain ITT at the Giro since the race was decided on the penultimate day in favour of Roglič in 2023, but at just a 4.4% average gradient on the climb – which is almost 5km longer – it isn't as vicious as the 11.2% average from three years ago.brings the 2027 Giro back to Naples for the sixth season in a row, and while it has typically been a sprint stage in that time, the profile points to more of a punchy finale, with several short kickers in the final 30km. The first week comes to a close with the second summit finish of the race, albeit on a mountainous with just over 3000m of elevation gain. After a flat opening 70km, the stage win will be battled out to Monte Livata (13.9km at 6.9%), where the hardest gradients are all packed into the first 4km of the climb – it hasn't featured in the Giro before, but was used in the U23 men's Giro last season, where eventual winner Lorenzo Finn won solo by 52 seconds. Monza time trial sets up final weekAfter the first rest day, the Giro gets back underway with two chances for the breakaway on and , the former finishing with two climbs in the last 30km and a long downhill run to the line, and the latter would be a certain sprint stage, if not for a final short sharp climb arriving with 28km to go.It doesn't take long for GC action to resume with another summit finish on , as the race heads through its one and only stage in Tuscany towards the Passo due Santi on the border with Emilia-Romagna. It's 8.7km at 8.3%, and could prove the next major point in the fight, with the final 2.4km to the summit averaging more than 11% in gradient. to Reggio Emilia is one of the almost guaranteed sprint stages, but the focus will quickly turn to those chasing the overall in Italy after a long transfer north into Lombrady. will he the hardest stage of the race so far when it arrives, taking the riders across just under 5000m of elevation gain en route to Piani di Bobbio. Four shorter climbs will precede the final 10.1km ascent which averages 9% gradient – a true brute in the Bergamasque Prealps, where if someone doesn't already have a commanding lead, this will be the best chance to take control yet.The second week concludes with the second individual time trial of the race, a 37.3km pancake flat race against the clock on from the Monza F1 circuit to Milan. If Evenepoel isn't present, then it should emerge as a day for the likes of Filippo Ganna, where all the GC hopefuls will need to have recovered from the day prior's big mountain test.Mortirolo double and Zoncolan to decide pinkIn typical Giro fashion, the hardest stages of the 110th edition are all backloaded into the final week, and there is no such thing as a slow restart from the second rest day here, heading straight for the queen on Tuesday, May 25, from Sondrio to Aprica. 192km in length, with 5,700m of elevation gain, and featuring some of the most feared ascents in the Italian Alps, the organisers have opened the door to the race being completely flipped on its head with the Passo del Mortirolo being tackled twice in the same stage, with a return to the Passo Gavia sandwiched between the double header. At 12.8km and averaging 10.1% gradients, the Mortirolo is a true icon of the Giro, but after the first time up, the riders won't have any respite as they descend back to the valley and begin the climb to the Gavia – a 16.5km brute with a more regular average gradient of 8%, but one which ventures to 2,600m in altitude. Following that with another rep up the Mortirolo and then a final climb to Aprica should make it one of the hardest races of the entire season, and where pink could be decided once and for all. If, and only if, the sprinters have survived this long, they could be rewarded by a sprint into Vó, but two late hills in the last 20km could complicate that, and after such a brutal mountain stage, the breakaway hopefuls may be more likely. With the legs still screaming from two days prior, the GC riders will have to go again on with a 4,450m elevation gain day to another summit finish at Madonna di Campiglio, but not before taking on the Passo Ballno, Passo Durone (twice), and Passo Daone. This final climb is much shallower at 5.7% average, so may be one for a break to get up the road as the GC favourites await the Zoncolan. should see the sprint teams come to the fore again, but early climbs heading out of Rovereto will give a strong break an opportunity to form – but the fast men will have been so starved of opportunities at this point that staying away could prove very challenging. The last time Monte Zoncolan characterised a route of the Giro d'Italia, it was barely seen in all its glory, with a foggy and cold day in 2021 being captured by Lorenzo Fortunato. The penultimate day of the race on will give someone a chance to join him, Chris Froome, and Michael Rogers as modern winners on this iconic mountain in the Carnic Alps. With the race returning to where it started in the Friuli-Venezia Giulia region, the 10.1km climb at 11.9% average gradient should provide one final chance to capture pink, or to reaffirm dominance on a backloaded final mountain stage, with 3,600m of elevation gain packed into the final 50km of the route. Whoever is in pink at the summit will be crowned the winner of the 2027 Giro d'Italia, with only the processional sprint circuit in Rome left to be completed on after a long transfer south to the capital.Misano Adriatico (Autodromo Marco Simoncelli)Scarperia (Autodromo del Mugello)Zeri (Loc. Passo due Santi)Monza (Autodromo Nazionale)The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Shimano Dura Ace C50 wheel review: Rock solid all-round performance and the update the flagship wheelset needed
item.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
item.content:encoded: $2,970 / £2,298.99 / €2699.98 1318 grams - F: 600 R: 718 (with tubeless tape)Internal - 23mm / External- 31 mm front / 32mm rear. 21 front and rear.Shimano launched its new R9300 Dura-Ace wheel range in late July after months of under-the-radar pro-use shots and speculation. I’d followed the wheels since the early spring, when we regularly saw Mathieu van der Poel racing on plain rims and hubs stamped ‘prototype’. Three days after Van der Poel’s magnificent win on the wheels in the final stage of this year's Tour de France, they arrived to market as part of an updated six-model range. The C50 has long been the most commonly used Dura-Ace wheel; as the range’s all-rounder, it’s the one that tends to be raced on the most. Its 50mm depth makes it likely the fastest across the widest range of terrain. The previous R9200 Dura-Ace wheels certainly weren’t boring, but it didn’t feel like they were many regular riders' first choice when it came to the best road bike wheels. I certainly didn't see many at all in the wild, and it's safe to say Shimano wheels are not as popular as their groupsets are.Alpecin-Premier Tech were the single team riding the wheels in the men’s WorldTour, and the fairly standard (by 2026 wheels) steel spokes, low-key Dura-Ace graphics and rim profiles were possibly just a little underwhelming. The new R9300’s seem to have been met with a positive reception all round, and their updated aesthetics have surely done some good.I’ve been using the wheels for months to see how they perform and how they are to live with. Big logos and carbon spokes might have been two of the best things Shimano could have done visually, but what about the rest of the package? Let’s start with what changed from the previous-gen R9200 wheels. The standout feature is the addition of Vonoa carbon fibre bladed spokes instead of steel ones. The spoke count has also decreased from 24 to 21 spokes front and rear to save weight. The spoke nipples themselves are still external. Carbon spokes aren’t automatically guaranteed to produce a good wheelset, but the weight savings and potential improved stiffness (depending on spoke count) that they provide are hard to ignore in a performance road wheel. On the topic of weight, the new C50's weigh in at 1318 grams on my scales with tubeless tape. A much more competitive weight than the previous wheelsets' 1461-odd grams.The rims themselves have also received an update; inner and outer widths grew to 23mm internal from 21mm. The external width is also now front- and rear-specific. The front rim is now 31mm wide, and the rear is 32mm. The wheels are optimised for 28-30mm tyres. Shimano is also said to have tweaked the layup of the rim, essentially to help produce the best overall performance for a rim of this depth. Dura-Ace is equipment designed for racing, so that means sprinting, hard cornering, changes of direction and the like. The wheels didn’t arrive with in-depth aerodynamic test data, though Shimano did cite a 2.7-watt aero drag saving at 48 km/h with 30mm tyres at the time of launch.We haven’t taken the R9300 C50’s to the wind tunnel for our own CN Labs wind tunnel testing yet, but we will try to get some data for them in the future. The previous-generation C50's finished at the bottom end of the table when we last took them to the tunnel in 2024.Dura-Ace hubs have long been viewed as precision, high-quality options, and notably the brand has stuck with a ‘cup and cone’, or loose ball bearing arrangement in its hubs, whereby the ball bearings sit in an open cage. Whilst the hubs use open caged bearings, sealed cartridge bearings can still be found in the freehub body. The brand believes that a cup and cone system provides advantages over a sealed cartridge bearing; this caged bearing arrangement incidentally is what Shimano's long-time rivals Campagnolo also use in its Record hubs. The R9300 hubs now have replaceable bearing cups, making pretty much the entire hub assembly replaceable if needed. I’ve worked on Dura-Ace hubs where pitted and worn bearing cups meant essentially permanently compromised performance (new bearings and/or cones would prematurely wear in rough, worn cups); this should now be a thing of the past for customers if it gets to that point. The hubs themselves are a classic Dura-Ace gunmetal grey, and have a big vertical wordmark on the shell. The end caps need cone spanners for removal; they don't just pull off. The freehub body is aluminium like the outgoing generation and has a 3.5 degree engagement angle which gives 103 points of engagement. The freehub body currently accepts a regular Shimano 12-speed cassette; we understand that when it arrives, the new Dura-Ace groupset will use 13 sprockets. This makes me think those 13 sprockets will fill the same amount of space as 12. I can't see Shimano rolling out some sort of updated freehub body for already launched wheels.Aesthetically, the combination of those bladed carbon spokes, matte rims, and a prominent ‘Dura-Ace’ logo on each side of the rim has really helped update the wheels' look and ‘coolness ’, in my opinion. In short, it strikes me as just what they needed. These are Shimano’s all-rounders, and I can report that the C50’s offer strong performance no matter what you are doing. I’ve done various training sessions, general Zone 2 rides and hard chaingangs on them, including flat-out max sprints, and they handle it all with ease. I set the wheels up tubeless with some 28mm Pirelli (deep breath) P Zero Race TLR SL-R tyres, for a full factory Alpecin-Premier Tech spec. The tubeless setup was very easy to do with a track pump, which I find is now the norm for modern road wheels and tyres. The tyres have held air well, with some normal drops in pressure but no leaks or seepage. The factory Shimano tubeless tape install was also, as you might expect, very tidy.The wheels' freehub is also quieter than most; there’s a recording below for you to listen to. It's actually a lot quieter than that in use. I’m a fan of a quiet freehub, but it’s down to user preference. Regarding performance, the C50 wheels haven't blown me away in any one key area. They don't feel hyper stiff or super fast; they are just rock solid across the board. Whether I've been out of the saddle climbing a double-digit gradient, sprinting flat out at the end of the club run, hunkered down and cracking on on the flat, or leaning them into fast corners, the C50's have handled everything without breaking a sweat. They feel fast and exciting to use, and for me, look very smart.They don't feel quite as stiff and taught as the Vision Metron RS wheels I tested last year, but out-of-the-saddle lateral stiffness, handling characteristics, and slow-speed acceleration are all good. Mid- to high-end road wheelsets are getting lighter and lighter, and I think the market is setting a standard for wheels to come with carbon spokes right now. The weight drop the Vonoa carbon spokes have helped provide is useful here, and helps the wheels feel light and zippy in use.On some rough tarmac, the wheels have felt slightly harsh at times with 28mm tyres; the remedy is going up in tyre size and down in pressure. A 30mm may well be the optimal choice for anything other than very smooth tarmac, but for me they didn't quite have the same luxurious ride quality as the Roval Rapide CLX III wheels.It's worth mentioning axle and bearing 'feel': the cup and cone system doesn't have quite the same buttery smooth, effortless feel as a quality sealed bearing. It's not bad, just different, and the wheels still spin very well.If you are buying a set, I’d recommend at least a yearly hub service. The best bet in the UK is to find and use an official Shimano service centre, where they should do things the right way, using the correct Shimano grease, etc.; these are top-end wheels and should be treated as such. These wheels have an RRP of $2,970 / £2,298.99 / €2,699.98. Expensive, but not as earth-shattering as some other top-tier models on the market; I think things could have been worse. For a quick comparison, the recently launched Zipp 202 NSW wheels are very pricey at £3.400/$4,200/€3,800, the DT Swiss ARC 1100 wheels I tested earlier in the year are $3,218 / €2,499 / £2,599.98 with tyres and tubes included and the Roval Rapide CLX III's are $3,399.98 / £2,999.98 / €3,498. Cheaper than some big-name competition, with solid performance and easily available spare parts. This is a good update for the Dura-Ace C50 wheelset. They haven't provided standout performance in one key area; they aren't the stiffest or the lightest out there. We also hope to gain our own wind tunnel test results for them in time to see how they fare against the competition. What they are undoubtedly is a quality wheelset worthy of the Dura-Ace name. The C50's are all-rounders, and that is what you are getting with these wheels: solid performance across the board, in a more attractive overall package.I'm expecting to see a few more pairs of these wheels out in the wild. Testing scorecard and notesSolid overall design in line with the Dura-Ace name. Replaceable cups is a nice touch. A much needed aesthetics boost too.Solid everywhere, not the strongest in one key area. Just great all rounders.Now a lot more competitive at 1318 including rim tape. Good for a 50mm rim and sensible specs.Very good, nice factory tubeless tape setup and all setups achieved with a track pump first time. Cheaper than some competitors from Zipp, DT Swiss and Roval. Not cheap, but there are lots more wheels out there that cost more than this.

item.title: Giro d'Italia Women 2027 route – The complete stage-by-stage guide
item.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
item.content:encoded: Race organisers, RCS Sport, revealed route details for the 38th edition of the Giro d'Italia Women at a presentation in Rome on Tuesday. The race is set to take place across the country's northern regions from May 29 to June 6 in 2027.For the second year in a row, the race will be held directly after the men's Giro d'Italia, with the first weekend of the women's race overlapping the final weekend of the men's.This year's Giro d'Italia Women will begin in Viareggio and include one mountain time trial, two mid-mountain stages, three sprint stages, and three mountain stages (including two mountaintop finishes), with the peloton racing a total of 1,132km before finishing at Monte Bianco.The opening day of racing is a three-star difficulty held on a circuit in Viareggio with a 124km race that includes 1,200m of elevation. The main circuit will include a climb up the Pitoro, which will be tackled four times, and the stage winner and the first pink jersey will be awarded in Viareggio.The peloton will take on another three-star hilly race from Massa to Genova on the second day of racing. They will compete over 139km that includes two categorised ascents over the Passo del Bracco and the San Martino di Noceto before the descent into the coastal city of Genova. The stage includes 2,100m of elevation gain.San Martino di Noceto, 112kmOn the third day of racing, the peloton will tackle the longest of all the stages at 171km from Cogorno to Viadana. Although they will crest the day's only categorised ascent, Passo del Bocco at the 20km mark, it is a two-star stage, and the race is mainly downhill and undulating all the way to the finish line in Viadana. There is 1350m of elevation gain.The first mountain test will be held on the fourth stage as the peloton takes on 131km from Credaro to the top of Passo della Presolana (Castione della Presolana), which the organisers class as four stars. The stage will include four categorised climbs over the Forcellino di Bianzano, Ganda, Colle di Zambla and then the mountaintop summit of Passo della Presolana, an 11km climb that averages 5.4% but reaches pitches of 10% near the top. There is 3,500m of elevation gain.Forcellino di Bianzano, 45.1kmPasso della Presolana, 131kmThe only one-star stage of this nine-day race, stage 5 will surely be one for the sprinters, with only 300m of elevation gain. The peloton will take on 140km in and around Cassano d'Adda.It is the first of two five-star stages and the second mountain finish of this race as the peloton tackles 137km from Bergamo to Madesimo-Valle Spluga. The route will include two major ascents, mid-stage over the Passo San Marco, a 19.6km climb with an average gradient of 7.4% but with pitches as steep as 15%, followed by the summit finish at Madesimo-Valle Spluga, a 19.3km ascent with an average gradient of 6.3% and maximum gradients reaching 13%. This will be a day where the race is won or lost with another 3,550m of elevation gain.Madesimo-Valle Spluga, 137kmStage 7 is another two-star day to give the peloton some reprieve from the climbing as they race 147km from Carugate to Rho, that includes 1,000m of elevation gain. There is only one categorised climb on the course at Sirtoti, located in the first quarter of the race.The peloton will be treated to a mountain time trial on the penultimate day of racing. The route is held along an 11km course at Valdigne Tudor. The mid-race checkpoint is located 5.7km into the race against the clock. The 11km climb will vary between 4.2% and 9% gradient with a total of 500m of elevation gain.The final day of racing at the Giro d'Italia Women will include 3,950m of elevation gain across 132km at Monte Bianco. There will be four categorised climbs at Doues, Verrogne, Saint-Nicolas and Colle de San Carlo, before the final climb to the finish line where the overall winner will be crowned.The two toughest climbs of the day will be over Verrogne and Colle de San Carlo.The ascent over Verrogne will test the riders with a stair-step ascent. The first section is 7.4Km at 7.9%, and the second section is 5.6km at 6.9%, with a 2km undulating downhill in between.The Colle de San Carlo is a 10km climb with steep sections at the beginning that reach 15%, and the overall gradient is 9.8%.Colle de San Carlo, 107.1km

item.title: Giro d'Italia Women 2027 route revealed – Uphill time trial and brutal final mountain stage feature on climber-friendly course
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: The organisers of the Giro d’Italia Women unveiled the route of the 2027 race in Rome on Tuesday, and while the race is shorter than last year’s, it has far more climbing, favouring the mountain goats once again.While this will be the 38th edition of the women’s Giro, the 2027 edition will be only the fourth organised by RCS, the company which runs the men’s event, and they continue to make the race more challenging. In total the race is slated to cover 1,132km, some 20km shorter than last year, but with 500m more vertical ascent on the cards, and with three stages climbing 3,500m or more, the 2027 Giro will suit the purest climbers more than ever before.Next year’s race takes place over nine stages, beginning with a lumpy opening day in the seaside resort of Viareggio on May 29, and concluding on June 6 with a brutal third Alpine road stage organisers have named the 'Monte Bianco stage', on the Italian side of Western Europe’s highest mountain, Mont Blanc. And it's a tough way to end the week the riders tackling almost 4,000m of vertical ascent.The entire race is set in the north-west, starting in northern reaches of Tuscany before heading along the coast into Liguria. There's a brief visit to Emilia-Romagna as the race moves into Lombardy for a first visit to the mountains. The final two stages, including a mountain time trial, take place in Italy’s smallest region, the Valle d'AostaWith such a challenging route, including two mountain top finishes, a mountain time trial and that brutal final day in the Alps, organisers will be hoping the route tempts the sport’s biggest star, Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ), to defend the maglia rosa she won last year, though whether she takes the bait is to be seen. After her second place at the 2026 Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, it’s a race suited to Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and her new Lidl-Trek team, while after her win at the Vuelta España Femenina, the new GC star on the block, Paula Blasi, may opt for the Giro, especially as the course is suited less to her new Movistar teammate Marlen Reusser. After finishing second overall in 2026 and with the Canyon-SRAM Scalable Capital team leadership in her hands, Antonia Niedermaier is another candidate for success, especially with the mountain time trial featuring again. However, such is the the amount of climbing , we could see pure climbers like Vuelta stage winner Petra Stiasny (Human Powered Health) and Sarah Gigante (AG Insurance-Soudal), who won two mountain stage on her way to third overall in 2025, among the suitors to the maglia rosa. But before we get too deep into who may win, here's what the route will look like next May.While the GC riders will need to be attentive over the three flatter opening days, the 2027 Giro will be decided over four mountain stages, which include two mountain top finishes, a time trial and the final Alpine day.Stage 4 features four classified climbs and 3,500m of vertical ascent and the week’s first mountain top finish, stage 4 is the first GC battle of the week. Covering 131km between Credaro and Passo della Presolana, the stage heads into the Bergamasque Prealps, the day’s final climb the perfect platform for attacks with its relatively even gradient edging between 5% and 10% over almost 12km.If one strong climber emerges on stage 4, we may see a procession two days later when stage 6 takes us into the Central Alps for another mountain top finish, this time at Madesimo above the Valle Spluga. With more climbing than the previous mountain day, the stage also includes the Cima Alfonsina Strada, the race’s highest point, the Passo San Marco, some 1,987m above sea level.A brute of a climb, the gradient averages 7.4% over its whopping 19.6km length, though the top comes still with 80km to the finish, and ahead of the ascent to the line, which also approaches 20km in length. The stage 8 mountain time trial will be crucial for those looking to challenge the general classification. It’s the second consecutive edition of the Giro with an uphill TT, and this is harder than the one Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime) won last year, even if it’s 1.7km shorter, there's no respite over the 11km, the gradient ramping up to 10%.The TT crosses the path of the final stage, and both will force some reshaping of the GC, though with almost 4,000m of vertical ascent in the shadow of Mont Blanc, the final day should be hugely dramatic, and could even see the GC turned on its head.Only 132km, the day takes in four classified climbs in total, though it is the final one, the Colle San Carlo, which is likely to have the most effect, not only coming on the final day, but averaging almost 10% gradient over its 10.5km. Interestingly, it tops out 25km from the line, with a descent and a short kicker to the line, creating opportunities for some fascinating racing.Despite the huge amount of climbing on the route, there are a good five opportunities for sprinters and opportunists. While we could even see five bunch sprints, at least three of the days are lumpy enough to upset the fast women, and after missing out on the pink jersey after being disqualified from the 2026 Giro when her bike was judged to be underweight, Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) is likely to be disappointed with the opening stage. Starting and finishing in Viareggio, on the Tuscan coast, the 124km stage takes place over four laps, each with an early climb, and though Wiebes may be able to survive, it will be far more complicated, especially with plenty of other riders aiming for pink.Stage 2 heads up the Ligurian coast between Massa and Genoa and is a similar lumpy day, though with much of the climbing coming early on, it’s more likely to end in a sprint than the day before. However, if a breakaway is still out front when the race reaches Genoa, the sprinters’ team will need to take care to bring it back. At 171km, stage 3 is the longest of the nine, though, along with stage 5, it's the first of only two where a bunch sprint is almost guaranteed. A long early climb will bring a fight for the breakaway, though it will be comprised of eternal optimists, as the final 150km are downhill and the day should be easy to control on the road to Viadana.With only 300m of climbing, stage 5 is the flattest of the week, flatter even than the time trial, and is the second nailed on opportunity for the fast women, especially if they’ve struggled for success up to that point. Another circuit race, the stage takes place around the town of Cassano d’Adda, closing with four almost pan-flat laps.Though on the face of it stage 7 looks like another sprint day, it's sandwiched between a brutal Alpine stage and the mountain time trial, so is ripe for breakaway success. At 147km between Carugate and Rho, there is only one classified climb and some gentle undulations, so any escapees will need to work hard to the line or they’ll tempt the sprinters to take control.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. Plus, the Cyclingnews app means you can stay up-to-date wherever you go!

item.title: British Airways lost my father’s vital life-saving machine
item.author: Anna Tims
item.content:encoded: He needs a dialysis machine to survive, but on a flight it was first damaged, then it was lostMy father suffers from terminal renal failure and relies on a highly specific dialysis machine every night to survive. British Airways’ check-in staff twice insisted on checking this fragile 20kg lifeline into the aircraft hold where it was first damaged, then lost.When his outbound flight arrived at Heathrow, it was returned broken resulting in a frantic search for a loan unit and hours spent in A&E so my father’s blood could be monitored. On the return flight to Rome, the machine could not be found. My parents waited until 2am before being told to go home without the equipment that keeps my father alive.Continue reading...

item.content:encoded: Marco Rose’s tactics are lifting Bournemouth, Roméo Lavia makes progress with Chelsea and Roberto De Zerbi gives youth a chance at SpursGood defending is the mark of champions. At Anfield, where Arsenal had not won in the past 13 visits, Mikel Arteta followed the orthodoxy of locking down once his team took the lead. This time around, it proved successful. Arsenal did not allow the occasion or the stadium to get to them as they have on previous occasions. In April 2023, Granit Xhaka entangling with Trent Alexander-Arnold energised home fans previously despondent that Arsenal were 2-0 up. It finished 2-2. On Sunday, Liverpool zipped around zestfully, as Andoni Iraola requests, though the final-ball quality was lacking. That owed a great deal to the organisation of the Arsenal defence. Ahead of the last international break, Brighton set a blueprint for getting the better of Arsenal in winning 3-0. Liverpool’s squad profile might have made a similar strategy possible though Iraola’s outfit is struggling to create chances in the same volume as Brighton or his Bournemouth team. item.content:encoded: Unusually, all clubs in the top flight have the same manager with whom they began the season – but the first sacking may not be far awayNo Premier League manager has yet lost his job this season. In only three of the past 10 campaigns was November reached without a club making a managerial change.The 2026-27 season commencing with 11 managers who were appointed at some point in 2026 has probably contributed to the early season stability. They have to be given a chance to fashion their side as they see fit. But with roughly a quarter of the season played and only one more round of fixtures before an international break, the first sacking may not be far away.Continue reading...

item.title: Michael Carrick insists he will still be in charge of Manchester United against Roma
item.author: Jacob Steinberg at Stamford Bridge
item.content:encoded: Defeat against Chelsea extends winless run to nine gamesCarrick clinging on to job after club’s worst run since 1988Michael Carrick insisted he would still be in charge when Manchester United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, despite the 2-0 defeat at Chelsea on Saturday. United’s problems mounted as their winless run reached nine games. Carrick is clinging on to his job after overseeing the club’s first such run since 1988 and tried to focus on the next game as he analysed his side’s defending when Morgan Rogers opened the scoring for Chelsea.“It’s never a good goal to concede,” he said. “Morgan went through the middle of us and at that point the game was right in the balance. To concede like that was a big moment. I’m just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now.”Continue reading...

item.author: Jacob Steinberg at Stamford Bridge
item.content:encoded: Get ready for another week of agonising over the sorry state of Manchester United. The legends of old will rage on podcasts, clips of a fuming Gary Neville will fly around social media and by the time United play again there is every chance a new manager will be in the dugout.There were echoes of Erik ten Hag’s final game in charge as the walls closed in on Michael Carrick here on Saturday. United missed chances at 0-0, just as they did when Ten Hag lost to West Ham a day before his sacking two years ago, and Chelsea exacted punishment after initially delivering a performance so bad it had you worrying for the nascent Xabi Alonso project.Continue reading...

item.content:encoded: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffectiveCora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.In late September, dozens of – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).Continue reading...

item.author: Niha Masih
item.content:encoded: Rubio’s decision not to meet Narendra Modi last week was seen by some as a snub – but by focusing on business leaders and oil, the secretary of state made American priorities clear. Plus: the artist bringing a female perspective to men’s clothingWhen the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.Continue reading...
